text:
Although not the first classic of the 50's (this was released in 1953, 'The Day the Earth Stood Still' was 1951) it was the first real big budget sic-fi of it's time. In color, with costumes designed by multiple Oscar winner Edith Head and directed by Oscar winner Byron Haskin (Haskin was also nominated 4 times in the 40's for special effects) and produced by Oscar winner George Pal (who was nominated an additional 6 times himself) this was the 'Avater' of it's day. Special effects of all shapes and sizes: floating wedge space ships, heat/death rays, protective force shields and Martians! Yes, little green (well, actually, they were brown) Martians! If you saw the movie "Back to the Future" and you remember the mind set of Marty McFly and the posters and things that his father had in his bedroom back in 1955, this is one of the movies that helped create that fear of aliens and Martians back then. Of course it's just your basic fear of the unknown, and now we know there are no Martians (maybe) but back 60 years ago it was as real as any other threat to people all over the world. Sure the dialog is a bit hokey, and a few of the performances are over the top, but this was the beginnings of the sci-fi genre, there wasn't a lot to base their performances on, and generally they did an excellent job.
Also, a few more things to note - the movie is a usual early 50's quick: 85 minutes in total. If you want to see some video of the 'Flying Wedge', a 1950's attempt at an early Air Force bomber that was just, well, a flying wing with no real fuselage or tail, this movie has some video of that plane, plus, the movie itself is based on a classic HG Wells novel from the turn of the century. Actually, if you get a chance, you should read the HG Wells novel 'War of the Worlds' for a fascinating look at how people in England would handle an invasion of the largest city in the world at the time, London, and how long it took just to send and receive simple messages from city to city before phones, computers, email, Facebook, Twitter or any of the other dozens of conveniences we now take for granted.

text:
It touched me when I read somewhere that NOBODY'S FOOL was Newman's favorite film. Those words mean a lot when you consider the likes of COOL HAND LUKE and the rest.

It's my favorite Newman flick too.

Someone in another blog asked me why I identified so heavily with Sully. Knowing is one thing; explaining it to other people is a different matter. I'm giving it a shot here, but I'm also curious about others who identify with this fascinating character.

Sully cared about everyday people, the powerless. He carried a load of emotional pain--symbolized by his injured knee--but instead of letting his pain defeat him, it seems to have sensitized him to the needs and struggles of others.

He was fearless, spoke truth to power and took the consequences.

Every day, he was a loving friend and his love was returned by the townspeople.

He was old and weary in body--symbolized by his old broken-down pickup--but world wise and willing, intent even, to share what he believed important. This was brilliantly expressed in the scene where Sully gives his grandson a pocket watch and explains how to be brave. Even his blunt face-to-face criticisms of Roebuck seemed to be cloaked with the loving intent of making a better person of the younger man.

There are two basic kinds of people in this world--those who like things shiny new and perfect and those who see the value concealed in the flaws that inevitably appear. Sully appreciates the latter and is no slave to the former. Mrs. Beryl's broken railing wasn't merely a chore; it was a link between her and Sully that allowed him to show is love for her and for her to show hers in choosing him to fix it, with no reciprocity involved.

There were dozens of these loving exchanges between Sully and the townspeople throughout the story, like when Sully helped the demented grandmother get back to the diner, walking sock-footed in the snow and ice; then substituting still sock-footed for her daughter at the diner where she waitressed while she attended to her mother.

Like Sully, I had a rotten childhood and it sensitized instead of hardening me. I see honor in the overlooked heroisms of everyday working class struggle. I see love where others are repelled by poverty. I had a rocky marriage but raised successful children. I don't allow money to control my life but am optimistic about the outlook for financial comfort.

(This is all based on the film. The book is on my reading list. I'm sure it will hold up to my expectations after reading EMPIRE FALLS. By the way, EF was Newman's last film, just as NF was Jessica Tandy's. What great tributes to Richard Russo.)

text: Unjustly written off by critics when it first arrived, Stardust Memories has only gotten better over the years. Acted with dangerous honesty, shot with surreal perfection, this film details the mental collapse of an artist struggling to find meaning in his work.  A long distended dream, SM is at times terrifying, and at times beguiling, Charlotte Rampling is particularly fine as the mentally ill Dorie, who flashes through this film like lightening.  Now that many years have passed it's easy to place this film among Allen's more dream-like productions, such as Night and Fog, which this film resembles in more than just it's film stock (both are in glorious B & W).  I remember when I saw this film when it was released, I was still an undergraduate, and not every experienced with the strangeness of life. text: The 1960's were time when wide-screen epics were all the rage, but few make the cut anymore.  Developed to fight the overwhelming presence of television, these behemoths, like Khartoum, boasted 70mm Super Panavision, entrance, intermission, and exit music, and an all-star cast.  The problem is that few had all-star directors.  Khartoum is a case in point, over-long, shot indifferently (as opposed to say any of Lean's epics), and somewhat boring.  Heston is not a great actor, and his portrait of the infamous Zealot, Colonel Gordon is a one-note performance.  Think what Peter O'Toole, or even Olivier might have brought to the role.  Ah well.  The diametrically opposed characters of Gordon and the Mahdi is intriguing, but the film hardly interrogates this double phenomenon and takes the position that Gordon is a martyr of some kind.  Basil Deardan directed some charming British comedies, but he hadn't the vision to make this film truly great.  I first saw this on tv, back in the 1960's, panned and scanned an cut to pieces.  Now, seeing in HD, and in one piece, I can tell that Dearden strived for some epic shots, but lit most of the sets like an indifferent television show. As for the subject, all I can is that history repeats itself again and again.  The Mahdi's speeches about his intentions can be heard this minute in the justifications of ISIS.  So the battle goes on.  It's tiresome.  The score, by Frank Cordell is actually better than the film, as is too frequently the case with these elephantine  exercises in widescreen.

text: I have great affection for this film and the novel too.  I saw this film in early young manhood, perhaps 17 or 18, and I liked the character of an alienated writer coming back to his small town and falling in with the demimondaines of Indiana.  I identified with Dave Hirsch, and still do. I attended a few lectures at the American Film Institute back in 1990, and the director under discussion was Vincent Minelli; the instructor for the class went through the film and demonstrated clearly how like one of Minelli's musical films (Carousel, American in Paris) SCR was.  Well shot, well acted, and scored perfectly by Elmer Bernstein, the film still falls somewhat flat.  Perhaps if Elia Kazan had taken this property on, the film would have been deeper.  Yet, the impossibility of love (and sex) is so rampant in this film that the tortured, self-destructive characters do take on life.  Certainly, Dean Martin never out did this role, although Sinatra sometimes phones in his lines. Shirley MacLaine, as the clueless trollop working in a bra-factory walks off with your emotions.  I honestly don't know what to make of James Jones, who wrote this mammoth book.  Nostalgia for me?  Perhaps.

text: Bertolucci's masterpiece spans the years from 1900 (hence the title) to film's present (1977), although most of the drama concerns the years leading up to the Second World War.  Is it propagandistic? Yes.  Is it symbolic?  Yes.  Does any of this matter?  Not really.  The cast is amazing, starting with two hoary American icons, Burt Lancaster and Sterling Hayden as the padrones of their respective clans, simply put the rich and the workers.  The two sons of these oppositional forces grow up together, played by Robert DeNiro and Gerard Depardieu.  Both experience the vicissitudes of the early 1900's.  In a telling scene, Ulmo (elm) goes off to WWI, while the rich boy merely dresses up. Other characters enter and leave, in particular Atila (Donald Sutherland) playing a swamy fascist.  Combine this with a brilliant score by Ennio Morricone, and this film builds and builds over its long, but never boring length.  I first saw this in LA over two nights, and I am still under this film's spell.  Not so much for the politics, but for it's complete accurate depiction of rich and poor, owners and workers, justice and injustice.

text: When a mainstream media figure starts talking on screen, I usually turn it off or switch to something else.  Most of them come off as woefully out of touch, empty-headed, or opportunistic.  They're not the scholarly investigative journalists of yesteryear.  In my opinion, John Meacham used to be that character, but it appears he has evolved.  In this documentary, he carefully reviews specific positive turning points in American history, then cleverly shows how those turning points were huge letdowns for various parts of the American citizenry because the leaders of those movements didn't go far enough.  He asks us to retrospectively look back at the lead-up and passing of the 1964 Civil Rights Voting Act as an example of what can be accomplished by the powerful and the average citizen when appealing to our "better angels."  Throughout the film, he parallels the current time ("The Soul of America" was made in 2020) and past events.  John Meacham is clever here.  He never blames any one American demographic outright, but if you're paying attention, it's clear who he's talking about and to.  It's delicate, but it works!

text:
How the Sci Fi channel nabbed this series has always been a mystery to me. Most of their programming over the course of their on air stint has been horrible. The re-imagined series of Battlestar Galactica was a top notch show akin to an HBO original series and I am so glad that it was on a network that was more affordable and accessible to the masses (lol).

With the exception of season 3 being a bit shallow and not quite as dense as the rest of the seasons, the new Battlestar Galactica was one of the best tv shows that has come around in a long time. The story line, though taken from the original, was far superior in depth, character development, morality and complexity. The characters were so well defined and the story written so well around them that as time passed they felt like friends and family. When a character was written out of the show in death, it felt like losing a limb! While on their journey, you were on the journey with them. It is a rare thing to watch a TV show that reaches into both the farthest areas of your soul and mind, but Battlestar Galactica did it with ease.

It took me a while to completely finish the series, as in between it I became a new mom and had other things besides TV keeping me busy, but I finally finished it and wept like a baby at the end. What a series! There needs to be more Sci Fi stories like this... way more!

text:
What a great television series this is. Though I'm an Idris Elba fan, I won't say something he's in is good unless it's ... well... good. "Luther" is really good!

The series follows the typical police/detective model of an emotionally unhealthy, but extremely savvy head detective (DCI ~ Detective Chief Inspector/British) by the name of John Luther (Idris Elba) and how he goes about handling his messy personal life with his professional one. While the aggressive, unorthodox, down and out cop story has been done and re-done a million times, every once in a while a producer, director, writers and cast get it right (Law & Order, NYPD Blue, Homicide: Life on the Streets, etc.) and with this show they got it right. Another interesting twist in the series is the unethical and strange, but meaningful and intriguing relationship the main character develops with a suspected murderer by the name of Alice (Ruth Wilson) who, at one point, DCI Luther interrogated. The chemistry between these two characters is fascinating and could only be due to the great acting these two pull out of their hats! I love it and hang on their every word and interaction.

"Luther" is an edgy series that often doesn't have a happy ending. It's well acted and solid. So far, they've created about 10 episodes which consist of Seasons 1 & 2, but it appears that they are starting a 3rd season (yay!). I don't know how long the series will continue, but I'd like to give a hearty Thank You to the BBC for consistently producing wonderful television series. It seems like these folks almost never miss!

text: It is hard to believe that it took me 50 years to begin to read and watch Hercules Poirot. I since have spent this last year reading and watching every book and every show/movie MANY TIMES over! David Suchet is Hercules Poirot personified. I can not imagine another actor playing this part, Suchet is perfect. I enjoy the early years with Captain Hastings. During their first years filming together it was almost comedy. When Suchet went on his own, changed Butler's and apartments it seems his personality and demeanor became serious to the extreme. Not wanting to go through every show, but wanting to state that their seems to be inconsistencies in Poirot s personality from one minute to the next. I imagine it was due to the writing. I have enjoyed watching 'my' Poirot movies over and over and seem to find that I missed a bit here and there, never tiring of my favorites. The Blue Train, Adventures of the Tomb, Death on the Nile and of course... The Orient Express to name a few... I am grateful that David Suchet played this very important character for so long, never worrying that it may pigeon hole him into only one role, THANK YOU MR. SUCHET. And the always fun 'Ariadne Oliver' are in some of my favorite shows. The settings where these were filmed were EXQUISITE and each and every item that appeared on film was original or looked original for that time period, BRAVO to the set designers, dressers and all the behind-the-scenes people who made it all come together. There will never be another Poirot, but I will continue to watch and introduce to my kids and grandson to keep Hercules Poirot alive. BON!

title_x: **VERY GOOD** FILM IF YOU REMEMBER PART OF YOUR SECOND HIGH SCHOOL BIO CLASS!!! IT'S EVEN **INTTERESTING** GREAT FILM!
text:
Exceptional film - BUT you need to have at least a good high school education in biology - AND REMEMBER IT. I have a couple of advanced degrees in the biological sciences (not human biology), and even I had to stop, rewind, and listen over again to make sure that I understood what was said.- and sometimes I remembered the concept and it was easy, other times I had to go back a couple of times an LEARN the concept and put the words together in MY understanding of the concept to allow it to make sense to me.before I continued watching and understanding the 'story arch' or how the concepts fit together into a whole.

This is not a FUN film, it's not a POPULAR film with easy to follow plot lines and easy to understand dialogue. Unless you are one who likes to learn. For ME it was VERY INTERESTING, and that made it enjoyable -- not FUN but enjoyable -- I would not recommend it to someone without SOME remembrance of high school biology - the kind you take your Junior or senior year, not the kind you took as a freshling where you passed notes and giggled a lot-- you'd miss a lot of the information and concepts being presented. This is because you need to know some of the basic language of science in general, and biology in specific. They DO try to make it intelligible by explaining concepts first by idea, then stringing many concepts together to present the whole.

I probably took about an hour and a half to let the completeness of the film sink in. I did a LOT of rewiding and listening again, and then again to be certain that I had a concept firmly in place before I moved on. And yes, it is a bit dated, but progress on the HIV is slow, and the film explains why it is slow, and why it WILL be slow for quite awhile to come. This, as I said is not a POPULAR film it is meant to educate on a very difficult topic -- from exactly what a virus is (or might be) through various kinds of virus's and how they work, and finally to HIV. -- and when you only have an hour to do it, you move quickly glossing over the complex parts and spending time on the basic concept of why it may be impossible to find a 'cure' one you have an exceptional understanding of the virus itself.

If you are not afraid of learning, and spending time to learn, this film is for you. If you want a very simple, easy to understand film about HIV this film is not one I would recommend for you -- you have to learn and remember information that is given in the first ten minutes all the way to the last ten minutes. So if you want to learn in a 20 second sound bite or a 30 second sound bite, just remember that it might take as long as one minute or two minutes to explain ONE idea and that a concept is many ideas, all related to each other, clustered abound a single subject.

But if you want to learn about HIV and WHY it's taken well over 30 years to learn very little about it - this is the film you want to watch. It puts you in the same ballpark that Science is in today and it explains MANY ways in which HIV is viewed so differently by people in the same field. It really is an exceptional film - but you do have to be ready to think, and be able to think, and to know when it goes over your head so you can stop and go back and understand what you missed the first time through - the film assumes that you understood the concepts as they are presented, If you pretend you 'got' it as it flew by over your head, you'll lose the most important part of the film: what it means and what the ultimate point is. But, for me, it was worth every repeat, it was worth dissecting the words into their root meanings so you understand something as simple as 'dendritic entanglement' as it applies to cascading immune systems and the defense of the virus against it. I loved the film - and hope that others watch so that they can at least understand WHY this is just one of those pandemics that can only be cured by throwing a LOT of money at it by every nation on earth. Some aren't worth the trouble -- this pandemic is because it WILL mutate faster and faster -- and unless you understand WHY you'll never 'get' the concept of public health funding and why SO much money has to go into something where no results ARE worth the money - real science is often NOT finding the answer as much as not finding the answer simply says, try another way -- which, when you are lost is a huge help.

If someone says to go to the third brick building at the corner that's across the street where there's a blue painted brick building - then turn right ---- it helps to know what a brick looks like, and it helps even more if you can find where the buildings are mostly made out of bricks. At least you know you are in the right neighborhood. That is what this film tries to tell you - only the bricks are made out of many different materials - so you need to know WHAT KIND OF BRICK was that guy giving directions talking about. =-- maybe a lousy way to explain it, but that's also part of the problem - if you don't understand the basics about the virus, you'll understand why the funding has to be there to 1) identify the kinds of bricks, and 2) put them together so you at least have a neighborhood to look for so you know you are still in the right area.

Again - and exceptional film - but not an easy one -- you have to pay attention to things you may not have heard about for 10 of 20 or 30 years - or they weren't even known when you went to school -- kind of like even with a couple of degrees in 'biological sciences' --some of the stuff was outside my field and I'd never even heard about -- so thining was a good thing for me. I now know I can still learn and think at the same time!!! (smiles)

text:
This one picked up a third star for the sole purpose of my wishing to stay on the right side of heuristics. The metrics and algorithms used by both Amazon and Netflix are--by what I've heard/read--quite effective at profiling the great majority of their customers. But, unfortunately, their respective 'pictures' of me are as though drawn by blind men. Therefore, I know that giving this series only two stars will only result in seeing fewer--possibly better--war docs in my queue. That said, then: it's plainly NOT a 3-star production.

Like other reviewers here, I'm annoyed by the seemingly forced biases against some subjects. Similarly, the favoritism towards others--most perplexingly towards Charles de Gaulle--comes across as equally forced. It seems 'forced' so as to present someone's definition of *fresh perspectives*--regardless of whether or not those perspectives fit into any trustworthy historical record. More than any overt political intent, the contrarian spin on certain subjects comes across as merely an opportunistic gambit by the show runners in their hopes of having the series stand out from others like it by way of gimmicks, rather than on scholarly merit.

Meanwhile, IMHO, the most jarringly distracting weakness of the series is its exceedingly poor selection of stock footage. Again and again, the narration is overlaid onto scenes that match up in the most painfully vague way imaginable. Film shot during the African campaign rolls while the narrator relates some episode from the European Theater. We're shown a first-person POV, rolling down some random street in Paris, with mid-1950's Peugeots lining either side, as the narrator talks about that city's liberation in 1944... Whilst holding forth on Germany's counter-offensive in the Ardennes--an event that occurred in a snowbound winter wonderland--we get B-reel excerpts of G.I.;s slogging down a muddy road somewhere in Southern Italy... After plainly identifying a still photo of the sweet, khaki colored, custom Cadillac used by Patton as his staff car, the next sight is an inexplicable clip of a late 1940's, two-tone, family sedan rolling down an exit ramp somewhere in America... These are, honestly, just a few examples of the rule. The very few images in sync with the narration are very much the exceptions to the rule. Without exaggeration, I've never, ever, seen anything quite like this series. Very disconcerting stuff.
description: ["Pacific Media have assembled a group of expert historians, researchers and analysts from King's College, one of mainland Europe's most prestigious educational institutions, to create the documentary series History's Verdict. From an up-to-the-minute viewpoint, and packed with fresh historical discoveries, their scripts deliver fair and wise verdicts on World War 2's most powerful figures."]

text:
John Wick (Keanu Reeves) is back and still needs a haircut. I enjoy the heck out of John Wick movies, though "Parabellum" probably wasn't quite on par with the earlier movies. But it still delivers truckloads of carefully choreographed carnage and develops John's backstory.

My favorite scenes are the sly homage to "The Good, the Bad and the Ugly" when John assembles an old revolver from other revolvers. Or the terrific "Blade Runner" bit with the dove in the rain as the "Bowery King" (Laurence Fishburne) waits for assassins to arrive. And the The Director's (Anjelica Huston) ballet of death is a visual banquet.

Sofia (Halle Berry) with her awesome German Shepherd land sharks delivers creative scenes of carnage; some truly skilled animal trainers really earned their paychecks. The chilling Adjudicator (Asia Kate Dillon) is terrific as she "de-consecrates" the hotel while the urbane Winston (Ian McShane) keeps things running "smoothly."

So many excellent actors appear in this movie. And, while I usually never pay attention, the lighting and photography in this movie is unusually lush--it really caught my attention on the second viewing when I wasn't quite as stunned by the action. I'll be interested in seeing what develops next, because now John is pissed.

If you don't like his acting, you might as well skip it. I was pretty much on the fence as to whether I would give this film a two or three star review. I'm going to give it three simply because I have seen so many horrible films lately that it was nice to see something with a half-way decent plot and acting.

The plot is fairly simple, but believable. Sizemore is a detective who just moved to a small Connecticut town from being on the NYPD. He soon runs into a case of robberies committed by a pair of women that he then tries to track down. A large part of the story centers on the relationship of he two robbers and their motivations for pulling the heists.

Jordan Ladd and Nikki Moore both turn-in pretty decent performances as the robbers. Sizemore is... Well, Sizemore. He basically seems to play himself. There is also a cameo performance from WWE wrestler Kevin Nash that is kind of amusing. Other than that, there really is not much of a cast of supporting actors in the film. Just other cops.

As I said, the plot is pretty simple, but there are some twists thrown-in that keep it interesting. This film seemed to have a decent budget, so there are no major problems with cheap sets, poor production values, continuity errors or cheap CGI. I don't think that there even is any CGI in the film. The direction was decent as well. Apart from being a bit slow at times and Sizemore's quirky acting this is a perfectly watchable film. Not a great film, but not bad. Sizemore fans will definitely enjoy it.

text:
If you think that Hollywood is the only place where big-budget, high-octane mega-disaster, action movies come from, think again. The Tower is absolutely on-par with some of the biggest hits that Hollywood produced in recent years, with some spectacular effects, non-stop action and excellent cinematography.

Throw-in some very decent acting, excellent character development and a dash of Korean humor and you have one excellent movie. Yes, you will need to read subtitles to understand the dialogue if you do not understand Korean. Fortunately, this is one of those films that even if there was no on-screen translation you could easily understand and sympathize with the film's characters.

The film seems to be a mix of every movie genre you can name, except perhaps as musical. There is action, drama, adventure, romance, humor and even some slightly spiritual moments. The action scenes are exciting and brilliantly directed. The drama is not overboard, but believable. The script is modest, letting the character's actions and expressions tell the story just as much as the words. The effects are stunning without being overplayed. Even the soundtrack is used to best effect. Honestly, if this movie had been shot in English with American actors it would have been the biggest hit in years.

I wouldn't hesitate to say that you will likely enjoy this even if you can't stand subtitled films. It truly is that entertaining. The story may borrow ideas from quite a number ideas from other "disaster" films, especially The Towering Inferno, Backdraft and The Poseidon Adventure, but it has enough original elements to keep it fresh and unpredictable. Definitely the best action movie I have seen in quite awhile.

This is a creepy, supernatural thriller that very slowly but surely sucks you into the plot. It starts off a bit slow but doesn't take long to ramp up to what turns out to be a pretty classic horror flick. The screenplay and direction of this film is excellent. It is well acted and keeps you guessing about what is going to happen until the end. There are a number of sub-plots that are never fully fleshed out, but only hinted at. It makes you think that perhaps a good deal of material in this movie ended up on the cutting room floor.

This is definitely not a slasher type of film with a lot of gore and cheap effects. It's more of a psychological thriller that has some scenes that fit into the horror genre. It reminds me a lot of M. Night Shyamalan's earlier films and I do not believe that is an accident. You'll definitely notice some similarities to his films in this, but I'm not going to mention wish as it would tend to give parts of the plot away.

I think that the ending of the film could definitely have been done better. I'm guessing that there is probably more than one version of the ending out there. I think that this film could have been better with perhaps better editing and more focus on the sub-plots. All in all I would say that it was pretty enjoyable though.

text:
Arguably one of the better films in the Star Trek franchise, First Contact features most of the original cast of Star Trek The Next Generation as they battle it out with the Borg. In a last ditch effort to save themselves, the Borg transport themselves back in time in order to disturb the current timeline. The Enterprise gives chase and follows them back to the 21st century on Earth.

That's about all of the plot that I am going to give away, in case there are any of you who haven't actually seen the movie before. The first time that I saw the film was on the big screen in 1996. It came out after the original series was cancelled and Star Trek Voyager had just started its run.

Although I am not a big fan of time travel movies, this one has a good enough script to keep it afloat. Perhaps this story was a bit easier to buy as it takes place only about 60 years in the future. In any event, the story shifts between the crew of the Enterprise in orbit battling the Borg and the efforts of the away team on the surface to fix any timeline problems that the Borg have already created.

Obviously, the original characters from the TV series are well established, so not a lot of time is spent developing their characters. I wish I could say that you don't have to know anything about Star Trek TNG to enjoy this movie, but I would be pretty confused as to what was going on if I hadn't been a viewer of the TV show. I think it's safe to say that if you enjoyed the TV series, you will probably enjoy the movie. If you didn't like the TV series, don't even bother trying to watch it.

Overall, the story is pretty tight. The acting is exactly what you would expect and there is plenty of action. I could pyschoanalyse this film to death with all of the possible interpretations that people can read into the script. You can decide for yourself the deeper meaning in the story. The important part is that it is fully entertaining on the surface and fun for all ages. It was definitely worth another look after 20+ years.

text:
It had been nearly 30 years since the last time that I watched this Clint Eastwood classic. I can't say as it lived-up to my past memories of how great it was, but it was definitely a film worth watching again.

Probably my biggest disappointment in re-watching this film was the special effects, especially during the flying scenes. Although the effects were o.k. at the time they seem pretty lousy when viewed today. The film was released about 5 years after the original Star Wars came out. So, there were definitely better effects available at the time. I'm pretty sure that this film was made on a much smaller budget though.

Eastwood gives a very decent performance in this film. His flashbacks as a pilot in Vietnam are a bit cheesy looking, but they were pretty common for the time period. Of course, Eastwood also produced and directed the film as well. I wouldn't call this one of his best films. The whole space age, sci-fi genre doesn't fit him very well. I think that he gave a convincing performance though.

Other than Eastwood, there really are not any other actors who get much screen time in the film. I doubt that anyone else got more than a total of 10 minutes of screen time. Eastwood is not only the central character in the movie, he is the only character really worth remembering.

From a realistic standpoint, the plot of this film is pretty ridiculous. The idea of the Soviet Union having stealth technology in the 1980's is laughable, as is the thought of them having weapons systems run by mind control. Even in 2018 there are still no fighter jets capable of reaching speeds of mach 6 as described in the film. The F-22 Raptor, which is probably the fastest fifth generation fighter in the world, only reaches a speed of about mach 2.

Honestly, the lead up to stealing the Firefox is more interesting than the aircraft scenes to me. It gives you a good idea of how tense that things were during the height of the cold war and how frosty relations were between the east and west at the time. It has the gritty look and feel of a cold war spy thriller. If you haven't seen the film before it is definitely worth watching. If you haven't seen it since the 1980's it's definitely worth a second look.

title_x: Venom Is What Its Name Implies
text:
I'm really surprised that this movie was ever released and not in a good way. This movie had one of the most uneven, badly written scripts that I have ever had to sit through. The pacing is outright horrible. Like it was written by someone with ADD. The CGI was so overwhelmingly annoying that it made my skin crawl.

From what I have read it seems that this film was not only the result of a really bad screenplay but was pretty much butchered in the editing process. It seemed as if there were large gaps in the story line that just didn't make much sense and the whole film just seemed kind of incomplete.

Then there's the confusing back-and-forth mix of what at times seems like your average Marvel Comic Universe story and when it begins to delve into the R-Rated format of the Deadpool films. This movie can't really seem to figure out what universe it fits into and as a result seems choppy and uneven.

Tom Hardy's role is played so over the top that it is pretty much a parody of itself. I have no idea what the director was thinking in this case. He just made the character end up being so unbelievable that you couldn't really sympathize with him or take the plot seriously. I know that the film is based on a comic book, but in reality comic books are not nearly this cheesy.

The film definitely had some amusing moments. It was mildly entertaining, but not something that I would ever want to watch again. I've seen many of the Marvel movies several times and still find them enjoyable. Honestly, I didn't really want to sit through all of this movie the first time I watched it, but I have this annoying habit of watching films to the end no matter how bad they are. This once I very nearly ended up turning off.

text:
I don't throw the word "brilliant" all that often when discussing movies, but this is one of the few than genuinely deserves that description. Although the names and some of the events shown in the film are fictional, the premise is based upon a very real program that was once funded by the U.S. Department of Defense. This film tends to make light of the work done in this program and the results that it achieved, but it was definitely taken very seriously by the military at the time.

George Clooney is really the glue that holds this movie together, even if Ewan McGreggor (and his attempt at an American accent) does the narration and tries to be the focus of the film. Clooney seems to steal every scene he is in and provides the best performance in the film despite being cast with the likes of Jeff Bridges and Kevin Spacey. To be fair, Spacey does not get a ton of screen time in this film and isn't given a lot of dialogue to work with. Bridges gets quite a bit more screen time to play with in a role that he seems perfectly cast for. He definitely makes the most of it and is probably the second most compelling character in the movie. McGregor gets more screen time than anyone, but gives a fairly lackluster performance.

To be sure, this is no documentary and a lot that happens in the film is contrived simply to make it more interesting. The Remote Viewing project was a very serious affair at the time. Some aspects of it were very quirky, to say the least, but no one was laughing about it at the time. I think that Clooney had as much to do with making this film as funny as it was while still being convincing as the script writers. Had he not been totally convincing in his role the entire film would have have fallen flat. Fortunately, he was able to convey exactly what the writers intended to get across with his character.

I only saw this movie for the first time earlier today, but I'm sure that it one of those films that I will end up watching over and over again in the years to come.

text:
This is one of those movies that I first saw as a teenager but am again revisiting in its Blu-Ray form. The Rookie is a rather by-the-numbers cop movie starring and directed by Clint Eastwood. He plays a cop that is a slightly toned-down version of Dirty Harry. The story takes place in Los Angeles where he is teamed with new partner Charlie Sheen to investigate high-end car robberies.

The main car thief is the late Raul Julia, who oddly is supposed to be playing a German that seems to hate the Mexicans and Italians he works with and has no love lost for the "Polock" cop who is chasing him (Eastwood). Sheen plays "the rookie" as the title would suggest. Keep in mind, this film way made during the peak of Sheen's film career, long before his TV shows and numerous drug scandals. He was a hot property on the way up in Hollywood at the time.

Unfortunately, his acting was pretty stiff in this film. His character really had no depth and came off as mostly unlikable. I'm not sure if that was part of the script, but that's how he came across. The plot is a rather simple cops-and-robbers story with the two cops chasing the criminal around throughout most of the movie, culminating with a showdown at the end.

The film is predictable, but has a lot of great Eastwood one-liners and plenty of action. The pace drags a bit at times, but doesn't drift off-track for too long. Tom Skeritt plays Sheen's rich Father who coddles his Son and who is trying to get him to quit the LAPD and get a "real job".

Other than Eastwood being at the top of his game, there really aren't any stand-out performances here. The movie cost about $10 million to make, which was a pretty decent budget at the time. The script was rather unpolished and even goofy at times. Characters would repeat things that they said and use slang that just sounds flat-out comical these days. Pure cheese at times. Still, if you have time to kill and just want an old-fashioned action movie to pass the time you could definitely make worse choices. It mostly boils down to how big a fan you are of Clint Eastwood movies.

title_x: Weakest Movie of the Airport Series of Films
text:
This was my least favorite among the "Airport" series and I am just barely giving it a passing grade. Although I really like the overall plot, the screenplay is bogged down by some sappy side stories that slow down the pace to a crawl at times and ruin the more exciting parts of the film.

While all of the other Airport films feature some sort of romance between the different character, this one seems much more like an old re-run of The Love Boat than it does an action-adventure or drama movie. If they had left in more of the action scenes and taken out all of the BS romance it would have been a lot more enjoyable.

The main actors in the movie do a pretty good job, including George Kennedy who seems to play one of the few likable characters in the movie. The numerous cameos and walk-ons are more of a distraction than anything. Charo and Jimmy Walker couldn't act their way out of a paper bag if their lives were dependent upon it. I would have to say that most of the cameos were more annoying than anything.

One thing that you will definitely notice if you decide to watch this film is the fact that there is absolutely NO CGI in it whatsoever. The reason behind this is simple. CGI did not exist at the time. Instead, there are a lot of live action scenes that had to include some really bad special effects, like things blowing up or doing things that it just would not be practical to do with a real plane. To say that the special effects are crude would be too charitable. They happened to be state-of-the-art SFX at the time, but they look horrible today, even compared to cheap-o CGI.

The plot makes enough sense and I really loved seeing the scenes that actually involved the real Concord at the time these planes were flying. It was an incredible aircraft that has become much loved and missed since the time the fleet was retired. It was cutting edge technology at the time and many of its features would still be considered state-of-the-art today. The Concord is the REAL star of this movie. Everything else in the film basically revolves around it.

If you have seen the rest of the Airport movies you should really see this one. You probably will not like it as much as the others, but it still has its moments and you won't likely fall asleep while you are watching it. Just as the movie starts dragging with soap opera type drama they cut to another scene where the plane is in some kind of danger. So, while it has lulls, they do not last too long.

If you haven't seen the other Airport movies, you should probably watch them first. Not because you will be missing any story lines (there is really NO continuity between the different films. They each have totally different characters and unrelated plots) but because the other movies are much more entertaining than this one.

text:
A thoroughly enjoyable documentary for anyone old enough to still remember the beginning of the era of "home computers". Commodore was my first introduction to computing and gaming (unless you count Pong). I first got a VIC-20 when I was in 7th grade and eventually moved up to the C-64 later on. I never did get my hands on an Amiga, but by the time the Amiga was introduced IBM compatible "clones" were the newest fad and I jumped on that bandwagon instead.

I must admit, I did not know all that much about the history of Commodore prior to watching this film, so I definitely learned a lot. There seemed to be a lot more information on the company's early history than on how it spiraled out of control in its final days though. Obviously, there were a lot of bad decisions made, but how Commodore went from being the largest computer company in the world to having to completely liquidate its assets is not covered in great detail. I guess that not many execs who were there in the end probably wanted to be interviewed.

If you have fond memories of this computer brand, you will probably be captivated through the entire 2 hour+ film. If you grew up in the post-Commodore age, you will probably just be shaking your head wondering what the hell these people are rambling on about though.

description: ["The Commodore Story is a cram packed feature documentary film that takes us through Commodore's evolution from the 70's to the 90's from the PET, Vic20, C64 to the Amiga and beyond including the very rare C65 and the retro wave of nostalgic events and Commodore/Amiga related products hitting the market today. We take a journey across Europe and the US interviewing ex-Commodore staff and end users."]

No spoilers here, but this movie started off incredibly slow, depressing and dark. I don't think that there was any dialogue whatsoever in the first 15 minutes of the film. I almost stopped watching it about 30 minutes in, but I'm glad that I ended up waiting it out.

While this is certainly not one of my most favorite time travel movie of all time it really started to pick up after the first half hour and presented a pretty interesting story about the paradox of time travel and its moral implications. There is not much science fiction involved here. The details of time travel are glossed over to the point of being almost beside the point. That would normally be a bit of a turn off for me, but the story was good enough that I was sucked into it after the first hour and wanted to see how things turned out.

The film seemed a bit low budget with almost no special effects, CGI or complex sets. It is a pretty minimalist production, but doesn't come off as cheap. The acting is well done and the characters are ones that it is easy to sympathize with. It wasn't the best movie ever, but definitely worth watching.

text:
One of the funniest and most entertaining films that I have seen in awhile. If you are expecting a run-of-the-mill action movie, forget about it. Machete is really a comedy disguised as an action movie. There are tons of stars in this movie, although few are known for their excellent acting skills. Lindsay Lohan does pretty much what she does best, play a sex-obsessed junkie that is naked in most of her scenes.

Steven Segal is hilarious (perhaps unintentionally) as a Mexican drug lord hell-bent on killing Danny Trejo's character. Steven Segal has tried passing himself off as a lot of different races and nationalities... Japanese, Native American, Russian, etc. Seeing him trying to speak with a Mexican accent is absolute comedy gold though.

Deniro does a spectacular job straddling the line between dramatic acting and comedy. Playing a politician in this movie, it reminds me a lot of the film Wag the Dog. I have no idea what Jessica Alba's family background is, but I am pretty sure that she is not Hispanic. Watching her trying to act Hispanic is just hilarious. She must have spent weeks in a tanning booth to get ready for this part.

The plot of the movie makes total sense, which is odd for what I would characterize as a B-Movie.The script was obviously custom tailored for the specific actors in this movie. Since Rodriguez uses the same actors in many of his movies, that makes total sense. The comedy timing and overall pace of the film is about as close to perfect as you can get. It was meant to be more of a parody of 1970's action films than anything else. Nothing in the film is really taken seriously and it's all 100% pure entertainment. You are either going to love this film or hate it. Anyone who hates it clearly has no sense of humor.

This is one of those films that I almost stopped watching a couple of times but held on to the end hoping it was going to get better. It didn't. The pace of the whole film is mind-numbingly slow with an occasional gun fight here and there to keep the audience from falling asleep. The script is horrible and there are so many holes in the plot that it seems like the script writers didn't take this movie seriously at all.

The acting is so-so, with Gina Carano being put in the position of carrying the whole film on the back of her performance. While I do enjoy her acting at times, she simply doesn't have the acting chops it takes to turn a flop of a movie into something that entertaining. The film itself reeks of being low-budget, which isn't always a bad thing, but certainly doesn't add to any charm this film might have.

To sum it up, there really isn't a lot to like about this movie. It seemed to drag on forever, with a predictable plot and a lot of corny lines. On the bright side, at least they did not stoop to using a bunch of cheap CGI for special effects. In fact, there were no special effects to speak of in the movie other than fake gunfire. Unless you are searching for a cure to insomnia, I would give this film a pass.

title_x: A review from an *actual* burlesque professional
text:
Same recycled plot line as almost every rom com, and it touches on most of the cliches - small town girl trying to make it, she and a guy like each other but pretend not to at first and then have a miscommunication and OH NO! What if they don't get together?! And there's a mean girl.

Music and costumes are undeniably fun, I'll give them that.

But apart from that, the writers and producers should be ashamed of themselves. Burlesque is a real thing in cities across the world with real humans doing it, and this movie decided to pay NO regard either to what classic burlesque was nor the resurgence that has happened since the 1990s.

Here are some things you should know:
•Burlesque is so much more than sexy dancing, it can be comedic, or emotive - rooted in vaudeville, it is a form of storytelling
• Most burlesque dancers are not professionally trained. And we come in a wide variety of sizes and shapes. It is an art form that in most communities celebrates feminism, consent and body positivity.
• There is literally nothing new or provocative about singing during burlesque. This happens in almost every show. (The movie would have you think it's like this jaw dropper novel idea.)
• Apart from showgirl venues in Paris, NYC, las Vegas etc, most burlesque performers don't perform nightly at a venue or have large production budgets. In most cities, it's hard enough to fill a weekly or monthly show.
• Most of us have day jobs and even learn to sew and rhinestone ourselves. Unlike stripping, it is usually done out of passion, not for money - it is hard to make enough just to break even on good costumes and props, let alone to live off of.
• in most cities, you can expect a burlesque show to have a mix of solos and group choreo, and typically, solos "peel" down to pasties and undies or merkin.

If you are intrigued by modern burlesque, for the love of goddess, go support your local performers and see what it is actually about before watching the dumb movie. Look beyond Dita and Suicide Girls, and look up videos on YouTube of Burlesque Hall of Fame (bhof), Michelle L'Amour, Ula Uberbussen, April OPeel, Vagina Jenkins, Jo Boobs, Lola LeSoleil, Rosie Cheeks.

Burlesque is at your finger tips and you don't need this movie to reach out and touch it (just don't touch your performers ;)

text:
Castle is brilliant. I love it - it's a brilliant satire and farcical parody of the entire genre and I look forward to season 3.

The characters, while excellent in the first season, become a lot more nuanced in season two. The stories revolve around the murders and mysteries, but Castle is, at heart, a story about people - warts and all. I'm not sure why the writers chose to change the character of Kate Beckett as they did (having her grow her hair out), because there was no need to make the character more feminine.

If this show were a dead serious cop drama, scenes with Beckett stripping for a bath or changing her clothes to bail Castle out of a sticky spot with Russian gangsters would have felt like the creators were pouring the sex appeal on and weakening the character - instead, they made her more complex and interesting through the dialogue, body language, and sudden tone shifts in those kinds of scenes.

Castle himself remains a fairly static character, but as he is the centerpiece, this makes a lot of sense - what's revealed about him is not new things about him, but how the character has changed from the first season to the second, and watching true, carefully crafted and subtle character growth is fascinating.

The writers haven't ignored the 'secondary' characters - Alexis, Martha, Esposito and Ryan all get handled well, treated with respect, and grow with the show, but never seem like their presence is forced into the limelight in order to remind the viewers they exist - they organically and naturally are added to the story when they're needed.

Despite the show being built on the concept of being a very subtle parody of an entire genre, the show still treats the people who are victimized by murder with respect, and does a good job of showing even bit characters or one-off villains as rounded, dynamic people - something I rarely get the chance to see in this kind of show.

And did I mention the fantastic dialogue?

Over all, a very enjoyable show. Worth the money and worth the time - especially if you have an appreciation for the finely crafted parody.
description: ["As Season Two begins, Castle wrestles with how to repair his relationship with Beckett. But a mysterious murder forces the pair back together. Though their relationship remains rocky, their passion for cracking cases keeps their collaboration cooking. Can Beckett forgive Castle for poking into her past? And can Castle conquer his writer's block and finish his book?"]

text:
"Good" - the special effects, including their skybase and the jetcopter, were visually stunning (which is expected from Hollywood).

"Bad" - the props and the thin plot. Tom Cruise' uniform and his rifle are cheap and phony to the point of distraction. The uniform Tom Cruise wears is right out of The Day the Earth Stood Still.... the 1950's version, and the rifle is obviously light plastic as he throws it around like a wiffle ball bat.

By design, the setting was one of isolation and loneliness, unfortunately this was combined with a thin, uninspired plot which exacerbated the movie's weaknesses. The visuals were striking, but once I adjusted to this I was looking for more substance and plot, which were only partially delivered. Under the circumstances, a deeper, more intriguing plot was necessary.

The pace picked up somewhat near the end, with some nice twists, but even these were recognizable themes that leave you with the sense of "I've seen this stuff before". This movie needed more Morgan Freeman and little less Tom Cruise.

It is not a bad movie. I enjoyed it...somewhat, but it never grabbed me. I was initially amazed by the visuals, but as this wore off, I was left with mild indifference to the simple storyline. I've been on a multi-year rant about Hollywood blockbusters that spend countless millions on special effects and big name actors, but apparently spend very little on writing, and in my opinion this is another example of my gripe. This blockbuster movie that could have and should have been much better with relatively little effort.

Way too much meaningless and vapid backstory, a very slow start, extended scenes of pointless "witty" banter leading to nowhere, overly stereotypical cop behavior, all leading up to about 10 minutes of an actual cohesive, and somewhat interesting, story.

Notwithstanding the 4 star rating here on Amazon, I think 2 stars is generous. I like a good cop show as much as the next guy, but this was a disappointment. I had to fast forward it a couple times, which is never a good sign for a movie, but at times it was that boring.

If you want a good cop show, buy every season of The Shield and watch it from the start. You won't regret it. One of the best shows on television ever. Even better than the Sopranos.

text:
This is going to be long. :)
As the sixth installment in the Paranormal Activity franchise, it was decent. It tried to tie in the obscurity that ended the first few movies. I appreciate that. As a horror movie on it's own, it was completely cliche and predictable.

Pros: There were elements, parts of the premise, that I enjoyed, especially the bits of past and future. I can't say much more without giving spoilers, but I felt this element very enjoyable. I'd love to see an entire movie done like this.

The jump scares were decent. Okay, so they were totally predictable, but you got to "see" more in this movie than any of the others, so that was good.

And finally, they tied in this movie to the first few and gave some semblance of a reason. The franchise was sorely lacking in that.

Some MINOR Spoilers Ahead:
Cons: Where do I begin? How about the writing? Like most haunted house/people movies, the characters made the stupidest decisions ever. First, there's the "one parent believes and the other doesn't" schtick. This gets so tired. Luckily it doesn't take forever for the other parent to believe, and it's cool that the roles were reversed from the usual, but it's still tired. Weird s*** happens, simply take it at face value, even if you're not a believer.

Then there was their reactions. Until Tobi was literally in their faces, everyone acted so blase about it all. The child is acting weird - oh well, she's just a kid. There's this weird, gross thing floating around when I look through this camera that is so unique from a year before technology was all that powerful - but hey, I'll get real close to it for the heck.

The above is also a part of what I call "ridiculous white parenting". Instead of demanding an answer from their now creepy as heck daughter who's acting completely different than normal, they ask nicely. They believe the entity is in her room, and they put her to bed, in her own bed, with a camera to watch her. That's comforting. The child screams that she doesn't want to leave, and they're trying to plead with her rather than yanking her ass up and carting her to where she needs to be. Stupid, stupid parenting. Everyone got exactly what they deserved simply because their parenting pissed me off.

I don't get this. For once I want to see a haunted house movie where the people act normal. The whole premise of an entity following a person rather than a home is supposed to give you that element. If moving won't make a difference then why bother moving? But these people had so little emotion, such stupid reactions that it didn't help. Everyone was just so dumb.

I'm also sick of "dark" entities being the opposite of Christianity. It's such a modern-day religion, let's do something else. Instead of calling the local priest, call the local witch. Witchcraft has been around a heck of alot longer. Just give me something original. But since this movie is the 6th PA movie, I wasn't expecting originality. For less than a buck to rent, I wasn't expecting greatness. I got what I was expecting. :)

Will the movie scare you? No.
Will it make you sleep with the lights on? Hell no
Will it answer some questions from the earlier movies? Maybe a little
Is it worth watching? If you're bored and don't mind yelling at your screen because of stupid people and idiotic endings, yes. ;)

And speaking of the ending, I read there was an alternate on Wikipedia. They should've used that one.

text: The opening of Finding Kim is a dreamlike collage of gorgeous nude bodies juxtaposed with childhood flashes of idyllic carefreeness. Then we are confronted with the shame and disappointment of older female Kim, who is trapped in a female body she does not feel comfortable in. Director Aaron Bear takes us on a psychological/emotional quest to find Kim’s new male body. In that narrative, we learn a litany of things Kim never told anyone about her true thoughts regarding her birthed body. We watch her step-by-step physical transition—testosterone shots in her thighs, an evolving elation after a depression, and a suffering inability to speak the truth to her 80-year-old parents. We not only witness Kim’s passage from f-to-m, we also hear other stories from other trans folks such as Buck Angel and see glimpses of Seattle’s vocal trans community—the city’s strong sense of activism. Bear carves Kim’s story culminating in the filming of Kim’s FTM reconstruction chest surgery, the contouring, resizing, repositioning, and nipple grafts, alongside the surgeon’s story of achieving the best results as if he were a sculptor sculpting a new body, a new person, a transformation of beauty. At the end of the film, Kim still chooses not to tell his family, and he is still the ultimate dog lover and lighthearted swing dancer. A bare-chested Kim deep dives into a public pool. He is no longer drowning in identity. The image of water leaves us with the symbolic cleanse of old-to-new skin. Bravo to Aaron Bear for his first documentary—this emotional, pained, transformative coming-of-truth quest.

Christians are to express God's love to others and to one another and that involves loving even when we have been wronged and forgiving when the transgressor seeks forgiveness. text:
My two favorite Austen Novels are Pride and Prejudice, and Emma, so I tend to be *very* picky about their screen adaptations. When I compared this version to Gwyneth Paltro's version, I was astonished to discover that I found it far inferior in many aspects. Usually BBC adaptations are vastly superior to anything Hollywood puts out. Don't get me wrong, the ability to dig deeper into the subplots and characters in the novels are a great thing, but somehow, the lighthearted satirical spirit that so categorizes Austen's style became mean-spirited, and too dark. The Bates' who are supposed to make you laugh, instead make you cry.

While Jane Austen admitted that Emma was a girl "no-one but myself would much like" I think writer and director took it too literally. Emma was *not* very likeable at all! Ms. Garai, displayed very little of the sweetness, and vulnerability that made you root for Emma to begin with. I also felt like she had none of the elegance and decorum that a woman of her class is expected to have. I'm not a fan of Gwyneth Paltro, but she managed to have both in spades. It felt like she was always shouting her dialogue whether she raised her voice or not.

I also found myself deeply disappointed with the costumes, and some of the sets (the ballroom in particular) when Harriet Smith and Jane Fairfax are both dressed better than Emma Woodhouse, something isn't ringing true.

However, there were also very good parts that I did enjoy... Mr. Lee-Miller's portrayal of Mr. Knightly was very well done, despite my issues with the adaptation from the book to the script. I thoroughly enjoyed Harriet Smith, when I usually don't. Kudos to Ms. Louise Dylan for making her so charming. I also enjoyed that we got to see the conflict and pain in Frank Churchill and Jane Fairfax's courtship, (even though I adore Ewan McGregor and Polly Walker more). Thankfully, the mini-series afforded the time to delve into John and Isabella Knightly, and their children too.

All in all, in spite of what I disliked I think it's great to get to see these marvelous adaptations on Amazon Prime.

title_x: Fantastic Performances, Intriguing Storytelling, and a Controversial Plot with No Real Answer
text:
I loved this movie. I just finished watching it via Amazon instant video.

This is a deep, dark drama that has a slowly gathering plot conflict. It is not for everyone. Many parents, particularly mothers, may have a hard time with Eva's (Swinton) lack of ability to bond with her son. Are maternal feelings a part of the natural order? Is this why her son Kevin "has no personality" and for all purposes is portrayed as a sociopath? Eva eventually has the ability to connect with her daughter who is about eight-years younger than Kevin.

So, the film asks questions about the nature of evil, or evil actions. Nature versus nurture. It provides the answer for you a few times in such quotes by Kevin's character as "there is no point," and not recalling if there was any impetus for his horrible criminal incident. Eva goes about her lonely life after the incident in routine fashion caring about the mundane in a losing battle against entropy as if the only point for her is waiting for her natural death.

There is beautiful religious and spiritual imagery throughout the film. The opening scene has Eva being lifted Christ-like bathed in red while on one of her many travels abroad; a baptism of of free spirit which will be tethered with the arrival of her firstborn. The color red and water imagery is prevalent; possible representing sacrifice and redemption (or change). Without giving away any major plot details - pay attention to one of the final scenes after Eva arrives home from the incident. She hears the sprinklers on, which are heard frequently during the film in memory and flashbacks, and there are three (3) non-automatic fan sprinklers on. Three is sacred number in many religions, and might be homage to the Holy Trinity here.

The performances from all are stellar. Tilda Swinton and Ezra Miller are amazing and convincing. It is worth watching just to see them maneuver through such ferocious chemistry.

The single thing that bothered me was the reaction of the townspeople. While I do believe that it would be human nature for a few individuals to treat Eva as horribly as she was treated in the film, I believe that we live in a world where most people would not place the blame on the parent and attack them so viciously.

If you are an action or a comedy buff, or need big special effects, this is not your movie. It will leave you talking and thinking about it for a while after. I will watch again to pick up details I missed before. It is the literary critic in me.

text:
This is an interesting and "arresting" study in Polygamy. THIS is how it works, for the health and betterment of this particular family dynamic. The polygamous household is a mostly mess in suppressive, manipulative, criminal behavior. It's a sickening headline in far too many scenarios.

That being said, the Brown family have my heart, and my support. They are awesome; their stories and struggles are as human, and as compelling as any monogamous marriage....but much more gripping. An unstoppable show. It's a eye-opener for any who question how this kind of family can possibly work. It works very, very well. No child of theirs is compelled to commit to polygamy. There is no coercion, nor force.

There is indeed, beauty all around. A big thank-you to the Brown family for sharing vulnerable and unscripted moments. You are brave. My hat is off. You are the best of family and of love. You show the world what COMMITMENT means. THANK YOU.

I think if you get too serious with making Godzilla a realistic movie like somehow it may happen then it could become silly in a negative way instead of a fun way. The older movies Godzilla is more like a WWE wrestler with almost a human personality (he's outright anthropomorphic) in some of his Showa flicks. This is a main reason people connect with him. In this movie he's basically a giant radioactive lizard with not much personality.

The movie was entertaining despite this even though Godzilla doesn't have much screen time. About as much as the original movie from 1954 from what I've heard. The cut aways can be annoying though, this was also done in the original like the scene where Godzilla is fighting MUTO on TV in the original Godzilla is shown destroying the city on TV. I understand this may have been for dramatic effect for the build up to the final battle and
to develop some character among the humans but at the end of the day people want to see Godzilla bash monsters and trample buildings and there's really no surprise in the revealing of a character who's been around for 60 years.

My biggest gripe with the movie is that it's very dark. I don't mean dark figuratively but dark literally. It's very hard to see a lot of what is going on especially during the final battle scenes. I was hoping maybe it would be lighten up a little on the Blu Ray but it's not. Not on the regular DVD either.

text: I love this show! I used to watch Flipping Out with my aunt weekly when I lived close to her in Dallas, but then I moved and cut my cable subscription so I lost my Jeff Lewis fix - what a bummer! I kind of forgot about the show after a while, but then my aunt told me about Jeff’s new show, and I was excited to find it on Amazon (along with more seasons of Flipping out!) I was happy to find I still love it as much as usual. Jeff and Jenni are so crazy! I love their dynamic, and even though they can be mean to each other you can tell they’re good friends - they’ve been through a lot together over the years! I love the crazy antics they get up to, and I think it’s so funny when they have their little pajama parties. I really like seeing Jeff work with clients - you’d expect him to be self centered like he is with his house flips, but he really listens to the clients, and I love how he really listens to both people in the couple rather than just the louder voice (and there’s always one of those!) He does such an awesome job with the remodels, and the time crunch just adds that extra level of craziness to it - it’s very entertaining to watch! I’m happy to see Zoila back as well, and that she’s still got her attitude. I haven’t finished the first season yet, but I know as soon as I do I’ll be back for the second.

text:
This is an over-told idea - a story of passion and love within the confines of stifling social obligations with a touch of class tension thrown in for good measure. To make matters more annoying, the story is told in two directions. While Weisz and Hiddleston are brilliant, it is difficult to care about their characters as the story opens in the middle of the conflict and provides only snippets of the characters' beginnings. As a result, the chemistry of the couple isn't established at all. There is no investment in the development of their relationship in this story. It was as if one is only viewing part three of a miniseries without having first watched parts one and two.

I would skip this one despite HIddleston's and Weisz's wonderful performances, and the film's rich sets and costumes. However, if you do decide to take this one in, don't waste your money on HD. The whole film seems to be shot in soft-lens so the crispness of HD is completely lost.

title_x: See it for the stunning visuals because the story is.....
text:
......and always has been, rather lackluster.

I have, oddly, yet to meet anyone who read and liked the book.

Friends and family of mine, have spoken about this movie in conjunction with the disappointment they felt after having to read it for English Class in H.S.

Back in the day, for many of us stuck reading THE GREAT GATSBY by school requirement, we all wondered how F Scott Fitzgerald could write a book with such a simple plot and one that contained no real moral to it, or at least some striking revelation about people/life, and still manage to win this very ordinary book much hype and acclaim.

If he had written this book today, I think he would not have been published.

There really is nothing outstanding about the story.

In any case, for some reason, his book stood out to those who read it, and he got published.

Eventually the book took off like wildfire.

BACK TO THE MOVIE: Dicaprio, who I do like a lot as an actor, is miscast here, in my humble opinion.

I kept waiting for him to comfortably slip into character, but something is amiss and I kept seeing Leonardo Dicaprio dressed up in Roaring 20's attire and not some figure named Jay Gatsby.

His constant use of the phrasing," Old Chap" is beyond annoying and seems unbelievable, coming from his mouth.

Tobey Maguire ends up really being the best and most interesting character in the movie.

I also feel he stole the movie from everyone as Nick Carraway- the one who narrates the story in the book.

The spotlight shines on the incredible wealth of the times and people depicted here, and it glows specifically on this particular place on the coast of the Long Island Sound.

While given a bogus name in the story, Fitzgerald was referring in general, to the location of Nassau County's North Shore of Long Island- which is still deemed THE GOLD COAST even today, as it does have many breathtaking old mansions that still exist.

The cinematography is fantastic and I felt it was worth renting it just to see how this movie was filmed.

The music is current music- which throws the film off kilter a bit.

Why this artistic license was taken, I am unsure.

You see the art deco decor and the timely fashions of the 20's, but throwing in modern music left me- and others- a bit puzzled.

But, I will say, that when you see the party scenes and hear today's music, the director definitely managed to pull it off. This might have been done to appeal to the younger generation of viewers.

I am sure some of the older segment of viewers will think the director should have stayed with a truer approach to that era's music.

There are some minor additions to the story-mainly the beginning and ending, that were not in the book. However, they do not affect the integrity of the original story.

All the actors did a great job with the role they were given, but Dicaprio just can't seem to pull off the role of a mature, mystery man of money.
It is not that he wasn't trying. I just don't think this role was meant for him.

With now 3 versions of THE GREAT GATSBY on film( ALAN LADD- ROBERT REDFORD & NOW LEONARDO DICAPRIO), I don't think we will see another version anytime soon.

I saw the coming attractions for this movie and I thought maybe, with a great all star cast and the very enticing visuals, it might- MIGHT- change my mind about the book.

Unfortunately, no.

Even awesome cinematography cannot save a basic story.

This movies definitely pads it out with looks, but in the end you are still left with the book you read in High School.

I will say, when it comes to the first opening scene of a party in progress, you are wonderfully bombarded by incredible imagery- and you DO soak it all in!

VISUALLY GORGEOUS IS WHAT THE MOVIE IS AND MAYBE THAT'S WHAT SAVES IT FROM BEING A TOTAL DISAPPOINTMENT.
description: ["Leonardo DiCaprio brings 'Gatsby' to new life in this stylish, colorful adaptation of F. Scott Fitzgerald's literary classic."]

I was fully aware of his lifestyle, the things he is interested in i.e. body suspension art, his extreme drug abuse etc.  I've followed his radio show "Dark Matter" for years and have watched many interviews with him so nothing said or shown in this film was shocking or bizarre to me, but I do enjoy darker artistic impression. I could see how some may feel this way if this is the first time they are exposed to things that are considered out of the ordinary. So many reviews expressing disappointment and confusion that it wasn't an entire documentary about the murder? And that he talked about himself in the film? The title gives it away for all those who have failed to grasp this. "Mourning Son", it's about him - the son. Geez  To say Dave is vain and egocentric after exposing his soul in a documentary about his life and loss is plain ridiculous. I enjoyed this documentary and thought it was very well done. text:
I see a lot of reveiwers that are confused and dissatisfied, leaving low scores.

This movie isn't really a horror movie or not a typical one. There's definitely a Sci fi horror subplot but the main focus is on human relationships and coping.
Through the entire film something is just off about the main character. He's obviously very depressed and obviously doesn't know it.
He makes a lot of really horrible mistakes along the way that are almost hard to watch but if you look at it from the right point of view they make sense. He has VERY innocent intentions from the start. He tries to express this at one point near the end of the movie saying "I had the simplest of intentions"
Something that started out as him just trying to have a touching moment with his little brother and remind him of a fun random memory from their childhood all of a sudden turns into multiple deaths. He is dealing with what growing up and growing apart is and he has found himself a fully grown adult that hasn't ever found anything worth while since his child hood and he is desperately trying to get back to how things were then. He wants the relationship he had with his little brother to be the same as it was as children and he wants to live in the house they grew up in and he despises his brothers wife and daughter for taking his brother from him. None of it is really his fault and it's a very realistic portrayl of mental illness, exaggerated by the supernatural element of the creature that has bonded with him.
The metaphor of burning down his house of lies at the end is amazing.
Basically he gets sucked deeper and deeper into this sick web, all the while he's only trying to protect himself b3cause he really hasn't done anything wrong. In the end he makes the choice to do something wrong to try to get back everything he thinks he's lost and finish everything for good. It's truly heartbreaking.
A very deep film. Very slow burn. Definitely not going to be for a lot of people. But it was very well done I think. I only took a star off because a movies main purpose is usually to entertain in some fashion and I don't feel like this quite dies that. But the message it's trying to get across does come across very well if you can take a minute to really think about it.
Overall phenomenal acting, good music, good lighting, realistic takes, and believable dialogue. Watch this on a bored rainy day when you need some introspection

text:
Review of Anything Goes
Hot Toasty Rag, September 13, 2017

Anyone, even a musical lover, will tell you that Anything Goes is a pretty silly story. A bunch of colorful characters are stuck on a boat together, and while he loves her and she loves someone else, and she’s marrying that guy, and he’s pretending to be someone else—well, it’s a hodge podge of musical comedy interrupted by Cole Porter standards and some tap dancing.

While Ethel Merman starred in the original Anything Goes on Broadway in 1934, she reprised her role for Hollywood in 1936, with Bing Crosby by her side. Almost twenty years later, she made a live television adaptation, this time with Frank Sinatra. Two years after that, in 1956, Hollywood ditched Ethel but kept Bing and made another filmed version! Anyway, the 1954 version was severely condensed to fit into a television event on Colgate Comedy Hour. While the plot is pretty truncated, I don’t think anyone is really watching it for the dialogue. They’re watching it to see Frank Sinatra and Ethel Merman sing live versions of “Anything Goes”, “I Get a Kick Out of You”, “You’re the Top”, and “Blow Gabriel Blow”. The two stars didn’t get along, and it’s pretty obvious when you watch it that they have zero chemistry together, but if you’d like to see them performing live, you can give it a watch. It’s only an hour long.
