title_x: Throw Horrible Bosses From a Train
text:
Interesting formula: Take Hitchcock's [[ASIN:B0002HOERG Strangers on a Train]] from way back in the 50s, add in equal amounts of Danny DeVito's 1987 spoof of that movie called [[ASIN:B005AIRCBW Throw Momma From a Train]], then mix 'em both with a whopping helping of [[ASIN:B001UV4XEW Hangover]] humor and that sets the stage for the dark comedy Horrible Bosses. But it wouldn't be the complete movie that it is without the absolutely perfect cast who act their own parts out with perfection, but also exhibit a chemistry together that is unparalleled in any movie that I've recently seen.

And hats off to the writer/producer/director team for putting together a familiar story line that is ultimately pulled off with originality, and most importantly, hilarity from start to finish. The humor is often rude, crude and probably a bit more than the average Jennifer Aniston movie fan bargained for. However I give Aniston a ton of credit for for adding to the success of this film by effortlessly making her character believable, funny and shocking. After all the goody two-shoes roles that I'm used to seeing Aniston in, watching her in a "bad girl" role only made the movie more refreshing and entertaining.

Colin Farrell was another great cast as one of the Horrible Bosses. He's transformed into a pot-bellied, balding drug addict and almost unrecognizable a la Tom Cruise in [[ASIN:B001H5X7KC Tropic Thunder]]. Farrell is Jason Sudeikis' boss. Kevin Spacey is Jason Bateman's boss, and Spacey is a natural crass meanie. Then Anistion is a the boss of a comical Charlie Day. The individual bosses deal out their own styles of harassment on the job and it's all darkly hysterical. So the three guys are given the notion that they could take each other's bosses out to make their lives easier. The events following this brainstorm of an idea are equally dark and laugh out loud funny.

If you're looking for laughs you'll find them o'plenty in Horrible Bosses. Perhaps over the top at times (but that's what the movie is going for), Horrible Bosses is one of the best movies that I've seen in 2011.

text:
As usual, I will try to write a spoiler-free review, but given that Freddie Mercury is such a well-known public figure, I feel somewhat disingenuous in making such a claim.

The movie, obviously, features Mercury as the central figure, which in some ways is odd, because two of the band members are executive producers of this film and were instrumental in the film's creation, yet they are only supporting characters, with none of their personal lives and little of their individual perspectives detailed. The time period covered is from the time right at the band's creation up through the legendary performance at Live Aid.

The film's primary mission seems to be to detail Mercury's demons/driving force for his oversized persona and his creative genius--largely the product of those same demons. Along the way, we're treated to insights of Queen's creative genius (this was an immensely talented roster--not just Mercury) that gave birth to truly masterful, innovate creations, the infighting and sense of family.

One thing I'll note is that the pacing of this film is truly excellent. Although it's 2 1/2 hours long, it doesn't feel like it, partially, I think, because it does take time to explain so many aspects of Mercury's life and career, but it doesn't linger too long. In that way, it's very economical so that by the end of the movie, you feel as though you've sampled fully, but not gluttonously, at the buffet and you emerge light, yet satisfied.

The emotional impact of this movie is also judiciously applied, eliciting genuine feeling at each step, but it's never overplayed in any soap opera-like fashion. The audience can sympathize and perhaps even identify with the subject, but the director nor Remy Malik ever elicit pity; there's a certain dignity to the performance and direction that I found refreshing and tactful.

I know that there's a controversy about how Mercury's sexuality was portrayed in the film, some saying that his homosexuality wasn't featured adequately. To that, I have two answers: 1. There were at least five scenes involving Mercury with men; 2. The film was more about his creative genius, his wit and oversized personality, all of which were highlighted more prominently, because that's how the average person interacts with his life and it more effectively portrays his relationship with the band--the central relationship of the movie.

My final verdict? Well worth the viewing AND its Academy Award consideration.
description: ['Bohemian Rhapsody celebrates the band Queen, their music, and their extraordinary lead singer Freddie Mercury, who defied convention to become one of the most beloved entertainers ever.']

title_x: “Inside Out” and the Lessons from Mister Rogers
text:
What more is there to say about a film that is “inventive, gorgeously animated, and powerfully moving” (rottentomatoes.com)? As I was watching and enjoying the film with my family, my thoughts kept drifting to lessons from our favorite neighbor, Mister Rogers. One thing that set apart Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood from most contemporary children’s TV programs was his focus on the importance of “growing on the inside”, versus the sometimes fanatical rush to teach young children letters, numbers, and vocabulary. Feelings are mentionable, and what are mentionable and more manageable. “Inside Out” followed this tradition and made the clashes of feelings inside Riley – particularly feelings of sadness that were difficult to express – both mentionable and ultimately more manageable.

As the film’s characters explored the inner world of memories in search of the few “core” memories that define who we were, it became increasingly evident that the joys and sorrows of growing up were intimately woven with the people we loved and people who loved us. The more disconnected Riley felt from her parents, the more disconnected her memories became to her self. As Mister Rogers would remind children and adults, nothing – not even the latest and greatest technological gadgets – can ever compare to the significance of the human to human connection. In all things that truly matter in learning and growing, relationship comes first.

“Inside Out” was produced in close consultation with neuroscientists to achieve a rough approximation of the workings of the mind. There is only one thing that made me wonder afterwards: as children walk away from the film with a greater appreciation for the feelings inside themselves, would they also come away with a greater sense that they have the power to manage their own feelings? For most of the film, Riley seemed to be at the whims of her conflicting feelings, functioning more as a “shell” than a person with her own will. Would some children walk away feeling that, when they are mad or sad, there is nothing they can do except to wait for their feelings to sort themselves out? Mister Rogers famously recited the lyrics of the song, “What do you do with the mad that you feel?” in his 1969 congressional testimony to advocate for PBS funding (you can find that footage on Youtube). After affirming that it was alright to feel mad and suggesting there were lots of constructive ways to express being “mad”, Mister Rogers wrote these words, “I can stop when I want to, Can stop when I wish, I can stop, stop, stop any time. And what a good feeling to feel like this, And know that the feeling is really mine.” While it is important for children to know the legitimacy of their feelings, it may be equally important for children to know that they own their feelings, and not the other way around. “Inside Out” is the kind of movie that can help families talk about these things long after the watching is over.

title_x: A romantic film that isn't stupid.
text: Most romantic films I find to be stupid and the women in them pathetic because they are so desperate for a man. In "Dorfman in Love", Deb Dorfman pines after Jay Cleary but not in a pathetic desperate way. So many women in romantic movies seem to feel they must have a man to feel happy in life and to have self-worth, as if not having a man makes them nothing. But in the case of Deb Dorfman, she goes about her life without feeling she has to have a man. Yes, she says she wants love, but who doesn't? Deb's lack of confidence isn't because she doesn't have Jay as her boyfriend, but because she sees herself not as someone who is fun, sweet, intelligent and beautiful. In this movie Deb eventually learns to live her own life instead of living it for others. She also learns to see herself as someone who is fun, sweet, intelligent and beautiful and although she didn't need a man to show her this about herself, it was a man who did. It wasn't because he's a man, but because he's the type of person who sees beauty and is able to turn it around for others to see. Haaz Sleiman as Cookie I think really stole the film; he truly shines in this movie. Sara Rue is adorable as Deb as well. The film is well acted and not too cheesy or too slapstick like so many romantic films are. I enjoyed seeing Los Angeles as I was born and raised in Southern California and I am homesick and miss my old stomping grounds. The only down side to this film are two things: 1. Having Haaz Sleiman's character, Cookie, go from saying he's gay to falling in love with a woman. In real life, this typically doesn't happen. I have had several gay friends and they don't suddenly just switch sexual orientation; and 2. The makeover of Deb. Before the makeover she looked like an average person. Then she was transformed into this model looking creature that barely resembled the first Deb. That's all well and good, but doing the makeover shtick is not only a tired romantic cliché (remember Toula Portokalos's makeover in, "My Big Fat Greek Wedding"?), but it implies that an average looking woman can't find love unless she's turned into someone who's pictures belong in Vogue magazine. But for what it's worth, this is a pretty decent movie. I really liked it. As far as romance movies go, this is one of the better ones I've seen so I'm giving it five out of five stars.

title_x: Well worth watching and eerily similar to...
text:
This clever plot concept and film most definitely doesn't deserve the term "schlock." It also happens to be the kind of plot that can be presented very well on a very low budget using stock footage.

There was in fact a DEW (Distant Early Warning) Line of radars in the far north of Canada, a component of the film. Their use in this film, which was released in December of 1958, of the term "Keyhole" as the name for one of those radar surveillance installations must have seriously freaked out anyone involved in the beyond top secret US spy satellite program at the time, that program having begun in 1956. Their first spy satellite in the KEYHOLE series, KH-1 (Keyhole-1), was launched in June of 1959, just six months after this film was released.

Another amazing coincidence which probably freaked out those involved was another top secret US military effort which began in 1955 - the Supersonic Low Altitude Missile (SLAM) project. That was a very large nuclear powered cruise missile that flew at supersonic speeds at an extremely low altitude. Because it was nuclear powered, it's range was estimated to be at least 113,000 miles which is over 4.5 times the circumference of the Earth. So, it was capable of flying around the Earth multiple times... just like the missile in this film. SLAM's nuclear reactor ramjet was not shielded to save a huge amount of weight, but it did not become seethingly radioactive until started up for doomsday use. The shock wave from its extremely low altitude supersonic flight would have caused damage on the ground, another similarity with the missile in this film, but not nearly as bad. Also, even though it would have been incredibly radioactive once running, it would have passed by any spot on the ground too quickly to present a serious radiation hazard.

Still, the similarity between SLAM's characteristics and the lost missile's are interesting.

Finally, any satellite or missile on a path highly inclined from the equator would, due to the rotation of the Earth, pass over most of the surface of the Earth over time or ALL of it if it was in a polar path or orbit. That's the other clever part of this plot concept because that's exactly the hazard this "Lost Missile" presented.

text:
My kids love magic tricks and they love cats. How can you screw that up? It wasn't easy, but directors Jeremy Degruson and Ben Stassen demonstrated why Pixar continues to knock it out of the park and nWave Pictures...doesn't.

This film has all the ingredients that my kids should love: a spooky magic house, a kindly old magician (Doug Stone), an adorable cat protagonist (Brianne Siddall), and a motley cast of characters that includes a rabbit (George Babbit), a mouse (Shanelle Gray), two lovebirds, and a host of steampunk-inspired robots. Cute, right? Poor Lawrence the magician doesn't realize his grasping nephew Daniel (Grant George) is planning to toss him into a retirement home and sell the magical house. Standard stuff for a kid's movie. Well, it would be except...

This is a movie where the bad guy shouts "damn cat!" over and over. This is a movie where Daniel tries to murder Thunder (Brianne Siddall) by shooting him with a shotgun. This is a movie where Daniel going into anaphylactic shock due to his allergy to cats is played for laughs. This is a movie where 3D is demonstrated at every turn by point-of-view shots and stuff flying at the screen -- and freaky Halloween sequence in which the movers are scared out of the house, but really it's like a creepy Disney ride instead.

It's got all the right elements, but it simply doesn't gel. My kids didn't like it at all, and if your kids are afraid of Disney's Haunted Mansion ride or aren't fond of attempted cat-murder, they won't either.

text:
Your opinion of this movie will likely hinge on how much you like Paul Rudd. Rudd's got something of a goofy everyman quality that's common to modern film-making, a non-threatening goofball that's just trying to get by in a crazy world. And make no mistake, the world of Ant-Man and the Wasp is nuts.

Remember the first movie, where former criminal Scott Lang (Rudd) took over the Ant-Man persona and suit while romancing Hank Pym's (Michael Douglas) daughter Hope van Dyne (Evangeline Lilly)? van Dyne is pissed that Lang stole the Ant-Man suit to help the Avengers, in violation of the Sokovia Accords. Lang lives his life in miniature, trapped in his house with an ankle bracelet, counting off the days to his freedom while he tries to keep his daughter Cassie (Abby Ryder Foster, who easily steals the film's heart).

But with such a rich Marvel universe, it's virtually impossible to ignore what's gone before, and this installment wisely embraces the past: Lang is haunted by his adventure into the quantum realm; the fact he returned gives hope to Pym and van Dyne, who begin working on a plan to rescue Janet van Dyne (Michelle Pfeiffer). Lang is the key to finding her, but that means leaving his house and his daughter, setting up one of the many tensions that twist through the film to keep us on our toes.

The entire concept of Ant-Man is gloriously wacky, but the first movie felt oddly muted, perhaps under the weight of introducing a new character to an already-crowded universe. Director Peyton Reed takes the gloves off and lets Ant-Man's bonkers concepts literally run wild, creating chase scenes that involve miniaturized buildings, man-size ants, and giant-sized men. The movie keeps things gleefully clipping along at an absurd pace, as Lang plays football with a string of opponents: the desperate (Ghost, played by the excellent Hannah John-Kamen), the clueless (hilarious straight-man Randall Parker as FBI agent Jimmy Woo), and the just plain bad (Walter Goggins as Sonny Burch, a low-level villain who just can't resist the billions Pym's tech might net him). Add this all together and Ant-Man and the Wasp delivers a bonkers, gleeful series of fight and chase scenes, interspersed by regular guys like Luis (Michael Pena) and Lang trying to figure out what the heck is going on.

None of this film stands up to the slightest scrutiny, and that's okay. The rules behind how shrinking and growing work are comic-book-levels of arbitrary, but there's enough jokes to make you feel bad about pointing them out. It's a fun summer popcorn flick...until it isn't. If you've seen Infinity War, you know why you shouldn't get too invested.

title_x: We'll stick with the series, thanks
text:
My family is a big fan of the My Little Pony franchise. We've seen all the episodes, my daughter has all the ponies, and we just wrapped up a Dungeons & Dragons crossover between the Princes of the Apocalypse campaign and My Little Pony where my daughter played a pegasus pony, my son played a dragon, and I played a griffon. We were even as HASCON, bought the special D&D/My Little Pony dice, and visited the My Little Pony booth when we were there. You might say we know a thing or two about My Little Pony...but this? I don't know what this movie was supposed to be, but it's not up to the level of quality we've come to expect from the series.

The film starts out in the traditional fashion, with a literal song-and-dance about a Friendship Festival that will involve all four princesses: Celestia (Nicole Oliver), Luna (Tabitha St. Germain), Twilight (Tara Strong) and Cadance (Britt McKillip). We get a long tracking shot that crams every character into the film, which fortunately includes Cheese Sandwich (Weird Al Yankovic, but no speaking part for him). That unfortunate trend -- shout outs to characters that should be rising to Equestria's defense but just show up in the background -- is part of what's wrong with the movie.

The movie is gorgeously animated, which proves something of a distraction. The ponies have absolutely massive eyes, but the animation in the series blends their eyes together with the rest of the bright background. Here, pony eyes glimmer and glisten with such intensity that it's hard not stare at their eyes even as the ponies say something important. This is one of those rare instances where a better animation budget was actually a detriment.

With the obligatory fan service out of the way (look, there's Derpy, uh, Muffins!), the tone changes abruptly as bad guys in airships show up, led by a pony with a broken horn, Tempest Shadow, voiced by Emily Blunt...with an American accent for some reason.

Tempest is after the magic of all four princesses to fuel the monkey-like Storm King's (Liev Schreiber) staff. Who the Storm King is, where he comes from, why he's after the staff (other than for, ya know, evil power reasons) is never explained. There are hints that the Storm King was supposed to be a sarcastic adult in a world of kids, similar to Hades in Disney's Hercules -- but Schreiber just doesn't have enough lines to pull off James Woods' level of acting work. So we get a generic villain with a minion who is far more interesting.

The Mane Six (Twilight and her five friends from the series) plus Spike the dragon know they have to ask for help from the "Queen of the Hippo--" but Luna is cut off before she can explain further. And thus the ponies, along with the audience, are pushed out of their comfort zone as we discover that outside of Equestria the world is filled with nasty humanoid fish and sneaky humanoid cats in Klugetown.

Our ponies are hopelessly out of their depth. Rarity (St. Germain again) doesn't have much to do but complain about the tired plot. Rainbow Dash and Applejack (both voiced by Ashleigh Ball) seem like they should be in better command, but at various times Rainbow Dash forgets she can fly. The other pegasus, Fluttershy (Andrea Libman) has one slightly humorous scene in the whole film and almost no other dialogue. The bulk of the movie revolves around Pinkie Pie (Libman again) and Twilight's conflicting philosophies on how to survive this new world of high stakes, with poor loyal Spike (Cathy Weseluck) caught between them. The question they both answer differently: is being friendly an appropriate response to the end of the world?

The reason the ponies are sidelined is because The Movie is hellbent on cramming as many celebrity guest voices into its 99-minute running time. From a plot perspective, Twilight Sparkle forgets how to teleport, never casts any spells, and the Mane Six never use their Rainbow Powers. In other words, this movie literally feels like the characters got dropped into another film entirely. In fact, there's an entire group of characters that seem to have no other purpose than to sell toys, since only one of them even bothers to help.

Most unforgivable of all is that the music is subpar. Songbird Serenade's (Sia) contribution is the lone standout, but it doesn't even match the quality of music that's played in the Equestria Girls films. My kids couldn't sing any of the songs or even quote the movie, but enthusiastically retold the finale of season seven that they watched the same day.

The Movie is a disappointment. In an attempt to create high stakes for the ponies, it feels like a cynical take on what made the series so much fun to begin with. We'll stick with the series, thanks.

text:
I had my doubts about “X-Men: Days of Future Past.” For one, it’s the seventh installment in the series (yes, really, counting the Wolverine movie). For another, it’s a mash-up between 2006’s retro “X-Men: First Class” and “X-Men: The Last Stand.” In a fashion similar to the Star Trek franchise reboot, “Days of Future Past” is an entire retcon of the events of “The Last Stand” – an opportunity to forge a new path with younger actors that isn’t beholden to the main storyline. Fed up with the many nonsensical plotlines of “The Last Stand?” Loved the ruthlessness of “First Class”? Then you’re in luck, true believers!

“Days of Future Past” features a dystopian future in which mutants are hunted by Mark II Sentinels, capable of instantly copying any superpower they encounter. Their directive: protect humans from mutants at all costs. Unfortunately, the definition of a mutant rapidly expands to include those with the potential to have mutant offspring, and it’s not long before the shapeshifters are killing off most of humanity. Desperate, Professor Xavier (Patrick Stewart) and Magneto (Ian Mckellen) team up with Storm (Halle Berry), to use Kitty Pryde’s (Ellen Page) powers to send Wolverine’s (Hugh Jackman) consciousness back in time to 1973. It’s all to stop Mystique (Jennifer Lawrence) from assassinating the creator of the Sentinels, Bolivar Trask (Peter Dinklage), which sets off the chain of events leading to Sentinel apocalypse.

This leads to a fun series of acting exercises in which young Xavier (James McAvoy) and young Magneto (Michael Fassbender) must be convinced by taciturn Wolverine (still Hugh Jackman) to work together. There’s just a few problems: Xavier’s a drug addict and Magneto is in a super prison. And oh yeah, they hate each other’s guts. Enter Peter Maxmioff AKA Quicksilver (Evan Peters), who is like the Flash with worse hair. It’s also the best part of the film.

The fun of a retconning film like this is that all bets are off. Older characters can die without permanently damaging the franchise, new characters can forge their own paths, and everything that was old feels new again. Although there are always plot holes in a time traveling film, it’s easy to forgive them as director Bryan Singer repairs the wreckage he left behind when he fled the helm of “X-Men: The Last Stand” to lead the dreadful “Superman Returns” and left it to Brett Ratner to pick up the pieces. I’m not sure this film is enough for fans to forgive Singer, but it’s a much improved course correction to the franchise.

text:
All-Star Superman is a pun on words. Here's a hint: it involves Superman as a superstar and Superman as a super star, literally. In a carefully orchestrated Lex Luthor plot, Superman is manipulated into being overexposed to the sun's rays with a special kind of cancer unique to his physiology. Superman is dying, and this animated film is an opportunity to look at Superman/Clark Kent's legacy.

With nothing to lose, Superman starts working on wrapping up loose ends. He tells Lois whom he really is, a truth she doesn't believe for a second. Being that this film is firmly rooted in the history of the Superman comics, it's easy to see why. Clark Kent has been "outed" multiple times with dozens of excuses as to why he's not really Superman, such that even when Superman plainly states his secret identity it's no longer believable. Nor is it really relevant in the big scheme of things.

What "All-Star Superman" does well is emphasize that Superman isn't an alien, but a god among men. What does a god do in his spare time? Collect dangerous but endangered alien creatures, synthesize super-power formulas, and rebuild the Titanic. This is Superman as a comprehensive being who is both endlessly compassionate and terrifyingly powerful. It's hard to conceive of Superman without his Clark Kent personality to ground him -- a fact brought into stark contrast by two Kryptonians who revel in their newfound power on Earth and carelessly abuse it.

There are other plots, led primarily by Luthor as an architect of destruction on death row that sees Superman's existence as an affront to humanity's destiny. But it's not until Luthor truly gets a chance to walk in Superman's shoes that he sees the world as the Kryptonian sees it -- and realizes how much he has wasted his life in trying to thwart someone who has only tried to help.

Although "All-Star Superman" doesn't have the luxury of truly digging into every plot point (there are two time travel superbeings who show up that feel out of sync with the rest of the film's tone) it culminates in a critical question: When you can witness the suffering of even the smallest blade of grass, wouldn't you do everything in your power to ease it?

Luthor -- and by extension, all of mankind -- realizes only too late how pitifully short we fall of our noblest goals thanks, in part, due to the limited perceptions of our humanity. This is powerful stuff.

text:
Bella is the winner of the 2006 People's Choice Award at the Toronto International Film Festival, and is refreshing in it's story and acting. This movie isn't about action and adventure, but it's a movie about life. Everyday life, and how two people cope with theirs. Part of what makes the movie so enjoyable for me is the acting feels real. When watching the movie I wasn't struck with the fake feel I get from so many typical Hollywood movies. This movie feels genuine, the tears and laughter seem real instead of put on to make money. I think a large part of that has to do with the case selected for this movie. They actually believe in the story and it's message, and aren't concerned solely about the money making aspect of the film. That makes this movie all the more real and powerful.

The movie is rated PG-13 (for thematic elements and brief disturbing images) largely for one scene. Most mature children probably 8 or 9 and up should be able to watch the movie and handle it well.

Bella has won several awards in addition to the People's Choice. Along with other accolades Edward James Olmos chose this movie to open the LA International Film Festival. At that time he said, "It is one of the most impressive landmark films to open our festival in 10 years ... a film people have to see, it really captures the heart and makes you think. It is one of the best films to come out in a long time."

I certainly agree, and highly recommend this movie.

text:
I started pulling up Sesame Street for my little guy awhile back. Watching this show as a little girl taught me how to read, well before I would have learned in school. Even though its changed a great deal in the style of content delivery and the set is more 'clean' (seriously, watch some vintage episodes, the Street was not so polished back then), I still find it has awesome educational value. I know not everyone would agree with that - tons of people I know look down their nose at the show now because its changed over time, but one thing I think every adult that takes issue with it needs to keep one thing in mind:

It is a show for children.

Sure, there are some jokes the adults would get, but it is a children's show. Its not there to entertain or educate us, the grown ups, about letters and numbers. We already know them, the young children that this show is geared toward, do not. Sesame Street still offers the same learning experiences to children that it did when I was a child, with some new things that they didn't do when I was a little one.

All in all, I'm glad that I can share this show that was special to me as a child, with my little man as he grows up.

text:
It leads up slowly to a terrifying climax, yet that is what makes it realistic. The last 30 minutes or so are brutal and will scare you, but again, this is what can actually happen to teens (or adults) who make the mistake of meeting someone they don't know.
It is a good teaching tool for anyone who is young or dating. People are abducted all the time by men whom they think are safe "He seems like such a nice guy" "He's very intelligent and sensitive"
There are ways to protect yourself- Meet people in public places. Have a friend come with you or watch from a short distance. Give a friend all the details you can - name, address, phone number, information on his car, etc...
Never leave an agreed-upon location. Set up a safe call - have a friend call (not text) you at a certain time. If you don't answer, they call the police. If you do answer and use a certain word, they call the police.
Teens are not going to listen when you tell them "Dont go meet someone you met online", but if you give them the tools to have a safety network with friends, you might avoid a horrible situation.

title_x: Too much embroidery, not well cast, not well written, maybe not necessary
text:
Just because someone can find another story about heroic resistance to the Nazis doesn't necessarily mean that yet another film is needed. If it is needed then try to stick to facts without embroidery - this does not. Further, it would be best to avoid inventing philosophic dialog about a time in which neither you nor anyone you know never lived and experiences which neither you nor anyone you know never had and placing the dialog it in the mouths of people you invent just to mouth your chosen platitudes. This is not "Schindler's list" this is not "The Wall" this is not "Sophie's Choice" - this is just hackneyed pandering and crass commercialism.

As to the casting: Jesse Eisenberg is a fine actor; among his most distinctive characteristics is his capacity for rapid, staccato speech - he makes Stubby Kaye, Lou Costello and Robert Preston sound like the founding members of The Slow Talkers of America. So, of course, let's cast him as a mime. Huh? First, he really didn't learn to mime credibly. Second Marceau was relatively short and stocky, he looked like a tough guy (and was, evidently) not so Mr. Eisenberg. There might have been something to be said for casting a French actor, n'est ce pas? Even better, a French mime. I'm sure there are a few who could have figured out how to escape their invisible box in time to audition.

Of course the casting director could have made Jesse seem tougher by creating a different contrast with the other actors. For example, instead of Ed Harris as General Patton they might have tried Michael Cera - that'd make Jesse look a bit tougher.

text:
This film was much better than I thought it was going to be. It was well-acted and characters were believable. It really captured the atmosphere of a back-woods community where people are driven by very basic emotions and there is little to do but hunt and feud over land. As some other viewers have said, the sparse conversation and darkness of the set add to the brooding sense of inevitability that the film is portraying.

The one biggest thing that struck me was just how much trauma this boy was subjected to in his short lifetime. He couldn't have been more than 9 years old and had seen more bloodshed and horror than most adults see in 80 years.

Unlike the one viewer who said he was whiney, I got a totally opposite impression of him. He was a good kid with a strong conscience, and he actually had more sense than the adults around him who used him for their own agendas.

It was clear that his Grampa knew that in that time he instead of the boy would have been the "responsible adult" charged with the accidental but reckless killing of the man, but rather than protecting the boy he was more worried about himself going to prison, and he further dragged the boy who already felt bad enough, into his plan to cover it up, out there in the middle of the night, risking hypothermia, coyotes, and risking himself and the boy being shot by the two men who were up to no good poaching on the land.

As others have said, I wondered why the mother allowed 1) The Grampa to take HER son out hunting at a time when visibility was low (she could have put her foot down and said "no absolutely NOT"), and then

2) Why she just stood there gravely staring when she found out that the boy had shot the man in the woods and her father-in-law wanted to drag him out there to cover up the shooting. Why she didn't insist on calling the sheriff right then and there and a lawyer to find out what they needed to do in this complex situation is a mystery to me. She struck me as a sad woman who just let things happen around her rather than being actively involved in making sure that her son was safe and cared for. I don't why she deferred to the Grampa who really did not have any legal authority over the child. I also noticed that she didn't hug the boy when he came home from being out all night but instead seemed in a trance with more of that sad resignation she showed throughout the film. It is possible that her husband's death was pretty recent (it was implied that the guy he was feuding with shot him but why that guy was still free is not explained).

I didn't understand the significance of a scene earlier in the film when the Grampa said to her that he didn't want to go into what happened with her late husband (as if to imply it was somehow her fault). Possibly she was from the family he was feuding with. That's the only reason I can imagine why her father-in-law would blame her in any way.

text:
This story of an autistic boy was extremely moving and it was well-acted and believable. Many autistic children (especially during the 70s when this took place) have been assumed to be retarded when in fact they're not. This is a common misconception and often leaves them vulnerable to abuse due to the stigma attached and the uphill battle to get those in a position of power to believe them when they're abused. The teacher/psychologist in this story accurately read the clinical test results as not a true indication of this boy's ability or intelligence. A savvy professional understands that people with autism have brains that are wired differently, so there are some tests that cannot adequately measure their function. I know this, not only from study, but I was one of those children, but unlike the boy in this story I was not directly diagnosed at age 5 (being a girl at a time when they believed only boys could have autism). The raw data was there but they left out the diagnosis and merely left prognosis open-ended; a question.

I know what it's like to be unseen and unheard. I went through both public and private school education and often encountered either low expectations or was told I wasn't trying. Unlike the boy in this story I had to teach myself how to survive in the world with abusive adopted parents who felt cheated but too embarrassed to return me to where I came from lest they be viewed as uncaring by the community in which we lived. There was nobody who had my back and it was very difficult being misunderstood about 90% of the time.

With the exception of the pedophile Jeff in this story, this boy had an amazingly good experience in the school he attended and a teacher who genuinely cared about his success in life and, like his mother, also wanted to create a safe environment where he felt valued.

Many live-in facilities (up until very recently) had horrible practices that not only didn't help kids with autism, but traumatized them, such as using electric shock as though they were research animals in a conditioning setting, or forcing them into situations that ended up destabilizing them and triggering them. The FDA banned the use of the shock devices but that decision was overturned and one particular school in New Jersey still uses it! https://www.nbcnews.com/health/health-care/appeals-court-axes-fda-ban-electric-shock-disabled-n1273572 Many who have had this barbaric practice done to them never got justice against the perpetrators who used it on them under the guise of "treatment" and developed Complex PTSD that they struggle with the rest of their lives. All it takes is one bad apple to ruin one's trust in humanity.

Justice is very important, especially for people with autism, and it was important that the boy in this story had the support to see it through and that the facility was up-front about it and took swift action to remove the staff member instead of covering it up, because many kids didn't get that and as a result were left to feel alone, defeated, and angry.

I don't know why the makers of this film felt the need to put a disclaimer at the end saying that facilitated communication doesn't help everybody. One could say that nothing helps EVERYBODY, but of course that goes without saying. Even so, technology has come a long way since the movie was made and this type of teaching does help the vast majority of people that are initially non-verbal. It can make all the difference in the world and communication is key to opening doors that would otherwise remain closed in a society that is based on communication. There are now all sorts of computer programs to help people that did not exist when I was growing up in the 60s and 70s. My communication is way better in writing than it is spoken and I'm 60 years old now. I use my computer for all sorts of purposes now.

There are companies that hire autistic adults in some states for IT type positions, but not near enough of an array of vocational opportunities that make the necessary accommodations given that there are always some things an autistic person cannot change in how one does things.

I would be very interested to know how the boy featured in this story is doing now that he is grown up and what he's doing now. I hope they will do an update movie about him. He seemed to be quite intelligent despite being unable to speak with his mouth. Some people just need to do things differently and if others have the patience and compassion to meet them half-way the world will be better for it.

title_x: Complex; You could Almost Miss Significant Points if You Didn't Pay Close Attention
text:
Some reviewers seemed to see this movie as boring, but I think the slow pace was done on purpose and not bad writing nor bad acting. It was done to create a somber, cumbersome mood, and it succeeded at portraying the gravity of the situation.

Petra, I'm sure, had Asperger's. She was direct to the point of insensitivity, but it was clear she really didn't know how to interact with others and seemed unaware of how she sounded to others. She failed to understand jokes, and loved the only way she could which was mostly expressed mostly as sexual behavior, as she didn't fully understand attachment and developing a relationship on an emotional level.

The main character, the father, was somewhat devoid of emotion as well, so that could be what made them a believable couple.

The circumstances surrounding the reason for the child's birth made him on one hand feel unworthy, but on the other-hand he felt in the beginning an obligation to raise his child, even though he was completely unprepared. He wasn't a bad parent, just underestimated the amount of work and commitment involved in raising a child alone. He probably didn't expect his wife to die this soon, so was blind-sided when it happened and he found himself solely responsible for the care of his child. It seemed as though his wife did most of the care-giving until close to her death.

Although he may have conceived her as a means to save his wife's life, I think he did grow to genuinely love her and by the end wanted her.

Petra probably mailed the incriminating letter in hopes he would focus on her or out of anger that he had rejected her. The two seemed to take turns rejecting each other. Often provoking anger is a way that some couples attempt to combat apathy in the other person and remove emotional distance and unavailability even if they get a negative response.

The sister-in-law seemed intrusive and selfish even though she couched everything as being in the best interest of the child. She clearly had control issues and ulterior motives. Being a former judge, she knew the rules of custody and knew how to say the "right" things. However, the law was not on her side, and as the attorney advised him, she really had no legal standing to take his child, since he was providing a good and safe home and had done nothing sufficiently egregious to warrant having his parental rights stripped from him. There are lots of parents who are not the best, but also not dangerous to their children and not unfit. They take care of them well enough, and may even improve with practice.

It seemed as though she ultimately didn't push the issue, although if she'd been especially vindictive she could have resorted to illegal/unethical ways to win custody. I know from experience that that does happen when a family member covets someone else's child, and when it does happen it's very hard to reverse. I think she stopped short of that line and at some point realized it was not her place to meddle in the natural father's decision.

Things seemed to work out in the end. It took some getting used to; being a single father, but it was not insurmountable and he learned to adapt.

If one has ever had the misfortune of meeting a psychopath (or worse; having one in your family) the creepy energy you pick up on from them is unmistakable. Someone like Kevin is capable of playing the part of a normal person when it's to his advantage, lulling those around him into a false sense of security. What tends to happen is that some people are fooled by them and others are afraid to cross them, so they tend to move through life unscathed while leaving a trail of havoc wherever they go that people can't quite figure out. Many of those people never get caught at doing the numerous kinds of damage they do to others. For every school shooter there are many more in all sorts of positions of power who manage to fly under the radar and manipulate everyone to their advantage.

The mother in this story had alot of strength to remain in this small town after a public tragedy like that and with really zero support even from her husband. Just as others have said in their reviews, the writer was really effective at showing how isolated she was and trapped.

I wondered why her son left her alive and killed his father and sister. On one hand it seemed as though he may have been trying to hurt her the worst way he could, but on the other hand it may have been on some level he respected that she was aware of who and what he was and that she did try to hold him accountable and set limits, unlike his father who was always making excuses for him and unknowingly rewarding his bad behavior. Maybe also he sensed that if his father were the one he left alive that once aware of the magnitude of the situation his father would not come back to visit him in prison because he needed his denial and once that was stripped away by such a heinous crime any support would likely end immediately.

What a waste of a popular character. The so called "birds of prey" are barely in the movie, and when they are you wish this wasn't about them at all. Everything around them is really really bad, including the casting. I think they knew that by the fact that the movie focuses on Harley more than the titular Birds of Prey- whom no one cares about and after this movie no one ever will.
There are a few saving graces to this film, for me, that I think you could possibly enjoy. Margot Robbie is fantastic. I love her characterization of Harley Quinn. I hope this movie doesn't kill her ability to make more movies as her because she's very solid in the film. She continues to prove she gets the character more than one would expect, and is even expanding on it in ways that are totally fine (even if I would love to see what Harley in an actual Harlequin Outfit would look like in a live action context- it's not a big deal).
The writing in this film is all over the place. I think that's because Margot and a couple other actors, are finding ways to make this trash interesting (both Margot and Ewen are putting in a lot of work to try and save this movie). It helps that Margot is actually believable as a funny female lead. She pulls off some bad jokes in decent ways. While a lot of character choices make zero sense, and plot holes and other writing problems really drag the film waaaayyy down I want to emphasize that this is not the actors fault. At least in a couple cases.
As I mentioned the casting on the B players (why are the birds of prey B players in their own movie? What a bizarre choice to make) is really bad. This isn't helped by the awful writing. However, the costume design should be reprimanded as well. I think they spent their entire budget on Margot and Ewen's character choices and everyone else got the scraps. I don't know who is to blame for this. If Margot Robbie or Ewen McGregor knew they were doing this and said nothing then that's not cool, but if it's not something they were aware of then it's not really their fault. It's like two films smashed together, though. One with a budget, and another with no budget. That being said, even with that, none of the costumes make any sense. Whoever made Harley Quinn's outfits should be tied to a clock work orange chair and forced to watch various permutations of Harley Quinn and then when shown what she wears in this someone should shout NO! in their face. It's complete nonsense. It's like they hired someone and said "make all the wardrobe complete nonsense- no you don't have to look at a single comic book (or DC cartoon). It's not like DC movies are having real trouble right now or anything. Why look at the stuff people think works?"
Another good part of the film is they accidentally had a good fight choreographer (the one from John Wick 3- I'm sorry I forget his name) for SOME of the fight scenes. When those scenes come up, again, it's like your watching a different movie. A competent one. Then you see the fight scene at the end and wonder why they don't just get the fight choreographer from the Schumacher batman movies. At least they had a weird kind of style to them.
Why is Harley Quinns Mallet, when she finally gets it, so tiny and useless seeming? She uses a huge mallet, just give her a large mallet already! How hard is that? Why does she get a hyena (only one :( ) and then it's never used in any meaningful way? What was the point of introducing it if it's just gonna sit in her apartment and never do anything? This is just more proof of the incompetence helming this film. It's a shame it's mixed with high quality because that makes the really bad stuff harder to laugh at.
It's so bizarre, but there is some sense to it. I think this film had reshoots (I don't follow a lot of behind the scenes stuff- that dampens the fun of a movie) because they could see how bad the movie was turning out, but it was too late so they had to mix good stuff with terrible stuff. The least shocking thing to me would be if Harley wasn't originally in this and they reshot it to be about Harley Quinn. I'm not saying that happened, but it wouldn't surprise me if it did.
This could've been the female Deadpool. It certainly starts out feeling like that's what it wants to be, but it just doesn't have the balls (sorry, no pun intended there) to go there. Even in the most violent scenes they use glitter instead of blood. I would argue, this is actually a cool idea and could still work, but then you have the problem of this not actually being a Harley Quinn movie even though it is a Harley Quinn movie? So it's so disjointed and moves around in time a lot because the writing was so bad they had to try and fix it, but whoever did that was brought in later so they couldn't do a whole lot.
When I think about this movie it makes me sad. They had so much potential and they wasted all of it due to ineptitude and probably ego.
At least Ewen McGregor got to try something different here. It's not good, but it's different at least. There is fun stuff like that, but you may have to sift through the annoying little girl, or the bad birds of prey scenes to get to any of it.

text:
I'm a big fan of Nicholas Winding Refn (Bronson is an amazing movie- everyone already knows Drive is), and I know what turmoil (mostly inner) that he went through while making this. He was concerned about it's appeal, especially since so many people (as he perceived at the time anyway) expected so much of him now. I think that was all in his head, and he'll be fine, but it puts a lot of what this film is into perspective for me as well as my feelings for it.
This is not Nicholas Winding Refn's best work (I love his name, I'll write it over and over- sorry for how repetitive that may be to read), but it is probably his most visually striking film to date. Nicholas Winding Refn has always had a very specific style (inspired by Kubrick mostly- I know). He is quickly becoming an auteur at least in the sense that you will always know when you spot a film he made. His style is so striking most of the time, especially but not limited to Drive, that people have been inspired to copy the way he uses this style in many different mediums at this point.
Now look- this is not at all a bad film. In fact it may be brilliant in it's own way, but it may be a difficult one for a casual film viewer (or even casual film buff) to sit through because of it's problems as well as it's his most minimalist film. It's not wholly a silent film, but there is very little dialogue as well so you never really know much about any character in the film. This both makes it a fascinating study in how well Nicholas Winding Ren's visual style holds a film (very well for the most part in my opinion) and a test in ones ability to maintain interest when nothing is happening or a scene is being dragged out with a slow motion shot for the 5th time in the movie.
Again it's not because the movie is completely bad, but Nicholas Winding Refn struggled so much to write the script for this film (which, what there is of it, is all over the place) that very little actually happens.
There is a plot. It's super bizarre (as you tend to expect from Nicholas Winding Refn). It's a very thin one, though, and it's told in a fascinating way. It makes the film almost an experiment in the way a story can be told.
I don't like to synopsis a film in a review (that's the laziest, and most horrible way to review a story of any kind), but I will say that I am unclear who the hero of this story is supposed to be and who the villain is. I have my own ideas, but the film isn't really one to tell you who to care about. That seems entirely intentional, and in a lot of ways I like this- the way it was told (in this particular film) is fun to ponder and think about. Next to the striking visuals I think I enjoyed thinking about the film as I watched it more than anything.
Anyway, I really can't recommend this film to just anyone because it is a little difficult to sit through it. Even though it is short there is very little to grasp or see here. While the visuals are gorgeous (and they are), and there are some good performances, very little actually happens and Nicholas Winding Refn overuses slow motion scenes to drag the film to it's credits.
I was also concerned by the way it seemed like Nicholas Winding Refn is mostly just ripping his own films off in this film. Look, yes he did invent a lot of the techniques that he uses (as well as being inspired by Kubrick, I know), but when you do them the same way again in a different film, with different context, it loses a lot because it wasn't designed for that moment. It becomes stale and meaningless.
I don't want to critique Nicholas Winding Refn too harshly. I am certain he knows the problems with this film, and he labored on this one a lot (for which I know he did because of the documentary his wife made while he was making this film). I just think it's important to know what you're getting into. Major Nicholas Winding Refn fans may enjoy this film for it's interesting concepts, and overall gorgeous visuals, but it's hard to say that anyone else will like it because it's very flawed despite some (possibly unintentional) moments of genius.

text:
A wonderful documentary showing how dedicated people can get laws enacted and/or changed to protect the voiceless. Being a long time volunteer at our county shelter and involved with rescue for over 15 years, the laws are horribly lacking when it comes to protecting animals. We as a country are on a slow (too slow in my eyes) road in the right direction. I have fostered several dogs that were victims of cruelty and the dogs are definitely the better beings. They just love unconditionally and forgive humans for what was done to them.

I usually cannot watch animal films but this was so well done that I found my interest in how the heroes went about fighting for Gucci and Susie within the court system enough to override the anger towards the perpetrators. We have to get involved and change our society to protect not just the voiceless animals but the children, elderly, the ones that cannot protect themselves. Too many times one hears first an animal then a person are victims of the sociopaths that commit crimes like this. Thank you for a wonderfully done film that is getting the word out.

title_x: Pretty Dull F&F Like All The Rest Of Them
text: F&F films make so much money that I always wonder what it is I have missed by skipping the latest one. I then break down, pay the streaming fee and suffer for the next two hours or so. This time around I think I have finally learned my lesson. All the F&F films, including especially F9, are dull as they come. There isn't much of a story at all. The dialogue is plain awful. I am sick of cars and the more gas-guzzling they are, the more they make me want to puke. Don't people know it? Electric cars dance circles around cars with internal combustion engines. Internal combustion is a spectacle of ancient history now. Internal combustion has given us never-ending fires and year-round smoke inhalation. They have brought the end of the world ever closer. There was a time when I was a muscle car enthusiast myself and helped a friend three-duce his hand-me-down 67 Pontiac GTO. I owned a Dodge Duster 383 for a time, but nowadays I just want to know how we can make mobility harmless but keep it still fun. We are succeeding on that score. However, even if F&F decided to go all electric, that would only solve a tiny part of its problem. The much bigger part of its problem is its phony baloney family of seemingly former foster home runaway kids and high school dropouts who have been stuck in adolescence and just refuse to grow up. There isn't even a hint that these characters are ever growing to grow up or just stop being so absolutely dull. Why so many people pay money to see these terribly uninspired F&F films and extremely laggard stories is a very sad tale about the state of our world.

text:
Let me start by saying the acting was excellent and that I could definitely live with more John David Washington action spy movies.

But that's the end of the positive things I have to say about this movie.

They didn't bother to write a character arc for anyone that would allow a watcher to emotionally connect with any of the characters. This movie tells you about things more often than it shows them to you. An early torture scene is blocked by passing trained so we're supposed to identify with why the protagonist would choose suicide but since he's fine every time we actually see him it falls extremely flat.

I think this movie relies on the audience to not understand it well enough for their brains to give up, suspend disbelief, and just enjoy the action. It often overshadows complex dialogue with loud sound effects and having actors ramble long speeches in low monotones. I believe they did that on purpose so that you won't pay too much attention to what is actually said and just think "now is a serious moment" and "this exposition is clever"

But if, like me, you actually paid close attention to the endless exposition the plot twists turn out to be incredibly predictable which, added to the nonsense premise, made how seriously it took itself irritating.

And then you have dialogue like
“Have faith.”
“Faith?”
“Whatever you want to call it.”
“What do you call it?”
...he just called it faith. Did the writers not have time to replace all the filler dialogue?

This movie didn’t make any sense but covered that up by trying to make it feel smart to enjoy it. It wasn't very good and I'm glad I didn't watch it in a theater.

I appreciated the candor of "Mister" in confronting his drug-using mother. Including an Asian-American as a co-main character, too, also shows that other minority groups experience devastating experiences in our American ghettos. The mom, Jennifer Hudson, played her drug-mom part well, and I was glad the story of, basically, living on the street, with reference to the two children, ended with her rehabilitation. Mister, the main character, is a master of facial expressions reflecting emotions, as also is his partner, Pete (a Korean). Most of these emotional facial expressions were reflecting fear, sadness, disappointment and despair. Mister was street wise and Pete was innocent and trusting, almost like a faithful puppy to Mister, but with good cause which we don't find out why until later in the movie. And how these two children interacted with each other was also amazing. Both wanted what their respective moms couldn't give them: love and guidance by example. At the very end, Mister's mother, played by Jennifer Hudson, was redeemed via rehabilitation, and Mister, though wary, it seems, accepted her as his "new" mom.

title_x: I can't get enough of Castle
text:
I got hooked on this show a few months ago. Kind of goofy, but still a good crime drama with romantic tension in the air. What more can you ask?

I tend to be a TV snob, watching mostly documentaries and movies that have some artistic or social quality. That doesn't mean I'm too good for some basic, fun to watch entertainment, and this does the job. Castle's character is a successful millionaire, but just goofy and vulnerable enough, plus ok looking but not over the top good looking to keep him from seeming somewhat believable. Beckett's character is so good looking, confident, and successful that it's hard to imagine her ever seeing anything in Castle, but the chemistry is undeniable and they use that to tease the viewer into coming back episode after episode and season after season.

The plots are, for the most part, original and refreshing, but far enough from reality that you have to just go along and stop reminding yourself that these things would never happen in real life and that nobody would survive the predicaments that confront the characters on each episode. I am former law enforcement and know that none of the things on this should would ever happen, but again ... I don't care. Sometimes you just need to escape reality for an hour or two.

One of the real surprises for me has been Susan Sullivan. After watching her as the uptight Kitty Montgomery on Dharma and Greg, I couldn't have imagined her playing any other character. In Castle, she plays Martha - Castle’s whacky mother, who is an over-the-top, past her prime actress, with a multitude of character flaws, but who is nonetheless lovable.

text:
This is a review of all three seasons of Lucky Man. These episodes were all created by the genius of Stan Lee.
He even makes a couple of very brief appearances in two of the seasons just like Hitchcock used to do in his movies.
This is a police procedural but with some supernatural overtones involving a lucky bracelet or two. The problem is that if one extends luck in one pursuit it may cause negative consequences someplace else for the person wearing the bracelet. James Nesbitt is the star and he portrays the goal directed take no prisoners type of approach that we see in some police detectives. He gets the bad guy but may break the rules to get him (or her). Each of the three seasons is different but with the common theme of the bracelets and luck and bad luck. The supporting players are all excellent. Another supporting player was the scenery of London. Some of the aerial shots were magnificent. An enduring presence besides Nesbitt is Siena Guillory who plays Eve who we could call the female lead or at least one of the them. Many of the characters are very complex including one from the second season who made the show.
Finally, Since Mr. Lee is involved in Marvel Comics the series seems to have a hyper reality to it which is almost cartoon like in the same way as Trueblood was as a series. Sure, since is is somewhat supernatural some things jump the shark a bit but it is still all fun and consistent with the storyline.
description: ['James Nesbitt returns as Detective Inspector Harry Clayton in the third season of the fan-favorite crime drama from comic book legend Stan Lee. In search of answers about his lucky bracelet, Harry journeys to Hong Kong, where he encounters some members of the underworld who are after more than just his lucky charm.']

text: I can't decide whether this new genre of gay films is modeled on the screwball comedies of the '30s or just well written romance comedies from the '80s and '90s, but whatever they're doing, it's working. For me, anyway. I think what I'm sensing in terms of the screwball comedies (Hepburn and Spencer Tracy or Cary Grant) is the comfort with gay characters and the willingness to present them as regular folks, like anyone else. And of course, there's the really tender angle characteristic of the more recent romance comedies (Richard Gere, Hugh Grant). If you want unrelenting camp, don't stop here. If you want things blowing up and people dying violent deaths right and left, don't stop here. But, if you want a romantic story well told, this is it. (And Big Eden, Redwoods, What Happens Next, even Coffee Date…) I'm discovering that it's no coincidence that several of my favorites feature Matthew Montgomery.

I kept watching. The other supporting characters were fun (can't give it away).

The lead (Annabella Sciorra)deserved to be the lead. You know the lead character has a big job and does carry the brunt of the story, does most of the action and if they aren't convincing and interesting to watch and if we're not caring about them or pulling for them then we lose interest fast and flip the switch. But she carried it. And we do pull for her. And we do feel her pain and confusion. And we want to shake her and scream, "wake up" this is just a bad phase you're in. Or, "snap out of it!" like in Moonstruck. The character's inability to not initially see that a temporary feeling - even a longer temporary state of feeling -does NOT have to be acted on makes for a tense situation, a tense life. You feel what she did. What her character did. What the writer wrote was to happen. You should watch it and experience this phase, this chapter with her acknowledging the strangeness and difficulty of it. And you understand her rebelling against it and wanting it to go away because you might want to do the same. The story will grab you and take you on a life ride and heart of hearts, it'll make you desperate for her to accept it, hold it and live it to its fullest.
