I found the docu slow and of limited interest. Not that the period and war are not interesting. It is that this focuses too narrowly. IMO
description: ['At a gallery in Croatia, Jeff Bowden walked in front of a photograph taken during the war in Kosovo of a boy wearing a ragged blue sweater. "It felt like a car wreck in my chest," Bowden told a friend. The image was captured by deceased French photojournalist, Alexandra Boulat. Years later, still haunted by the photograph, Bowden sets out to find the boy with the help of a grizzled wartime fixer.']

text: “Who Killed Lt Van Dorn?” asks a legitimate question and deserves an honest answer. There won’t be one. Some have said that when you sign on the dotted line, you agree to accept what comes your way. While there is truth in that, it doesn’t take away the question of equipment. One way the US evaluates foreign military capabilities is by assessing the state of their combat equipment. So, shouldn’t ours be the best possible? When you read the incredible prices our government pays for top end ‘toys’, is it so unreasonable to ask why an existing asset isn’t maintained? I think I was wrong above; there is an answer to the question: the lion’s share goes to the military industrial complex. President Eisenhour warned us.
description: ['The grieving widow of a Navy helicopter pilot spurs an investigation that reveals the American military’s inner workings and a long history of its failings.']

text: This is a good nature documentary with plenty of information, good camera work/natural vistas, and a good narrator voice. Nature lovers, give it a try.
description: ['Namaqualand - the setting for an annual wildlife fairytale. Every year in the narrow window between the cold wet winter and scorchingly-hot, dry summer, flowers of all description bloom in carpets of colors unimaginable, insects of equal diversity pollinate and predate, and everything form meerkats to ostriches breed.']

text: I couldn't get past the thirty minute mark. I wanted to. Christian mysticism is interesting to me, but this was boring. Talking heads tend to bore me, and talking heads who think they know so much about someone long dead turn me off. How can they know, authoritatively, all they profess to know. If it is from her writings, then let's hear the relevant portions of the writings and not your opinions dressed up as knowledge.
title_y: The Unruly Mystic: Saint Hildegard of Bingen
description: ['Discover why many consider Saint Hildegard of Bingen to be the patron saint of creativity and her continued impact today. This 11th century abbess became famous as a Christian Mystic and visionary, as well as a musical composer and writer, and whose medicine is still practiced in Europe today.']

text: Have you ever wanted to witness real determination, persistence and courage? Watch this documentary. It will alternately sadden and enrage you, then it will give you a glimpse of the power of those three things above as well as the power of hope and love. Highly recommended.
description: ["In Ethiopia's Omo valley, children are being killed under an ancient tradition known as mingi. One young tribesman strives for change through education and adopting the cursed children. But challenging tribal superstition isn't easy and as he battles to save lives, things are not all that they seem. This clever film will stay with you long after you watch it."]

text: I don't know of another movie with such an incredible cast. Love Sally Field in everything she does - what a superb actor. The others are also far above the run-of-the-mill actors. Great scenes with layered emotional content: love, friendship, anger, hurt, pain, redemption. Great movie.
description: ["A wedding is about to take place. The bride is Shelby (Julia Roberts), and her mother, M'Lynn (Sally Field), would do anything for her. Dolly Parton plays Truvy, the owner of the beauty parlor. They provide each other with friendship."]

text: The Kent State documentary was well done. It did a good job of showing the schism within the US during those years. The archival footage and interviews gave a good sense of the hostility and maybe even hatred that existed between the two camps. I’m glad to have lived during those years. I have great memories of the late fifties and early sixties, but there were problems in our culture. Did Vietnam cause them? I don’t think so. I think Vietnam just gave a focal point to issues which would have arisen even if there had not been a Vietnam to blame it on. The hippie movement and other utopian undertakings would have happened anyway. The Manson family would have found a rock to come out from under anyway. There would have been a heightened level of angst even if no one had ever heard of Vietnam, IMO.
description: ["In May 1970, four students were shot dead at Kent State. The mayhem that followed has been called the most divisive moment in American history since the Civil War. From college campuses, to the jungles of Cambodia, to the Nixon White House, The Day the '60s Died takes us back into that turbulent spring 45 years ago."]

text: I got fifteen minutes in and was bored to death. The documentary is amateurishly done and the subject is not sympathetic or relatable. Skip this one.
description: ['"Falling Up" is a powerful story of the transformation that occurs for Johnny Popp, a Vietnam Veteran from Michigan who is a crack addict on the streets of "Skid Row" in downtown Los Angeles.']

text: The US Navy on D-day, 1944. I had read before about the destroyers coming in as close as they could and taking out machine gun nests, etc. that had the troops pinned down. The target pool for this documentary will be pretty shallow, made up of old swabbies and war/history buffs. It’s not badly done. Some of the first-person accounts were moving. My only complaint was that the narrator’s voice was almost irritating. He sounded like a skit newscaster on SNL. If you’re a Navy veteran, you might be interested.
description: ['Operation Neptune-Overlord began the largest amphibious landing assault in the history of WWII and was critical to the success of the Allied invasion.']

text: “The baby died that night.” I got drawn into the stories of the mothers and babies, and when that baby died, a tear rose up. I’m not embarrassed; I’m human. For the queasy, “Sister” shows scenes of actual Caesarian Section and of real childbirth. The documentary was quite informative and poignant. There is a need. I would help if I knew how. Yes. It’s time for me to do some research.
description: ["Madam Bwa has never been formally trained, yet she's delivered over 12,000 babies. She works on filthy floors and in crowded slums, from Ethiopia to Cambodia to Haiti, while her mothers-to-be eat dirt to survive. In this beautiful doc the difficulties of childbirth are laid bare, and the strategies to improve Third World maternal health and mortality rates are explored with an affecting clarity."]

text: I know this is a parody of 1950s scifi flicks, but it isn’t funny. It might have made it as a short, maybe twenty minutes or so, but at ninety minutes, it’s way too long. In some shots where some of the actors are not speaking or acting, they actually seem to be bored. I think you can skip this one without missing anything. I wish I had skipped it.
description: ['This hilarious, award-winning (and loving) tribute to 1950s B-grade horror flicks concerns a college professor, his sexy assistant and five neato teens as they discover that atomic waste has transformed a World War II soldier into a hideous monster. As the nuclear beastie creates havoc throughout their small town of Mukwonago, Wisconsin, our heroes try to save the day.']

text:
Korean with English subtitles, which sometimes go by too quickly to read -- stop and back up.
I got 25 minutes in and had to let it go. It was silly and frivolous, but I didn't find it comedic. There were good production values, but the acting was too over the top. I know it was supposed to be over the top, but this was too exaggerated for me.
description: ['In this offbeat comedy, debt collector Mo Fellini and neurotic accountant Zha Xiaodao are brought together by a nefarious guru. When the unlikely duo comes across 3.2 million yuan, they have to put their heads together and find a way out of a sticky situation.']

text: The movie shows its age. The cinematography was good due to the lovely settings. The story was predictable and the acting only average, especially among the extra kids. It’s a feel-good movie, a coming of age story about love and loss. It shares some kinship with Old Yeller and The Yearling, but not as well done as either of those.
description: ['A boy’s yearning for two Redbone Hound dogs, which his parents can’t afford during the desolate times of the Depression in the Ozarks, is the setting for this truly triumphant film.']

text: “Memories of a Penitent Heart” is a ‘family reveal’ documentary. That is, it reveals a family’s histories, expectations, failings, animosities, etc. It failed to draw me in. At about the twenty minute mark I was bored and I did a lot of skipping. I’m not sure I understand one’s desire to expose family secrets; I don’t get the point. Does the title reveal the underlying reason? Whose is the penitent heart? Perhaps there was repentance and a purging of guilt for the filmmaker and/or for other members of the family. If so, then one must say it was worth the effort.
description: ["Twenty-five years after Miguel died of AIDS, his niece tracks down his estranged lover and cracks open a Pandora's box of unresolved family drama."]

text:
I think “The Field” is a sci/fi movie dealing with interdimensional travel. That’s what I got. I have to say before going any further: Ben, get a different pair of pants. He wears the same pair for three fourths of the movie. Sorry. I had to get that off my chest.
Anyway, some say this is a horror movie, but I don’t see the horror aspect. There are a few pseudo-scary moments, but that’s not what the story is about. Admittedly the story is all over the place. Lydia, Ben’s wife, found photos of some sort of cult rituals carried out on the grounds, but cult rituals play no part in the movie or in the resolution of the story. Also, there’s no explanation for all the negative reactions of the town’s residents, and the sheriff is over the edge, which brings me to another point. Early on the sheriff is on Ben’s case, so Ben knows what he’s up against. Why doesn’t Ben, the electronics whiz, carry a recording device so that when the sheriff threatens his life, he has something to play to state or federal authorities? And why doesn’t Ben just play the camera footage of the ‘bright light’ as soon as the sheriff starts asking about Edith and Lydia? And what was special about that field that allows interdimensional travel? The closeup of the baby at the end, WTH? There was nothing in the movie that will lead us to any conclusion, except the director had a wild hair at the end of the filming. There are just too many unanswered questions. On the positive, there is no cursing or sex or nudity, so that’s something.
description: ['A long-empty farmstead holds secret worlds, accidentally unlocked by an amateur photographer and his wife.']

text: Tom Papa’s special was mostly family friendly. There are a few PG-13 moments, but it was mostly clean and didn't rely on sexual jokes. He was occasionally humorous, but there were no laugh out loud segments for me. There were a few light chuckle moments, but not enough to warrant many stars. He did have good timing and facial expressions, so I think he could be funny. I suspect that this was not his best work.
description: ['Famously upbeat comedian Tom Papa delivers a stand-up performance that includes his observations on the perils of raising daughters, and more!']

text: Excellent, very family friendly, three-part documentary. Wonderful landscapes and seascapes, great shots of various land, air and sea creatures and their interactions with other creatures and with the challenging environs around them. Great narrative voice which does not bore or lull to sleep. Highly recommended.
description: ['"Wild North" moves through three biotopes; vast forests, rugged coastline and interior highlands shaped by shifting ice ages. These landscapes resonate deep within the Scandinavian soul, floating into view like illustrations from shared fairy tales. And so do the iconic animal species that feature strongly in each programme, stirring ancestral memories and reaffirming our connection with the land.']

text: “Alien Trespass” is a fun throwback to 1950s sci/fi movies of cosmic wanders and monsters bent on devouring humanity. It was an enjoyable hour plus. The plot was predictable, the monsters were elementary (was that even CGI?) and the acting was delightfully hammy though sometimes just hammy. The scenery was nice, the settings were period appropriate and the clothing was, I think, true to the times. It’s not a bad way to spend a little time if you just want to be amused, but don’t expect anything of Oscar-worthiness.
description: ['After crash landing on the outskirts of a desert town, an alien enlists the help of a waitress to recapture a monster that has escaped the wreck.']

text: UFOTV’s “Crop Circles” is an interesting dip into the waters of our ignorance concerning this phenomenon. There are various theories and little proof of any of them. I found the ‘interdimensional shadows’ theory thought-provoking. The least attractive theory to me was the theory of the superior intelligence playing with us, teasing us, instructing us. Is this pass/fail? Where’s the manual? Shouldn’t there be some sort of manual? I suspect that the only enlightenment most will find here will be in the theory that they already subscribe to. One severe negative to this film is the fact that music often overwhelms the spoken words, but one might just turn the sound off and enjoy the pictures of the circles. They are remarkable, beautiful.
title_y: UFOTV Presents Crop Circles Quest for Truth
description: ["Signs indicate that some form of non-human intelligence is communication with us ... What's the message? Academy Award nominated documentary filmmaker William Gazecki offers a compelling and provocative look at the mysterious phenomenon of Crop Circles."]

text:
English subtitled.
I understand a little Spanish, so I listened closely to the dialog. Some seemed Spanish and some Portuguese and some maybe even Guarani. Whatever the language(s) you’ll have to pay attention to the subtitles. Despite some rave reviews I had to stop halfway through. I don’t enjoy dark filming and much of it was at night. I get it that it is a modern-day Romeo and Juliet. I was aware of the war during the 1860s in which tiny Paraguay stood against Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay, and their male population was decimated. I read once years ago that only ten percent of Paraguayan males survived that war. I don’t know if that’s accurate, but I get that there would be residual animosity on opposite sides of the river. I just couldn’t get into the movie; I found the acting wooden and amateurish. I wanted to like it, but it never hooked me and halfway through I don’t care about any of the characters.
title_y: Don't Swallow My Heart, Alligator Girl!
description: ['Joca, a Brazilian boy of 13, is in love with Basano La Tatuada, an indigenous Paraguayan girl living on the border between the two countries, marked by the waters of the Rio Apa. He will do anything to win her love. Official Selection of the 2017 Sundance Film Festival.']

text:
Portuguese with English subtitles.
Who does the Amazon belong to? Does it belong to the state or the mining/timber interests? Does it belong to the indigenous tribes who’ve lived there for millennia, or does it belong to the world? Cases have been made for each.
Interesting and valuable documentary looking at the lives of the last three members of an Amazonian tribe, two of whom still live in the jungle, in a reserve maintained just for them. The only piece of background was about four women who were shot and killed sometime in the remembered past. I would have liked a little more of the history of the tribe. The documentary is done well enough considering how hard it must be to film in an environment like the Amazon. My one real complaint is that it could have been significantly shorter without losing any of its impact. For example, there is a two- or three-minute segment of the two indigenous men talking in their tongue with no translation. What benefit was that? And there were a surprisingly large number of closeups of the characters, in total probably five minutes or more. Again, what benefit? The hour and twenty-one minutes run time could easily have been cut to one hour.
description: ["The last two surviving members of the Piripkura people, a nomadic tribe in the Mato Grasso region of Brazil, struggle to maintain their indigenous way of life amidst the region's massive deforestation. Living deep in the rain forest, Pakyî and Tamandua live off the land relying on a machete, an ax, and a torch lit in 1998."]

text:
Not family friendly due to language.
This movie reminded me of “The Thirteenth Warrior”, though not as good. My limited exposure to Swedish movies has been of quality. This one is the same. I enjoyed the movie. The production values were good: setting, wardrobe, and the lovely landscapes. Some of the translations were clumsy, making me wonder if the dialog had been translated correctly. For example, I don’t know why the curse was attached to the girl. It was probably revealed in the dialog but ‘lost in translation’. There was conflict between the girl’s family and some others, but we don’t know why. And I had some issues with the writing. After the first skirmish, our group escapes across the river and their shields are shown floating away on the current. No seasoned warrior would have been so easily relieved of his shield; it’s part of his clothing, in a sense. Then we get a scene of ancient waterboarding. At least we now know where it came from. Joking of course. And back to seasoned warriors, what idiot would follow his foe into a dark, narrow cave, at night? To make it worse, they’re carrying lanterns, giving any archer a clear shot. Still I enjoyed the movie and recommend it as a good way to pass an afternoon.
description: ['In 11th Century Sweden, a missionary went missing in the dark forests that separated the North from the South. The King sent out a group of soldiers to find the responsible bandits. What they found was something worse. Much worse. (Please note this film is in Swedish with English subtitles.)']

text: “Wild North Sea” was fascinating. Beautiful scenes, landscapes and seascapes, and camera work. The narrator had a good voice, not one that would put you to sleep. And it was just fact rich, but not like in a lecture. Highly recommended.
title_y: Wild North Sea: Footage Never Seen Before
description: ["This film presents the North Sea's diverse fauna and visits the people who live on its shores. Breathtaking landscapes, unique underwater footage and beautiful aerials bring this land to life."]

text:
If you find the following offensive, I apologize. It isn’t intended to offend.
These spokesmen/women seem to be very much products of their generation. In them we see the progress of New Age philosophy. I found it interesting that people can speak with such authority about subjects that have no scientific foundation. Don’t get me wrong; I believe that the body dies and the soul passes into another realm, but I have no proof; it is only my belief. I hope they are right, but there is a niggling in my spirit brought on by the attitude of elitism among these ‘enlightened’ that puts them above the masses, an attitude of “Look at us. See how evolved we are.” I found that off putting because understanding of life’s deep mysteries, in my opinion, should be accompanied by an equal measure of humility. I saw none of that. How can intimacy with the divine (personal spirit guides/spirit teachers) not pierce the heart and bend the knee?
title_y: Life to AfterLife: I Died, Now What
description: ['Craig McMahon asks leading spiritual experts about the afterlife. What happens when we die, where do we go, and what is important to know about the afterlife.']

text: I’ve always liked “Charade”. I guess it might be because I like Grant and Hepburn and I like them together. Some reviewers cited a lack of chemistry between the two. I respectfully disagree. In fact, I read once that they tried to get Hepburn to play opposite him in “Father Goose” (another good Grant movie), but she wasn’t available. As much as I like this movie, I always wondered about some writing choices. It seems to me that the likely assumption would be that Charles’ murderer made off with the money, but of course then there’d be no movie. And when Regina says, “Carson Dyle is dead” and “Carson Dyle had no brother” why didn’t the Grant character ask how she knew that? I know it’s for the movie’s sake, but it seems to take a little away, IMO. One last point, come on Amazon. This isn’t an “uncut version”, as is indicted in the blurb. A little more honesty would be nice.
title_y: Charade - Cary Grant, Audrey Hepburn, Uncut Suspense Classic!
description: ["After Regina Lampert (Audrey Hepburn) falls for the dashing Peter Joshua (Cary Grant) on a skiing holiday in the French Alps, she discovers upon her return to Paris that her husband was murdered. Soon, she and Peter are giving chase to three of her late husband's World War II cronies, who are after a fortune the quartet stole while behind enemy lines. But why does Peter keep changing his name?"]

text: First of all, let me say that I love Shirley Maclaine’s work; I think that she is a fabulous actress, just fabulous. She was terrific in Terms of Endearment and Steel Magnolias. But I got a sense from this bio (which is more of an autobio), from her words and from her projection of herself that Shirley Maclaine is very much a child of her age. I doubt that she would like to be thus typecast, but there it is. You can clearly see the strong focus on individualism and the irreverence for traditional values that were some of the powerfully attractive themes of the 1960s and you can also see the New Ageism of the 1970s and 80s and following. She seems to see herself as specially chosen by the cosmos. For example, she makes the observation over and over that things just fell in line for her throughout her career. There’s no problem on the surface. It’s just that such an outlook can make one feel separate and apart, better than, mere mortals. I could be wrong, and certainly mean no offense.
title_y: Hollywood Collection: Shirley Maclaine: Kicking Up Her Heels
description: ['Shirley MacLaine was the product of a strict middle-class background from which she and her brother, the future actor Warren Beatty, escaped into the fantasy world of show-biz. Her ballet training and her long-legged pixie charm led to rapid success on Broadway in musical comedy.']

text:
Not family friendly due to F word.
I’ve read the books, seen the American version of book one and all three movies in Swedish with English subtitles. That was much superior to this dubbed version which was only moderately interesting and which cut out huge portions of the original Swedish version which had a lot more about The Section, about Gunnar Bjork’s murder, and which fleshed out some of the characters more fully than this one. My advice is: avoid this one. Watch the Swedish movies with subtitles. They’re more engaging and don’t leave so much of the story untold.
title_y: The Girl Who Kicked The Hornet's Nest (English Dubbed)
description: ["THE GIRL WHO KICKED THE HORNET'S NEST is the third and final film adaptation of the best-selling Millennium trilogy written by the late Swedish author, Stieg Larsson (The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo and The Girl Who Played With Fire). In this last installment, Lisbeth Salander (Noomi Rapace) lies in critical condition, a bullet wound to her head, in the intensive care unit of a Swedish city hospital. She's fighting for her life in more ways than one: if and when she recovers, she'll be taken back to Stockholm to stand trial for three murders. With the help of her friend, journalist Mikael Blomkvist (Michael Nyqvist), she will not only have to prove her innocence, but also identify and denounce those in authority who have allowed the vulnerable, like herself, to suffer abuse and violence. And, on her own, she will plot revenge - against the man who tried to kill her, and the corrupt government institutions that very nearly destroyed her life. THE GIRL WHO KICKED THE HORNET'S NEST brings back Noomi Rapace in the starring role of the pierced and tattooed genius computer hacker Lisbeth Salander, Michael Nyqvist as Mikael Blomkvist, the crusading journalist and publisher of the magazine Millennium, and Lena Endre (Erika Berger) the editor of the magazine and Blomkvist's occasional lover."]

text:
Korean with English subtitles.
There’s one shot of the F word on a vehicle of some sort. I don’t remember any others.
“Horror Stories 3” is a weird movie, or weird movies, for it is three separate and seemingly unrelated stories. But I guess they are related since someone (editor/writer/producer) put them together for this film. The message, as I got it, is that humans are a contagion, an cancerous epidemic upon the planet and the sooner we’re gone, the better. It’s bleak, but that’s what I got. The three stories were awash with dark camera shots which seem to be requisite now days. I don’t get the need by filmmakers to make the shots so difficult to see, but there are far too many of them for it to be accidental. The films show good production values and fair acting. In as much as the are three separate stories, the actors vary from story to story, and some are better than others, as you’d expect. On technical merit alone, the movie may be worth four stars, but jeez it’s so dark and depressing, I can’t give it four. Three is the best I can do, and with a very lukewarm recommendation. Watch it if you want to be depressed. I need to find something sweet and funny now.
description: ['When a woman escapes to Mars, on the run of her life, she explores a world of human fear with a group of cyborgs.']

text: Wonderful old movie. Some things didn't jive - like very young Grace Kelly and considerably older Gary Cooper. Should have been closer in age. And a little more action would have been good, not that the anticipation, heightened by the regular shots of the clock, wasn't well used. Highly recommended.
description: ['Classic western tale of a lawman whose retirement plans go awry when a revenge-seeking gunman and his gang arrive in town - will anyone stand with the marshal? Winner of four Oscars, including Gary Cooper for Best Actor.']

text:
Not family friendly due to language, nudity and rape scenes.
I didn’t see Saturday Night Fever when it came out. I learned tonight that I had not missed one thing. Lousy, disjointed plot - what was the point of the brother/priest or ex-priest? An awful show. Terribly misogynistic, racist, sexist and promoted racial stereotypes, and worse than that it promoted a culture of rape. Terrible. I don’t know how this ever became a classic. The dancing and the music were good, but not nearly good enough to make up for all those other faults. Depressing. You should skip this one.
description: ['Brooklyn teenager Tony Manero rules the dance floor on Saturday nights. His confident swagger and fluid hips have made him the champion of Disco, which helps him cope with the harsh realities of growing up.']

text: I watched for twenty minutes or so and couldn’t continue. The landscapes were wonderful, but there’s no joy in watching someone walk and talk into a camera. If you're a hiker, it may for you, but it wasn't my cup of tea.
title_y: Figure it Out on the Hayduke Trail
description: ["The Hayduke Trail is an 800-mile route across Utah and Arizona. It's one of the most challenging hikes in America and most of the time there is no trail. The southwest is canyon country and it's extremely remote. Figure it Out is about more than just hiking though, it explains how we can use the lessons learned in the wilderness to live happier and more resilient lives."]

text:
In my opinion this movie is not for younger children, and perhaps not for young teenagers either. There is some profanity and some recreations of murder victims as they were found.
This is a sober retelling of horrendous acts committed by a serial killer in the USSR before and after perestroika. More than that, it is a tale of determination and resilience in the face of roadblocks constantly set in the way. The film had good cinematography and good story flow, a commendable accomplishment since the actions depicted occurred over a dozen years or so. Donald Sutherland gave his usual solid performance. I found Stephen Rea’s performance to be a little stiff. I don’t want to be unfair or ungenerous, because he was portraying a man ridden by an unknown, savage serial murderer of children, and ridden as well by a system that demanded results yet gave little material assistance for most of those years. Perhaps he was spot on, it’s just that I have trouble visualizing a man who so very, very rarely smiled, even though he had a supportive spouse and lovely children. This film is probably mostly for those who enjoy TV shows like FBI files or CSI and the like.
description: ['A Russian police detective faces almost insurmountable odds in his search for the most savage serial killer of modern times.']

text:
Enduring love – that’s the theme of “Lovely, Still”. It is a wonderful motion picture experience but be warned: there are raw edges. Everything works together in this movie to bring you, the viewer, an uplifting experience. But before it lifts you up, it will first throw you to the ground. Again, be warned: the story is disturbing to some. I’m a senior myself and saw things familiar, and it is terribly sad, but in the end, it helps you up again.
Superb cinematography, story, script, dialog, settings…everything is superb. And we dare not forget the actors. Ellen Burstyn and Martin Landau are as commanding as ever I saw either. This is, quite simply, just an exquisite movie experience. I cannot recommend this highly enough. With this rave review some may question the motivation. I have nothing to do with any aspect of the film or the actors. Oh, be sure to have some tissues handy.
description: ["Lonely in life and love, Robert Malone (Martin Landau) braves the wintry snow on the walk from his job at the grocery store to his home, only to discover a stranger (Ellen Burstyn) in his house. What begins as an awkward encounter quickly blossoms into what appears to be a new chance for romance, and the elderly couple's love affair takes us on a heartfelt journey that reveals an unexpected twist."]

text: Hanna was better the second time. It’s a nicely told story, a little slow at times and seemingly off track briefly here and there. The cinematography was quite good, especially the early scenes in the wintery forest. The story held together well, and there was no superfluous dialog. The acting was the best aspect of the movie. Ms. Blanchett, always wonderful, did not disappoint, except in the future she should pass on doing a southern accent. Why a southern accent anyway? Mr. Bana was the best I’ve seen him, and Ms. Ronan developed her character very well. I’m sure she will make her mark on the industry. Recommended.
description: ['A sixteen-year-old girl who was raised by her father to be the perfect assassin is dispatched on a mission across Europe, tracked by a ruthless intelligence agent and her operatives.']

text: There is enough information to allow the viewer to feel like he/she knows a little more about one segment of ancient history. Surely what was presented, however, was only the tip of the iceberg. As for the documentary, itself, I found the narrator easy to listen to. The sites were quite stark and beautiful in a sharp, rigorous way. The film quality wasn’t great, and the blurb does mention 1998, but not sure of filming date. Recommended to lovers of history, archaeology, epistemology and other similar disciplines.
description: ["The gigantic geoglyphics engraved in the soil of Pampa never cease to intrigue explorers and archeologists. In the autumn of '98, two passionate archeologists, Giuseppe Orefici and Egla Barone, decided to undertake an impressive excavation campaign on the huge site of Cacuachi in an attempt to solve the mysteries of this little-known civilization."]

text: “Legally Blond” is just a fun movie. I suspect that’s all it set out to be. Yes, it’s cliched, yes is predictable, yes it’s corny, yes it’s fluffy. But it’s also fun. We all like to cheer the underdog on, even when we know she’s going to win in the end. Ms. Witherspoon is quite attractive, but I believe she carried the movie on her talent and not her looks. After you’ve watched all those thriller, killer, spiller movie, take a break with something that’s fun just to be fun.
description: ['Reese Witherspoon stars as Elle Woods, a sorority queen who rallies all her resources to follow her ex to law school, determined to win him back. While there Elle must wage the battle of her life: for her guy, herself and all blondes.']

text:

What is was NOT was edgy even though a show with a gay couple as part of the regular cast was expected to be. So why did it all seem so comfortable right out of the gate?
The reason is that you've met them before :
1) in the comics they were Mutt and Jeff - a big guy and little guy who quarrel but are inseparable
2) in the movies they were Laurel and Hardy and later Abbot and Costello
3) and in TV sitcoms they were the Skipper and Gilligan - the "little buddy"
The couple in MF were not so different in the way they were drawn. We recognized them right away and felt comfortable with them. The writers never tried to have them do anything that would make us uncomfortable and so we felt at home and part of the family from day one.
Other relationships became more problematic with time. Gloria and Jay were also a familiar cliche with the older rich guy and young girl. But as the seasons wore on it became a bit uncomfortable for all of us and when it was announced that a character would die in the last season many thought it would be Jay to put the relationship out of its misery.
They didn't seem to know what to do with "Lily" and shot much of one episode with her behind a door, and gave her few lines/scenes generally - eventually ending her arc as a family member who is a bit odd, but everyone ignores of chooses to find eccentric.
Hope that something comes online soon that is as well-written.

title_x: Will it End with a Bang or a Whimper ?
text:
Why it was Great:

The show had a following like no other because it solved the enduring sitcom problem of having a show about adults, but still letting them act like children( that is still being entertaining). The show FRIENDS tried to solve it by having the characters loosely employed and shooting most of the scenes in a coffee shop at a indiscernible time of day- so we wouldn't notice that they never worked.

BBT solved the problem by having highly intellectual people with serious jobs who never lost their childlike wonder while they studied the real universe. This made them interesting and entertaining at once, and provided for a large number of plot lines that had never been used before.

But we loved BBT not because of the plots, but because of the WORLD that the characters created and inhabited inhabited:
--The world of Dungeons and Dragons, Comicon, Paintball, Fun with Flags, Star Wars/Trek, sci-fi movies, and online gaming.
--But also the world of CERN, Richard Feynman, George Smoot, and Stephen Hawking

The writers also paid attention to character development and it is interesting to see that character growth was made in small but necessary steps, although occasionally abrupt changes were made to fit long-term goals. Stewart was actually a confident artist who dated Penny before they made him ( too much of a) joke. Bernadette was mousy before they decided Howard needed a domineering woman to replace his mother.

Writers say that the true hero of a story is the one who undergoes the most change. If so it could be argued that Sheldon deserves the title, while Penny (who's lack of development is demonstrated by her lack of a last name) remains largely unchanged into the start of season 12 without any real interests and expressing no goals.

Since the writers are scrambling to complete an originally projected 3-season character arc in 1 season we are likely to see Raj married ( I still think he should have ended up with the "vet named Evett" from an earlier season) and Leonard and Penny will hopefully grow out of what has become a depressingly flat relationship with the same tired jokes about her settling for him, drinking too much, and not wanting kids.

And this is now it should end :

The gang boarding a plane to go see Sheldon receive his Nobel Prize. As the others buckle in Sheldon points to a seat and says, "thats my spot".

Oh, and maybe Howard can use his MIT Masters in engineering to fix the elevator ??

May 17 UPDATE - BBT ended last night with a 2 part finale and I think I was pretty close with my predictions. I'm glad that Penny is shown embracing becoming a mom. I did think they'd reveal her last name, but then even the strangest name might have been anticlimactic. I thought they should have made her made her "Penny Einstein" of something ironic.
And I answered my own question - for me it ended not with a Bang or a Whimper, but with a tear, I'll miss them and I'm sorry that it ended too soon.

As Winne the Pooh said, " I would have liked it to to go on for while longer

text: SPOILERS: The first 3 seasons probably deserve 5 stars. Brooke is great as Deb in Jane's body. The series is pretty successful in winding us through her life now as Jane while asking for a lot of wiggle room for the fantasy, including the idea that a "guardian angel" is only there for one reason: to prevent new Jane from exposing who she really is to Grayson (which the writers seem completely ignorant of later when Grayson feels betrayed by the secret but neither Jane or Stacy offer this game-changing explanation) . This series is for everyone who loves romantic comedy. April Bowlby was perfect as the ditzy bff in the first few seasons, who is probably best known as the unlikely trophy wife of Allen Harper. Also included were entertaining musical skits that were clever and fun.  But later those musicals were completely omitted along with trying to make Stacey seem more grown up and almost shy compared to the fun, dumb but loving bff we were introduced to (no fault of April's) .... and that really sums up what happened to the remaining seasons: the show becomes too entrenched in the coiffed law-firm persona and less concerned with making us laugh. Josh as Jay Parker is believable as the egotistical, smart elect controlling partner but completely unbelievable as the romantic playboy. Jackson as Grayson was never that believable but we definitely wanted HIM and Jane to get together, so when Jane gives him the cold shoulder when he finally admits his feelings it's a big let down. That's your soul mate, girl, wtf? Then the show had him die and resurrect in the body of a killer.... By then the guardian angel -- successfully played by Feldman -- had been replaced by 2 other guardian angels who were completely unbelievable (although Deeley was fun and nice eye-candy). I'm old-school in the idea that if an actor leaves a show his character should simply be taken over by another actor, not do away with the character and bring in a new one, especially not with a supporting part like Fred. They should have replaced Jane's mom with a different actress, Elaine was one of the least likeable characters, played by Faith Prince, a Broadway actress, who bares a striking resemblance to Grandpa in the Munsters. And of all the pet peeves I might have, the show was remiss in bringing Jane back for a couple of shows while failing to make her look like old-Jane but instead she now had the same hair and makeup as new-Jane. Really guys? But Drop Dead Diva is a great series to a point, worth the watch. If they had stuck to the original formula it might have continued for more seasons. A truly novel show that is mostly entertaining with fun and personal drama and some pretty unbelievable but well-played court room antics and outcomes.

text:
I have to give this movie high marks for sustaining the tension throughout without taking recourse to the panoply of shopworn cliches. The film deals with (at least) two very difficult subjects: family and memory. Contested memories, especially those involving loved ones, are part of the lives of many people. Still, it's a difficult subject to broach, all the more so in film and theater. Judd Hirsch isn't a stranger to this idiom -- there were points it was like he was reprising "Ordinary People," or so it struck me. The de facto protagonist does a competent job, and the family dynamic is convincing both in terms of acting and dialog.

This film reminds me of plays by Ibsen and Pinter. By a stretch, you might add to that Edward Albee. Actually, if you've seen the film adaptation of "Who's Afraid of Virginia Wolf" and enjoyed it, you might like this, notwithstanding that it's not quite in the same class.

text:
This is really a 3.5.

This is a fairly deep movie, fairly complex for it's being taciturn (which is understandable given the subject). I add "fairly" to qualify it, because it strikes me that for all the thought put into it, there is something lacking.

Despite a few points where it's decidedly on the nose, it holds together through an inexorable progression to the end. And, man, inexorable is the key.

Where it succeeds is in gritty realism. And to that point, it might rely a little too much on gritty realism. It's worth noting that there is a nonlinear aspect to the film that doesn't so much add to the suspense as it does break up the relentless drive. Btw, if you find yourself identifying too closely with the protagonist or other characters, please seek help immediately. ;)

This film is way more about ambiance, and the dynamics of human relations, than it is about individual character development at an internal level. I mean, it works, but you're still watching characters, not people. I'd be curious to know what wound up on the cutting room floor, to this last point.

This is a good movie, not a great one. Not one you'll likely remember in late 2018. This isn't Memento, nor is it American History X, nor by any stretch Goodfellas. It reminds me somewhat of Drive, which I think is superior (if you'd allow for the comparison), but that I also felt fell short of its promise. Flip side, there's only so much cinematic flamboyance of the sort of, say, Oceans 11 etc. I personally can take.

Last, I want to say that this is an original film, but there's a retro quality to it I can't pin down. Something like Dog Day Afternoon stylistically, but unlike the latter, I don't think the actors here were given too much latitude for expression intentionally. With that said, I think this was the point, to leave much to viewer's imagination. Not a date flick, not at all. lol. Trust me on this. Word!

title_x: Bowing to the Sacred Art of Nature
text: Like all artists Andy Goldsworthy has the ability to see beyond what is easily seen to and help us to see what we cannot. Through the simplist of shapes and repetitive forms he invites us to rethink our relationship with the natural world. I believe, he is asking us to bow to the might, majesty, and ineffable beauty, inherent in the forms of nature. One small example is a scene where he is lying down on stone area in the city. Beautiful old dark, small, beautifully placed stones which form a walkway, or a standing area. So there he is lying down, spread eagle, arms apart from his sides and legs spead as well. It is drizzling lightly. In a few moments he sits up and leaps from the spot where he was laying. The stones around him are darker from the rain, but the spot he has protected, is still lighter and contains the outline of his shape. In minutes as the rain continues, the dry stones fade away, as they become wet. He has the playful heart of a child, held powerfully within the brave heart of a man of vision. THis is a rare opportunity to see, something you have never seen before, to see the world as you know it with fresh eyes and and to be invited to see inside the soul of a compassionate artist who adores nature and being playfully serious in all of his work. There is so much more to his art involving the moving of large boulders or covering steps in leaves to form a completely straight line going up or down a set of stone steps... This is one of those rare glimpses into seeing something unique that approaches the sacred, but demands nothing more from you than your attention and an open heart. Offer it and you will be richly rewarded.

text: I haven't read the book, but after reading some reviews online we decided to watch this on Valentines Day as our romantic movie night flick. I suspect that the film is trying to convey a lot more than what actually comes across, as it leaves the viewer wondering about many elements of the film. It is still a good watch, however the movie isn't so much a romantic film as it is a drama. The ending is very "Pride and Prejudice" and whilst it does end on a happy note it still leaves a somewhat depressed and melancholy impression. The heroin Bathsheba wasted her life by making bad choices, pushing away those who cared about her, and ruined two men's lives through her inability to commit and return their love. She comes across as self-centered, bratty and indecisive throughout most of the film, leaving the viewer with a poor impression of her and making it difficult to empathize with her plight. Her character is portrayed as being a desirable and beautiful woman, however the actress portraying Bathsheba is in actuality rather plain and average. Overall, good acting and great story, but it could have been done better. Watch it once and decide for yourself.

text:
The whole concept is fascinating. I believe some of the abilities of the Alphas cross over into spiritualism rather than super-natural ability, especially when the individual loses control of his abilities. I felt that the second season became rather dark and bled into the occult. For example, why did Dr. Rosen's dead daughter appear?

The success of the Stargate series and the Eureka series is that the audience knew that they were always going to be in a comfort zone of discipline, properly applied principles, personal strengths and a team working with good leadership. The Alphas team is breaking out of standards of appropriate behavior in some cases. Human frailty is certainly normal and acceptable, but it seems to be becoming the theme rather than the exception. Escapism entertainment should always leave the audience feeling better about themselves for having shared the experience with the characters. I hope the Alphas can get back to that formula. The audience cares about these people. Give them a great reputation to live up to.

text: I've recently watched Platoon for the first time in years and it holds up very well. Charlie Sheen's confronting tour of duty in a vicious war in a very foreign land in a fractured army is searing stuff. The war violence and language is suitably graphic - the brutal reality of men under extreme pressure is clear. There are some very confronting scenes, particularly the platoon’s descent into a Vietnamese village (but also, almost into Hell) where atrocities take place. By the end, the idealistic Sheen is thoroughly disillusioned. The battle scenes are very effectively shot; mistakes cost lives, people go mad. The other powerful aspect is the duel between the sargents played by Berringer and Dafoe. In some ways this was the perfect film about the Vietnam War. Some of the images are more powerful than those taken during the war itself. 4 1/2 stars
description: ['The film probes the psyche of the young soldiers who fought in Vietnam. Their camaraderie, their struggle for survival amid terrifying violence and madness of combat. title_x: A fascinating take on an astonishing time.
text: This is an excellent black comedy of a particularly unfunny subject – Josef Stalin. I had thought that Stalin’s murderous ways were generally consigned to the 1930s and 40s but here it is clear purges and execution lists were still all the rage right up to his ‘none-to-soon’ death. This is made very clear as his immediate lieutenants strive to stay alive, while conniving to undo each other. Ironically, the diabolical system imposed by Stalin, serendipitously comes home to bite the man himself. There are many moments of dark humour before a necessary (and appropriate shift in tone) sees the despicable Beria get his comeuppance. There are some liberties with actual time lines but it hangs together very well. Indeed, it is a clever script that makes the most of its extremely well chosen cast. ‘The Death of Stalin’ is a slightly bizarre but very entertaining film that tells an astonishing story.

text:
Witness for the Prosecution – Dastardly Murder

Tyrone Power is in a fix. He’s charged with murder and the evidence is stacked against him. The only thing he has going for him is his wife. But she’s German and it’s just after WW2 and the jury doesn’t like her one bit. Only his imminent barrister, sees some hope.

This film is based on the Agatha Christie novel. Accordingly, there are twists aplenty. Please note it is a film of its time, so it features the British social strata with its courtroom pomp, societal formalities, servants and the death penalty. It’s also in black and white.

Now, I found it quite fascinating but I watched it with a room full of fifteen year olds, who were not so engaged. Sure some of the characters seemed completely archaic but it worked well enough for me. The various twists were well delivered and I was genuinely surprised at some developments. text:
If you’ve seen Season 1, you know the score. Aliens have invaded Earth and appear unstoppable. The focus here is on a group of survivors who are engaged in ongoing resistance. They are the 2nd Mass’, a fairly rag-tag assembly reminiscent of the revolutionary militias. Their story is told predominately through Tom Mason and his three sons. The aliens are more complicated than usual and have the capacity to enslave humans with a harness device. Following a very successful counterattack by the humans, the previous season is concluded by the aliens taking Mason aboard one of their ships to ‘try and understand’ us.

It’s been several months and quite a bit has happened before Mason is able to rejoin the regiment. After being in alien hands, his return is greeted with some suspicion. Indeed, there are quite a lot of trust issues given the number and scope of human relationships and the pressure they are all under. The war is not going well but a very interesting opportunity presents itself.

I feel this series is getting stronger. There are quite a few fascinating developments. The aliens are becoming ever more interesting and nuanced. This really reflects well on the writers. There are some really great ideas coming forward and the foundation is laid for an intriguing series 3. Sure, some conversations are still in clichés but there is grittier action and confronting developments. There are new characters and the exits of others, which is all to the good! It is still a family show but not for younger children. Recommended 3 1/2 stars.

text: The first astronauts on Mars are driven from their research by a massive storm. They flee the planet but leave Matt Damon behind. This works though as the number of people needed to run a space program is pretty extensive. What is interesting is the common will to do the right thing. It’s good to see people working together on something so complex. There are some surprises here. Damon’s story remains central though. Showing him ‘sciencing the hell’ out of things to give him a chance to live. There are successes and failures. Altogether it is an inspiring (if pretty improbable) effort that keeps your attention. text:
As most people are saying, the opening sequence is astounding! It is visual and vicious. Unfortunately, the focused choices made there are not so evident in the rest of the film. Frankly, too much happens. The makers try to fit in action sufficient for 1 ½ films. There are several unnecessary scenes that do nothing but add to the body count. The tight story evident in Casino Royale is discarded in favour of explosions and shifting locations to yet another continent. The motivations of the lead villain are unclear and his ‘connections’ to earlier events completely unbelievable.

Too the good, Q, M etc get to do a bit more but the chance to bring in, even notionally, other 00s is lost. There are some funny lines and clever gadgets of course and the female lead is stunning, of course but predictability reigns. The suspension of belief is a prerequisite in Bond films but too much is asked here. My frustration stems largely from the excellent first and largely good third installments of Craig’s stint. With a more disciplined approach to the script and the sense of freshness evident previously, this film could have been on a par with those. Overall, it is entertaining, particularly early on but in this case more is not more…..

text:
This is my favourite Clint Eastwood Western after The Outlaw Josey Wales. Eastwood is again the man with no name, who rides into a situation where impoverished gold panners are being forced off their claims by LaHood, the local major landholder. He is ruthless towards them and in a clear nod to the rise of environmental concerns, a destroyer of the land with his industrial mining methods. He has a number of thugs and an odious son to do the nasty work. The arrival of Eastwood, seemingly a preacher, gives rise to one of my favourite Eastwood scenes. He saves co-star Hull and deliciously deals out some just deserts to the thugs, enabling him to take a place with the downtrodden panhandlers. This sets him against LaHood and leads to a climactic gunfight conclusion. Some very old scores are settled.

The plot is a basic one, seen before in Westerns. Offsetting this, there is intriguing colour with some religious symbolism and the enchanting Sydney Penny as the maiden Megan. Eastwood's character is a mystery, almost a ghost. Preacher or not, he is supernaturally deadly. This is the classic Western and classic Eastwood. A hero confronts the bad guy and saves the innocents. A very satisfying film on that basis.

text:
The story is set in an apocalyptic America, thirty years after a devastating war. Washington plays the lead who is wandering `west' to deliver a book of great power. He is a fearsome warrior who deals very violently with the assortment of cannibalistic thugs who roam the roads. The crux of the story is his encounter with Gary Oldman, who is trying to re-establish civilization, though his methods aren't terribly civilized. Oldman wants the book and Washington refuses. More violence.

The basic story is not new. Many stories have explored the dim days following the collapse of order and the scavenging needed to survive. Human principles are disgarded by almost everyone and cannibalism is the new fast food. The fresh element here is religion. Washington has a purpose greater than personal survival and he must defy the forces that seek to exploit it. Even so, it is at best only average fair. The fight scenes aren't too special and if you think about it too much, there are some perplexing plot issues.

Personally I welcomed the religious element, though I suspect it's not developed sufficiently for the faithful, and it's probably still too much for those who are resistant. It was kinda undone for me anyway in the last scene. The gore and sexual elements are reasonably limited, though there's a bit of language at times (THAT word will apparently outlive anything!). So overall sound enough entertainment but nothing special.

text:
An inspiring film, perhaps the best I’ve seen on Amazon Prime and definitely the best I’ve seen in years. A far cry from the woke, politically correct drivel Amazon promotes and creates left and right. As another reviewer said, it’s so refreshing to see characters who are willing to make extreme sacrifices for principles of a greater good. Lessons such as these are sadly rare these days, and people (old and particularly young) need to see them so they might learn from them. The film is also valuable for its stark portrayal of what life was like in the Soviet Union. In my lifetime, I’ve come across many brainwashed, naive Americans who have a romantic notion of communism, with no idea of the harsh realities of the perpetual distrust, corruption, and betrayal it breeds.

The film is remarkably clean, free from endless profanity, violence, and immorality; another refreshing change from most of the choices on Amazon Prime. I was deeply moved by the acting and the true story that is convincingly told. Do yourself a favor and watch it, and have your children or some young friends join you.

Enough real history to make it almost like a documentary. Perfect production and acting all around. The periods are replicated in exact detail, all the way down to the music, cars, props, sets and decor. Thought it was fascinating how it brought historical figures and events that I had read about to life: Al Capone,  “Lucky” Luciano,  Arnold Rothstein, Johnny Torrio, George Remus ... a dozen more. Even Joe Kennedy. I'm fascinated by organized crime and especially it's role in prohibition. There is some serious violence but it's not gratuitous or overly graphic. But even the most violent of the characters (Al Capone) showed moments of tenderness and compassion. As real as it could be. Everything clicked like clockwork. The final season was a perfect wrap-up. No complaints at all from me. If all shows were this well done I would hardly ever extricate myself from my TV.

title_x: Guess who's Coming To Dinner and Guess who's Leaving as Someone Else.
text:
I watched this at my sister's house and both my sister and her daughter liked the movie. I liked it as well, but I was a bit more critical of the movie as it reminded me of a 1950's B-rated horror movie. Now, if people are not familiar with B rated movies, they are all not bad. They just need a little improvement. The movie was extremely boring in the beginning as the plot slowly developed, and the action evolved. The director made an attempt to use symbolism by the scene where the car hits the deer, and the deer dies. The police officer shows up to add an element of racial animosity, to cement this concept in the viewer's mind. This is a foreshadowing event that is tied in with the scene in the basement where Chris is tied up in the chair and he looks up to see a trophy deer displayed on the wall. This is a metaphor that basically sums up the movie, that black people were being used as trophies by the aging wealthy Southern elite who hijack their bodies through brain surgery and hypnosis to prolong their lives. A single family is responsible for luring black men and women into this situation and making a living on doing this surgery. There are many slight connotations and metaphors here, such as the ability of one race controlling the other race through surgery and hypnosis, basically a form of racism in that you are using black bodies to prolong the life of elite upper-class white people.
The ending of the movie gives the viewer and blood and guts of your standard horror movie, with Chris lashing out and killing all of those involved in this devious plot, with the rage that has built up inside him. The scene was Chris takes the deer head and kills the surgeon says it all, that he will not be used as a trophy. Very unique, but something that is very basic that you learn in film class on day one. So Chris takes care of the situation and dispatches everyone in this whole bloody mess, with Granpa making the statement with his suicide, that he's through with this life as well. His TSA friend adds an element of comic relief, especially when he arrives at the end of the movie when all of the action is done, just like the TSA. One could argue that this movie has subtle racial overtones in the sense that trying to make someone conform to your beliefs and lifestyle is a form of racism. So, a very good attempt as a director and picked up by Universal movies is a great thing, since Universal is the king of horror movies, perhaps we will see more of Mr. Peele, who needs a lot of improvement regardless of all of the high scores. Just like in life, you have to earn scores on your own merits through hard work, and not be given them from others too freely.

text:
This is a dystopian film based in the future (2027) in England. The story line is to get a pregnant girl to the Human Project in a world where infertility has left humans without children, and possible human extinction. The movie is set in a world where the rich have isolated themselves from the rest of the world, were pills and video games rule their day. The poor are left to survive in a world with pollution, dirty water, filthy air, and lack of food, surrounded by intense overpopulation, immigration, anarchy and basic tribalism. Terrorism hits home as the main character, Clive Owen, (Theo) just misses an explosion at a coffee shop on his way to work. The police have militarized and use extensive force to round up immigrants and deport them, sometimes in a brutal manner. As the world reels from the weight of these problems, Britain soldiers on. When the youngest person, Baby Diego, dies at the hands of a fanatic, the world mourns his death, the weight of hopelessness settles in and creates an atmosphere of gloom and no possible future for humanity. The pregnant girl happens to be an immigrant which adds a twist of irony to the film, since the English government is rounding up and deporting immigrants in a brutal and efficient manner. The movie is filmed with dark colors with lots of gray tones surrounded by an atmosphere of damp and wet surroundings.
An activist group lures Theo into getting transient papers to move this pregnant girl to the Human Project, the last bastion of hope for the human race since governments can no longer be trusted, and the activists don't trust one another, and the proverbial uprising is always around the corner, never fully getting a start, as the government and the police squash any hope of resolving societies ills. But through all of the chaos, Theo manages to get this pregnant girl to her rendezvous by a buoy in the ocean. Some of the main ideas in this movie are relevant in today's world, especially England. The themes of immigration, terrorism, militarized police forces, government surveillance, anarchy, and activism are salient issues found throughout the civilized world. Overpopulation, pollution, Global Climate change, are featured in the movie as well. But out of the fog comes the boat, Tomorrow, to rescue the pregnant girl.
The movie never asks why the human race has stopped reproducing, an issue about the science that once helped humanity, is now lost in the hopelessness that pervades the landscape. This movie has a strong message about issues that are going on in today's world. What is evident is that the groups of people in the movie have assembled into tribes, for lack of a better word. The government and the police versus the anarchists and the activists. The activists rying to get the baby to the Human Project and fight with each other. The terrorists fighting the police forces, and the immigrants herding animals into their living quarters. All great civilizations have one thing in common - they were organized, designed and built by the group of people with the dominant gene. They were also undermined through immigration, when the lesser gene moved into their cities, and began to mix their cultures, leading to the fall of that society. A perfect example is Rome. Whether you want to believe it or not, society is a racial construct.

text: A very good movie with minor scientific inaccuracies such as the wind storm (Mars has 1 % the atmosphere as earth), no protection from solar and cosmic radiation (Mars's magnetic field is dead), and water production (the soil is frozen, no need for rocket fuel production).  Of course, all movies are based on some form of drama, such as man against man, or man against nature.  Of course, this is really about man using science to stay alive, while battling one of the most inhospitable places for humans - space. The pressure on Mars is 150 that of earth (14.7 psi), and the pressure on Mars would kill a human in approximately one minute, when fully exposed.  It was interesting to see the pressure, temperature, and oxygen icons displayed on his instruments.  Very spaceadelic, indeed. I also noticed how China helped the NASA in this film, but this is inaccurate, due to obvious security concerns, and from a personal nature, their technology is horrible, and they still produce junk, and I think it would hamper our rescue efforts if indeed this was the case. Another aspect of the movie that was right on, was the structure of government, with bureaucrats running the show, like the Alpha Male, (Jeff Daniels - excellent performance) bowing to his superiors and so on down the line.  I also liked the young astrodynamics student, with no social skills, trying to explain his theory for the rescue attempt. text:
This was two-thirds of a great movie, but my god what a two-thirds! The media satire and the romantic comedy elements are where this was strongest. The expedition to find the lost brother didn't add too much for me except make this at least 20 minutes longer than it had to be, although they did find a way to tie it back to the opening scenes. Gable and Loy were obviously great. Walter Connolly was a hoot, although I could have used a little more of him. Where the film doesn't age as well is in its approach to primitive cultures, although this would have been par for the course when this was made. It was more than a little ironic to have an isolated South American tribe's ritual being filmed as entertainment and then have them (in the context of the film) react to watching film clips as if they were dark magic. Overall, while a bit overlong --particularly dragging in the middle-- there was plenty of madcap banter and surprisingly au courante digs at #FakeNews. Most of the journalists staging newsreels for public consumption would not have been out of place as CNN field reporters covering the first Iraq War.

Random aside: There was a throwaway line about "Dromedary Cigarettes." Oblique reference to Camels?

text:
"The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much." (James 5:16b)
"Verily I say unto you, except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven." (Matthew 18:3)

Those two Bible verses perfectly encapsulate what this film is all about, in a way that the 1990's remake (which I grew up with) was not. More generally, it is a good example of the difference between old-school and modern Disney. Once upon a time, Disney stood for and provided wholesome entertainment that promoted family values and moral uplift. Now they just seek to provide entertainment for its own sake (or other things which I don't need to elaborate). And it's not new. This has been going on for at least 30 years. All that aside, I found this film to be outstanding. It is simple, yes, and the conclusion is telegraphed from the very beginning, but it understands that a child's sense of wonder and ease of belief are laudable things that should be protected instead of dismissed out of hand or reasoned away. It also shows the possibility and power of redemption. All of these are reason enough for me to return to this again instead of the remake, entertaining as it may be.

text: As the last of the Astaire/Rogers films (and the only one in color), this was always going to be bittersweet. Never again will I be able to watch these gems for the first time. They have been able to transport me to another world in a way that few other films can, and for that I will always be grateful. The plot this time, different from the others (except Vernon and Irene Castle) has the duo already being married, falling out of love, and finding each other again, which seemed very appropriate for them at this stage in their careers. I don't think one should read too much into this metatextually, but the parallels are still there. For me, the best numbers were 'My One and Only Highland Fling' and 'They Can't Take That Away from Me'; the former for its elegant simplicity and "cute" factor; the latter for its lush romantic quality, recalling the best of their 1930's output. In terms of the whole body of work, it's somewhere in the middle, but I'd be lying if I said I didn't have a lovely time. And before I forget, while Astaire and Rogers were the main course, Oscar Levant was a tasy side dish.

text: Much like real life, this docuseries starts out great but fumbles the finish. There was so much about Cosby's early career that I had never heard before, and which actually deepened my respect for him in some ways, having known him mostly for his eponymous 80's sitcom and Kids Say the Darnedest Things. All of the interviews with survivors also felt important, if a little hard to stomach. Where it fails, in my estimation, is in what larger message it wants us to leave with. Discussions about the corrupting effect of power, America's fraught racial past, etc. are important issues that need to be reckoned with, and in some ways, we are doing that. The question that never seems to cross people's minds is just how much we are still reaping the fruits of the sexual revolution in terms of what kind of behavior we tolerate as socially acceptable, irrespective of the circumstances. Until we are able to directly confront questions of sexual morality and its effect on culture, stories like Cosby's will continue to need to be told. We need to talk about Cosby, yes, but there are much deeper things that should be explored as well.

text: I've been a little hesitant to keep up with every new release this year for a couple of reasons. First, there are so many older movies that I haven't seen yet. And second, there hasn't been much this year so far that really grabbed my attention. I have to say that I wasn't that drawn to this one based on its trailer and marketing, but after having seen it I'm glad I gave it a chance. The story is about is simple as one can be, and doesn't really need recounting. Where this film really shines is in its pitch-perfect execution. Every beat is played just right. The soundtrack was on point. Even the editing and cinematography, though clearly done in a more modern vein, was extremely appropriate to the material and tone they were going for. It's only 91 minutes and not one was wasted. It also has a great, sardonic sense of humor. Although this will most clearly appeal to action fans, I think that has broad enough appeal for a wider audience, helped in no small part by Bob Odenkirk. If you're on the fence, just go ahead and see it. You will not be disappointed.
description: ['After failing to fight for his family during a robbery, an unassuming father calls on skills from his hidden past to become a lethal vigilante blazing a wild ride to revenge.']

text: I will confess that I know next to nothing about Fred Hampton and the Black Panther Party. That being said, films like this rarely set out to be objective or unbiased. As is clear from the title, JUDAS AND THE BLACK MESSIAH wears its politics on its sleeve. It has a point of view, and I can understand and appreciate that. That being said, there really was no narrative drive. People talked, things happened, but there was little sense of urgency or creeping doom. There were good performances, particularly by the two leads, and a few conversations that do a better job at polemic through subtlety than the sloganeering and rallies. What the FBI did to the Black Panthers (and many other "subversive" groups) was pretty horrible, and yet I find myself wondering whether or not Fred Hampton was a person worth lionizing in the way this film attempts, not unlike the many attempts of the media nowadays to turn the latest victim of a police-involved shooting into a martyr but leaving out the context of why they were in that situation to begin with. Overall, I will say that this film was never boring, yet oddly tame considering the explosive potential of the real-life source material. On a more positive note, I loved the soundtrack, which was very evocative and earthy.
description: ["Bill O'Neal infiltrates the Black Panther Party per FBI Agent Mitchell and J. Edgar Hoover. As Party Chairman Fred Hampton ascends, falling for a fellow revolutionary en route, a battle wages for O’Neal’s soul."]

title_x: "I've got the best dais, the yuuugest entertainers. Believe me!" (if only...)
text: If anyone deserves a good roasting, it would be Donald Trump. There are only two factors which make this comedy special not as funny as it could have been: 1) They did it too early; just think if they'd decided to roast him AFTER he lost this election in a landslide, not to mention all of the many outrageous things he's said and done over the course of the campaign; and 2) They didn't go far enough. With the exception of a few zingers, the dais handled him with kid gloves, you know, the kind that Donald Trump wears. From a big-picture perspective, the roast was funny and I laughed a fair amount. There was only one true bomb, courtesy of Mike "The Situation" Sorrentino, one of the no-talent hacks from the Jersey Shore. Of course, maybe it's fitting that a failed comedian come from one of the many places where Trump had a failed business. Who knows? For my money, fortunately not much of it, the best routines were by Anthony Jeselnik (?) and Snoop Dogg, who acquitted himself quite nicely in a performance format for which he's generally not known. If you're one of the many people checking this out a second time now that Trump's threat to run for President has become reality, you might find some laughter here. However, your best bet would just be to follow the news as he continually provides fodder for jokes much funnier than what you'll find here.
