title_x: Sandler does a great job going against type but the Safdie brothers’ manic story fails him.
text:
I went into seeing Uncut Gems with very high hopes after hearing about all the great reviews. Adam Sandler’s comedies are generally slammed by critics, but I almost always find myself liking them. Billy Madison and Happy Gilmore are excellent.

In Uncut Gems, Sandler plays Howard Ratner, a crooked Manhattan jeweler, degenerate gambler and failing husband (and boyfriend to the woman he’s cheating on his wife with). With those traits, it obvious that Ratner is really a dislikeable guy. But Sandler does a nice job making this dislikeable guy somewhat likable. This character obviously goes against type for Sandler and he does a nice job pulling it off.

The other actors in the movie are generally very good. Idina Menzel is excellent portraying Howard’s wife who is in the midst of making the final decision to divorce him. Julia Fox is also good as Howard’s immature and promiscuous girlfriend. Eric Bogasian is also good as Howard’s (loan shark, bookie?) brother in-law, Arno, who Howard owes a lot of money to throughout the movie.

The story, which is pretty simple, gets very convoluted with the way the directors, the Safdie brothers, chose to tell it. Howard owes lots of money to Arno. He’s set up an auction for a long sought after Uncut Gem (a rock containing numerous valuable black opals) that he’s finally acquired from Ethiopian miners after almost two years. Howard believes the gem is worth a million dollars, more than enough to pay off Arno. But, Howard is up against the clock, because the collectors that work for Arno give him deadlines that are before the auction. Into Howard’s store walks in Kevin Garnett (playing himself and is actually pretty good). Garnett was led to the store by Demany (LaKeith Stanfield) who brings athletes to Howard’s store for a commission on what they buy. For some reason, Howard shows Garnett the gem. Upon touching the gem and looking into it, Garnett feels a mystical connection to it and feels that he needs it for luck in the upcoming playoff series with the 76ers (the movie takes place in 2012). Oddly enough, Howard is convinced to lend Garnett the rock with Garnett’s championship ring left behind with Howard for collateral. I won’t keep going with the plot, but Howard uses the ring to get some cash to spin into bets (based on Garnett’s and the Celtics performance) etc. which leads to many confrontations with Arno’s goons.

I had heard a lot of praise for the Safdie brothers work...although I’d never seen any of their other movies. I have to say, I’m not impressed. The story was a mess with ancillary characters thrown in to give a vibe of the New York diamond district and the types of people Howard deals with (and two times). Most of these characters just convoluted the story and took attention away from the real plot. I know they did it on purpose, because they wanted to show that Howard has his hands in everything and goes a mile a minute. But this forced hectic pace was too much for me. The Safdie brothers are no Quentin Tarantino, that’s for sure. The choice of music was absolutely horrendous. It pretty much ruined a couple of decent scenes, including the opening. They mixed in some kind of New Age music that didn’t fit in with what I was watching on the screen (at least for me).

I’ll stay away from spoilers. The ending of the movie is tense, but not in a good way. It is overdrawn out and unsatisfying. It’s funny, I wonder if this movie would have been better served as a short miniseries on Netflix. Half hour doses may have been easier to take and would have allowed the story to unfold a little better. Of course I say this while thinking the MOVIE was a half hour too long.

To sum it up, Sandler is very good (but in no way should he be mentioned in a best actor category that should include Joaquin Phoenix for Joker). The other actors are all generally good as well. But the story of the degenerate gambler, spiraling out of control was messy, tedious and eventually left me shifting in my seat for it to be over. If the messiness was deliberate, then the directors need a few more movies to master their craft because they aren’t nailing it and they did a disservice to the talented actors cast in the movie. One person in the theater walked out mid-way through. Two people behind me said “that movie was horrible” as the credit rolled.

I’m usually the one saying ignore bad reviews from critics because many times I find myself in disagreement. I don’t like writing bad reviews of people’s work, I know it’s art...but man, this one bothered me. Rotten Tomatoes critics score as of today, 92% favorable. Audience score, 52% rotten. I think the audience got this one right.

title_x: A satisfying, albeit not perfect, ending to a 42 year old saga. NO SPOILERS.
text:
I’ve seen Rise of Skywalker (ROS) twice since it opened. Both on IMAX screens. As with many blockbusters, I find I enjoy the movie more on the second viewing. I guess with the anticipation gone, I focus on the movie a little more the second time around. ROS was no exception. I truly had a FUN experience watching this concluding installment to the 9 episode saga. I’ve seen all of the Star Wars movies in person during their original theaterical screenings. Nothing, obviously, compares to the awe I had as a kid watching A New Hope for the first time in 1977. Nothing like it had ever been made before. ROS didn’t give me that sense of “never been seen before awe”, but it did keep me interested and entertained throughout the entire movie.

It appears as though ROS tries to correct some of the story issues from the Last Jedi. I think the plot was extended probably about 15-20 minutes longer than it needed to be to change some of the story lines from that last movie. I think J.J. Abrams does a nice job doing this in a sensical way. I enjoyed the nostalgia of Abrams’ first entry, the Force Awakens. I wasn’t too pleased with Rian Johnson’s Last Jedi because I felt he purposely crushed the nostalgia/character arcs that old time fans like me enjoyed. Abrams gets ROS back on course. The first hour is a little slow as he does this, but while doing so, he actually makes the characters of Rey, Finn and Poe the most likable they’ve been in this newest trilogy.

The story moves along nicely and the plot twists make sense (with, perhaps, a little leeway given to some plot holes). The set pieces are excellent with the action maintaining the viewers level of excitement. The cameos are all well placed and will be especially appreciated by long time fans. The new characters, including aliens and droids, are all fun as well.

The performances are all really good. Adam Driver is the standout to me, but Ridley, Boyega and Issac all do fantastic jobs wrapping up their characters.

The movie, for me, ended in a satisfying way. Could they have come up with a better way to end it?...maybe. But for someone like myself, who’s vested 40 plus years of being a fan into these movies, if I can say I was “satisfied”, then that is more than good enough for me.

I’m not sure where I’d rank ROS in the series. For me, Episode 4 will always have that number spot because it was the first. Empire Strikes Back is always near the top because it was one of the first movies to leave you on a cliffhanger where the good guys didn’t end up on top. Rogue One had probably the best 45 minutes of any Star Wars movie as it kept fans emotions ratcheting up on a rising dial to its conclusion. The origin of Vader made Episode 3 a standout as well. ROS was, to me, the most visually stunning of ALL of the Star Wars movies. Abrams has a wonderful flair for how he films the movement of the spacecraft, in space AND on ground level. Some of the coolest scenes involve Kylo Ren’s amazing looking Tie-Fighter. Do yourself a favor and try and catch this on an IMax screen. The visuals AND sound are simply amazing in this format. I’ll be pre-ordering the 4K Blu Ray once it becomes available.

Until they come up with the next inevitable installment...May the Force be With You....lol.

text: I have seen just about every documentary on America's space program so I'm gonna be a little tough here.  It is a good summation of the space program, and overall I give this one 3.5 stars (didn't have a button for 3,5!).  I give it 5 stars for production quality which is very good.  Although it is full of stuff that I have already seen and already knew about the space program, there are quite a few things I have not seen (video clips and commentary by the astronauts), which is why I give it the 4 stars overall.  I give it 2 stars for commentating format, however, for the typical need today it seems for the producers of historical documentaries to pick commentators less qualified for the subject but ticking all the right boxes of gender and race.  I know more about the space program than the young girl commentator they include in this documentary!  But heaven forbid we don't pander or else get called the "r" word!  However, they did include present day interviews and commentary by the few remaining astronauts and engineers who worked in the space program, so I give them credit for that.  It could have been so much better, and I am still waiting for someone to produce a very detail series on the space program.  Don't get me wrong; there are a few out there that are outstanding in detail... I'm talking about a comprehensive series getting into the design of the vehicles and into the real nuts and bolts, i.e., how did they design the separation firing bolts to separate the vehicles?  Or who were the folks who designed the launch towers and how did they work?  etc etc...  Overall, it's worth watching this documentary even if for the video footage that has never been seen.  If you are a space buff, you will enjoy it like I did.

text:
Sadly, it's easy to complain about the Hobbit movies. The term "fan fiction" has been thrown about repeatedly.

It's clear that Jackson and his colleagues have added plot points - quite a bit of them. However, the goal of these films for me has always been to create a visual universe to showcase Tolkien's creations, and Jackson does it beautifully. Although the first film in the series got a bit tiresome (I probably don't need to see the dwarf drunken meal scene again), there are no scenes in this film that feel extraneous. Some of the dialogue seemed a bit forced (Gandalf to Radagast with a '90's cop-show -like "Don't try to come in after me" seemed poorly written), but the scenes following the dwarves and Bilbo were constantly good.

title_x: The Crazy, Irate Woman in Black
text:
Arthur Kipps is a lawyer in London whose wife has died in childbirth. He has a four year old son and a nanny for him. However, he is in danger of losing his job at his law firm because apparently he has done nothing but mope around for the last four years. He is given one last chance to redeem himself, to go to a remote village and Eel Marsh House, where the owner has died, and sort out her many papers.

He meets a man, Samuel Daily, on the train on the way there, and despite Arthur's very rarely opening his mouth to speak (ever), Samuel becomes his one ally in the town. Arthur goes to Eel Marsh house to look for, and at the papers of this woman, and get them in order and locate her will. How he is expected to do this, I do not understand, because even in the daylight, with candles, that place is dark as a cave.

The important papers (birth and death certificates, adoption papers) are placed conveniently on top so that Arthur finds out what he needs to know right away - about the ghost, The Woman In Black (what wearing black has to do with anything they don't say). Every time he goes to the house, there is always a lot of unexplained sights and sounds, which never faze Arthur in the least. He's still just so stunned from losing his wife four years ago.

The ghost, Jennet, really does seem to be taking her anger out on the wrong people. After so many deaths, you'd think they'd move away or hire an exorcist or something. As is usual in these movies, what the living person thinks/hopes/believes/is sure will appease the out of control ghost does not work. I didn't really care about any of these silly characters, and watching Arthur go from being covered in mud/dirt/or soaking wet to being dry and spotless wearing the same clothes, was irritating.

Something that perturbed me: on the adoption papers those involved are referred to as Mr., Mrs., and Ms. (the unmarried ghost). But from all the period British novels I've read, there was no use of "Ms." back then and periods after honorifics such as Mr, Mrs or Dr were not used, and still are not. Jennet should have been referred to as "Miss" on the adoption paper.

Janet McTeer was wasted, but I guess it's a paycheck.

text:
There are many ways to tell a truth. It can be directly, through symbolism, or simply from satire. The cinema, in its narrative omnipotence, appropriated them and has played to mix them in all possible ways. From great directors we have seen a few good combinations, and one of them is, without a doubt, Guillermo del Toro.

In 2006 we were surprised by del Toro's Pan's Labyrinth (El Laberinto del Fauno), a fable set in midst of the Spanish Civil War. Twelve years later, the Mexican director is back in form, this time with The Shape of Water (La Forma del Agua). The film may very well be this year's best, but not only due to the Academy's 13 nominations.

This fable, although with suspicious similarities in his narrative technique with Pan's Labyrinth as the two share a similar "structural formula", makes you fall in love and invites you to reflect upon its extraordinary script and cast. Of the latter stand out Sally Hawkin, Olivia Spencer, Richard Jenkins and the wonderful Doug Jones, the man behind the "creature".

Things from this world have a common place, an "aleph", a space/time where they gather and be one and all at the same time. The history of the United States in the sixties. The Cold War, the not-so "cold wars": the struggles for civil rights, the unstoppable technological innovation, the entertainment industry, the American dream... that being the case, Guillermo del Toro could not find better setting for The Shape of Water.

"Silence" has a strong symbolism in this film as those who literally cannot speak are the two main characters: a mute woman (Elisa) and an non-speaking aquatic creature that fall in love. Little by little it is revealed that their friends (a black woman, a gay man and a scientist tied to ideological commitments) are also mute in a society that does not accept them.

Elisa elegantly sums up all the others "good" characters, but del Toro takes her further and turns her into the hero of the story, one with no power other than the will to smash her loneliness. The silence remains in the film as a child of loneliness and not as an evil in itself.

The monsters of Guillermo de Toro always have something interesting to say, especially this one, although it cannot speak. The Shape of Water are not only two hours of pure joy and entertainment, but an opportunity to immerse oneself in our thoughts through its symbolism. The word "immerse" has probably never been better used.

title_x: Slow-paced movie that never arrives, or maybe wasn’t supposed to
text:
For someone who missed this film at the time of release and wanted to see what the hype was about, Lost in Translation was mostly disappointing. The film seemed much longer than it was (1 hour, 42 minutes), maybe intentionally. The slow pace captures the ennui of the 2 main characters as they struggle to fill time in Tokyo while going through the motions of a second-act job (Bill Murray) or as the wife of an up-and-coming photographer spouse (Scarlett Johansson). The viewer struggles to find some meaning in their trivial escapades and deep-but-shallow discussions, and sees the clichéd ending coming by halfway through the film.

In 2021, the movie is more difficult to stomach because of caricatured, racist portrayals of native Japanese professionals and entertainers, and needless typecasting of Scarlett Johansson as a needy wife whom Murray’s character chides for wanting to be the center of attention. Why would Johansson’s character, a Yale philosophy graduate, need to tag along after her husband, then Murray? The father/mentor figure flanked by the adoring, smiling and giggling female follower gets tiresome for a female viewer, surely much more so for Johansson, but she plays the role flawlessly. At the end of the movie, the two characters have a long discussion including some of Murray’s best dialogue about how parenthood changes one’s life for good and for bad. After a week of insomnia, they finally drift off to sleep while making this emotional connection. This seems symbolic until we realize that after a week overseas, jet lag is starting to wear off.

At best, one could say my “what is the meaning?” response to this movie IS the meaning – that we struggle to fill time all our lives, trying to follow a loose script with occasional companionship from another lost person. At worst, this was the expected result of a “sparse” script that “allowed a significant amount of improvisation in dialogue, especially from Murray” as described in Wikipedia. Glad I found out what the hype was about, but my curiosity ends here.

title_x: Survival of the fittest in a record-breaking movie
text:
This film’s title is “Parasite” (singular), because the survival of the Kim family depends on its ability to operate as a single organism, capitalizing on the gullibility and self-indulgence of the ultra-wealthy Park family. In the opening scene, we see the Kims in their cramped subbasement apartment in the South Korean slums where son Ki-woo/Kevin (Choi Woo-shik) and daughter Ki-jeong/Jessica (Park So-dam) find free Wi-Fi next to the toilet in the back of the apartment. Father Ki-taek (played by Song Kang-ho) seems like a hopeless optimist who finds opportunity in the mundane (e.g. free fumigation for stinkbugs in the kitchen) and teaches his children they must always have a plan. After the Kims’ failed attempt at folding pizza boxes for income, college student Min (Park Seo-joon) visits the family and changes their lives forever. Ki-woo agrees to replace Min in an English tutoring job for the Park family. Ki-woo also accepts Min’s gift of a special stone meant to bring fortune to its keeper. Indeed, the stone is part of the rise and devastating fall of the family as all 4 members intertwine their lives with the Parks’.

When the Parks leave on a camping trip, the Kim family enjoys a rare night of luxury in the empty house. A heavy rainstorm leads to a Darwinian struggle with the Parks’ past housekeeper (replaced by Mrs. Kim), who returns to rescue her husband hiding in an underground chamber of the Parks mansion. In a long, nightmarish sequence in the dark, the Parks unexpectedly return early, and Ki-taek, Ki-woo and Ki-jeong narrowly escape. Returning to the slums to find their apartment flooded with sewage, they spend the night with others in a school gymnasium, and Ki-taek discloses his “plan.” In complicated events the following day, the divided classes violently clash, but ultimately coexist.

The 2020 Academy Awards got it right in the unprecedented sweep for this movie (Best Picture, Best Director for Bong Joon Ho, Best International Feature Film, Best Writing--Original Screenplay). Don’t be scared away by the subtitles. This is a masterpiece you need to see.

title_x: “I won’t be a rock star. I will be a legend.”
text:
Freddie Mercury said, “I won’t be a rock star. I will be a legend.”

And then he was.

Watch this movie, see a documentary on Queen (e.g. “Queen at Live Aid—20 Minutes that Changed Music“), and listen to Freddie’s exquisite vocals in as many music videos as you can find. Look for these 3 scenes in the Bohemian Rhapsody movie that are significant but easy to miss:

THE BROKEN MICROPHONE STAND. During one of Queen’s early performances, Freddie tried to detach the microphone from the stand and the stand snapped apart. Freddie kept singing and running around with the half-stand as if it was part of the show. For the rest of his career, he continued to perform with a broken microphone stand--maybe his way of saying, “put anything in my path, and it won’t stop me.”

NO ONE EXPECTED QUEEN TO TAKE LIVE AID. In a documentary about the 1985 Live Aid concert, organizer Bob Geldof said, “This <global venue> was made for Freddie.” But because of discord among the band members at the time and their lower prominence since their “A Night at the Opera” album, Geldof also said “the last people anyone expected to come out of that gig as being the memorable ones were Queen.” By the end of the concert, the audience was enthralled, and Geldof said the performance “seemed to me to be of another order.” Brian May (Queen’s lead guitarist) commented, “Freddie knew exactly how to get across to a stadium audience. The guy right at the back of Wembley Stadium still felt that Freddie had a connection.” You will also feel the connection over 30 years later as you watch the Live Aid sequence in this movie. Thank you, Rami Malek, for studying and performing Freddie’s every move so we could relive it with you.

RAY FOSTER AS HE WATCHED LIVE AID. Mike Myers is unrecognizable in both appearance and demeanor as he plays Ray Foster, an EMI executive who made the biggest mistake of his career while managing Queen early on. A wordless scene at the end of the movie says it all.
---
Less well-known Queen videos will show you the astonishing range and creativity of their work, and the raw talent of every band member. “Love of My Life" (with Brian May's unforgettable guitar solo), “Under Pressure” (see John Deacon's famous guitar riff at Wembley Stadium on July 12, 1986), “In My Defence, and “I’m Going Slightly Mad” (recorded as Freddie felt the onset of AIDS dementia) demonstrate their strange and ever-changing style. Roger Taylor drives Queen's Live Aid performance with his precise but unbridled drumming and intuition about when to play one more chorus for the crowd. You’ll discover many more treasures from Queen’s 15 studio albums released between 1973 (“Queen”) and 1995 (“Made in Heaven” released posthumously after Freddie’s death in November 1991).

Long live the Queen! We love you and miss you, Freddie, but you will indeed “live forever” through your band and your music.
description: ['Bohemian Rhapsody celebrates the band Queen, their music, and their extraordinary lead singer Freddie Mercury, who defied convention to become one of the most beloved entertainers ever.']

title_x: Seth Breedlove Has Lost His Mojo
text:
This video is bad. It’s awful; a complete train wreck. It consists, almost in its entirety, of people reciting the most ridiculous, completely over the top stories you can possibly imagine. Most (all) of which are total fabrications.

About 2/3rds of the “documentary” revolves around Land Between the Lakes, a peninsula the straddles the Kentucky/Tennessee line. I live near LBL, and am an avid trail runner. I probably run 1,200 miles a year in LBL. Not only have I seen or heard nothing that is out of the ordinary, none of my trail running friends have either. All those stories of massacred families, children, hunters, etc.? It’s all complete BS. Even if you buy into some arcane, NPS conspiracy to hide the truth, the fact that newspapers around the area have reported no such stories says quite a bit. The hometown newspaper of poor M/M Smith and the kids’ mysterious disappearance while camping at LBL would surely be reported, wouldn’t you think?

Plus, there is a very large bison and a very large elk herd at LBL. Yummy food for an apex predator, wouldn’t you think? But no depredations have been reported, and the herds are very healthy and growing.

Finally, Boy Scout Troops are very active in LBL. Not only hiking and camping there, but building projects such as nesting areas and arbors. And guess what? Nothing. No Boy Scouts have mysteriously disappeared.

And then there is the scene from the emotional “witness” who finds a female’s blood-stained clothes and reports it to the police, only to have the police shrug it off as nonsense. Yet, according to the teller of this fiction, a young girl had gone missing while jogging several days earlier. Surely that was reported to the police. So do you still think the police would shrug off the discovery of blood-stained girl’s clothing and not investigate given a girl has gone missing? Really? Again, I’m tossing the BS flag on this one.

So where does Small Town Monsters come up with this stuff? Why would a company create such an outlandish mockumentary? Well, that answer is obvious. It’s to separate people like me - who used to think the company created quality products - from their money.

I’m very saddened to see where this company is heading. It’s first documentaries on The Mothman, Chestnut Ridge, and The Minerva Monster were excellent productions. I really hate writing a review of this nature. But unfortunately, it’s deserved. It’s bad……

It’s more a documentary - if you can call it that - of the people and personalities investigating this subject. And even that might be a stretch. There is just not a lot of credibility in this video, whether from the supposed witnesses or the investigators.

This just seems to be a “filler” of sorts; something done quickly and inexpensively to release between more serious STM productions. However, if it is, STM shouldn’t do it again, because it will eventually hurt its brand. Quality over quantity, as it were….

If you are a die-hard fan of STM, then by all means buy the video. Generally, STM does good work, and financial backing is important. But if you are looking for a decent video about this subject, I’m afraid this just isn’t it.

text:
I feel it is important to offer the disclaimer that I wear my bias on my sleeve. I am a longtime fan of the series having played all of the Warcraft games and have read a number of novels and extended lore. With that said I feel that if you are a fan of the property like myself you will find a lot to love with this big screen adaptation. It certainly is one of the more faithful adaptations of a video game property.

You might wonder if someone who has no prior knowledge can enjoy the movie. I think the answer is dependent on whether you can keep an open mind. There is some fan service but it never comes across as being too on the nose. The acting is decent, and the visual effects are quite spectacular. If the film is guilty of anything, its some of the pacing and characterization choices. The film does jump around a bit in the beginning, but it does present some great establishing shots of notable locations in the Warcraft lore. Some characters I think could have been better fleshed out (like King Llane). There is a romance plot arc that feels a bit shoehorned in. The biggest takeaway would be that I feel the film would have benefitted from a longer run time. I certainly would have loved to have had that director's cut. For fellow lore affictionados there are some changes made in the film. However I never felt they detracted from the film, even if I know they don't quite match what I know from the games.

All in all I really enjoyed Warcraft. Duncan Jones has succeeded in establishing the world of Azeroth, and I do hope we see a sequel. I want to see Tauren, Gnomes, and Nightelves along with the story of Arthas and his rise as the Lich King. If you have a love for high fantasy give Warcraft the chance to entertain you.

The 4k looks great and it has a number of extras as well. Its well worth a look if you like high fantasy.

text:
Like the movie, this review of Warcraft has two sides to it. One is from a fan of the video game franchise, and the other is from a movie critic.

Starting with the fan boy: Even though the critical reviews and number percentages from websites like Rotten Tomatoes and Metacritic are barely above a certain superhero movie, I think this is the official best video game movie ever created. Why would I state that? It’s because the devil is into the details and like video game development, Director Duncan Jones was pushing for that. Yes, as a fan, I did notice things left and right that were literally designed to be ripped straight from the video game. I applaud Jones's team for wanting to do Warcraft like this. The games were always about the grey area of between the humans of Azeroth and the Orcs of Draenor. (aka, 50/50). I never got to play any of the first game: Warcraft: Orcs and Humans, which this film is literally based from. This movie will be the next best thing unless I find a novel about it. I cannot stress this enough, but as a fan, I was literally hook by the first segment of the film. Viewing how the Orcs first stepped foot into Azeroth was everything I hoped it would be. it gave me chills and I was immersed as if I completed a series of missions and Blizzard was treating me to a CGI cinematic as a reward. When the main title appeared after the segment, I wanted to clap. I wish that part of the film was in my cinematic section of the World of my Warcraft login screen.

Anytime there were scenes with orcs, I could not take my eyes off of them. The facial animations and done graphical detail is, in my opinion, is the best motion capture CGI work since Avatar (I know, that story was dumb, hush!). Also, the camera work or scene editing involving their segments is leagues better and clearer than anything that Michael Bay’s production company will ever fart out. Even the cinematography of well known areas with the orc effects meshing together helped make Warcraft stand out among other CGI heavy films. It was a relief to view these characters and see them be believable instead being a chore to focus on. You could see and feel the conflict between Durotan's traditional Orcish honor and Gul'Dan's brooding evil schemes. Side note, Jones totally nailed Gul'Dan, and watching him made me want to play an Orc Warlock in World of Warcraft. I didn't' think that Jones's productions team wanted to have "other fluff" like elves in this movie....and yet, we actually see High Elves along with Dwarves and many other "icing on the cake moments." While the story isn't anywhere like Lord of the Rings, it was so awesome to actually see magic in a recently release fantasy movie. None of that just light spewing from Gandalf's staff, but actual magic spells of arcane, fire, and even Fell and it look pretty great! I heard this movie was actually decent in the 3D version. I’ve sworn off those versions for years, but I’ll admit that I wished I got to try Warcraft out that way.

I could go on and praise the CGI orcs and other fantasy elements, but that wouldn’t be fair and be very uninformative. So the big flaw to this 50/50 type of movie? While, the performances are not completely terrible as reddit.com will state, with also a story not completely as absurd as certain released super hero stories….I just couldn’t be that engaged with the human characters. Which is funny because I could never do that when I’m playing the actual video games from Blizzard. Travis Fimmell was a decent Anduin Lothar. However, he kept channeling his more well known character from the TV show Vikings a a bit much. It felt distracting and almost any humor present seemed a bit off. The movie thinks you want to have Paula Patton’s Garona (half orc half whatever green lady) be something to push the story forward, but it’s more distracting. It becomes almost into too forced on, pretty cheesy, and pretty awkward at one point. Ben Foster as Medivh is almost the same. It’s evident that his and Garona’s scenes needed reshoots while I’m sure both actors are pretty good in general. However, Ben Foster swings kind of lifeless at the worst times. I was thinking that Ruth Negga and Dominic Cooper were going to really ham up their performances in favor of just a paycheck. I was actually surprised when they didn’t. But there is nothing special about their parts and it’s painfully easy to tell their fates. Besides the actors, the story itself seemed that it needs to be 1 hour longer. I know from a certain other film that I argue it’s dumb that it needed to be long to be good…but Warcraft definitely needed some extra time to help flesh out stuff that I assume made non fans not like it.

I understand how passionate Duncan Jones was with this project. You can tell he let it get in the way of making a cohesive story that general audiences had trouble finding common ground on. Fans of the series, I can definitely see how they could absolutely love parts about it while wishing others were better constructed. Things were strange in favor or some weirdly placed humor and pointless other exposition, it's obvious. But to say Warcraft is completely terrible as some website journalists claim? No! Oh Fell no. It’s not (insert that certain superhero movie) levels of absurdity. Visually, it’s a work of art on many levels. It’s just that the story bits are a bit underwhelming and it depends on the audience too much. If you like more "high fantasy" in your movie, then this could hit your desire to see something that isn't just the Lord of the Rings type of films. Although, you'll be wishing they did try oomph up the narrative arc like it was Fellowship of the Ring. Watching characters actually perform magic was still awesome in my book. The fan in me wants to either pre-order it now or wait for the hopeful Director’s cut. The critic, I maybe pay a slightly discounted price for it off of Amazon Prime or VOD. I’m literally swinging both ways. I do know that I can’t wait to watch it again because I actually had fun and don’t feel the need to pull my hair out. I just hope that there is a possibility of a sequel….

Work, errands & chores all took a back seat until I finished this.  The reader engages with the characters immediately, and the intricate plot is both imaginative and darkly compelling.  Its depiction of the intersection of the art world with corporate corruption is extremely timely in our "1% World," and the longing of the characters, whether for a baby or money or world domination, is coolly yet compassionately portrayed. It's written with such a highly visual style, I immediately started "casting" some of my favorite actors into various roles.  Then, I was thrilled to find the film version on Amazon Prime, terrific also. I'd say Nesbo is more literary than Baldacci, less complicated than LeCarre, but I'll be reading more of his books soon. -- Diana

Blizzard seems to have dropped the ball with regard to its franchises and movies. Diablo, Warcraft, StarCraft, all excellent plots with a millions strong built in fan base. There should have been a dozen or more animated movies, raking in billions, over the last 20 years. Heck, much of the CGI used in movies was first used in cut scenes and promos for some of these games. For whatever reason that did not happen.

Which is why I was quite cautious when one finally came out. Incredible opportunity for cheese, selling out, using up the last gasp of meme, before it fails.

Instead, this movie is one of the finest of the genre with a solid plot, rooted in the games and books. Just the right amount of special effects but standing firm on the acting (which is superb) and the plot. The plot is one area this movie could easily have failed. There is so much to the Warcrat storyline, it would be easy to get too ambitious and screw everything up. The plot here is modest. It introduces the Orks....who they are and why they have invaded another realm. And shows them as relatively conflicted and complex. They are not monsters....but they are desperate and the victims of corrupt leaders preying on that desperation. The movie sets the tone of whom is who and introduces the conflict and is obviously the first of several movies.

The one mistake I think is it assumes a lot is known already by the movie patron. Which is to say the Burning Legion and almost all aspects of the world the Orks are from is left out. That world is dying. The orks kill a bunch of slaves to empower a gate to the human world with Fel magics but whom they enslaved is left a mystery as is the source of the Fel magics. The Light is not even mentioned.

A good hour could have been added to this movie to introduce such things. Another hour for the various other races involved. Yet another hour about the undead. In other words, these are all great ideas for the next half a dozen Warcraft sequels I hope they are working on these and prepared to link them to this one.

text:
No it isn't really a comedy. It isn't slapstick and it isn't meant to be a comedic celebration of Stalin or his demonic Central Committee. It highlights the gross incompetence, terror, and cowardice of the Central Committee through a human lens. Because they were human. The horrors they perpetrated, the horrors perpetrated by those that followed them, WE are capable of the same. They were as human as us, and that is dangerous.
By writing charismatic characters, the director warns us of what placing trust and power in the hands of a few does to the many. We all have the potential to be monsters.
The Soviet Union really was this depraved. Shooting a man while an officer yells for you to stop, just because you are desensitized. Herding all of the staff off to be murdered, only to get shot in the head yourself.

Read the Gulag Archipelago or listen to "The Cold War: What We Saw" podcast for a more in depth discussion of how truly monstrous they were. How truly horrendous humanity can be.

title_x: A fun ride, but don't think about it for too long
text: I'm a Fringe fan and before that X-Files, so I am comparing this work to those.  Lunopolis is for the most part a fun ride best taken with suspended disbelief.  For when you mull this over the next day, it really makes no sense at all.  The filmmaker must have had a blast writing this, throwing in just about every sci-fi cliche short of swamp monsters.  UFOs, Roswell, immortals, moon cities, time travelers, flying cars, time machines, "haunted" houses (of a sort), alternate dimensions, space/time distortions, and more.  SPOILER: for example, the story states that a lunar dweller turned himself immortal, then went insane and fled to earth, where he is on a quest to end his immortality (for reasons unstated).  In the story we find out he had access to the power gem, and a time machine, so... why didn't he go back to the moon and use the device to go back in time and inform his previous mortal self to not go through with the immortality process?  See what I'm getting at here?  And later it is shown that the films(and camera!) of the documentary makers somehow survived the dissolution of a time dimension. What?  How does that happen?  It doesn't matter in the end because the filmmaker succeeded in making an entertaining yet slightly disturbing thriller that has some really nicely done parts.

text: I really enjoy watching these documentaries & seeing everything they catch. The small percentage of people that say everything is fake just annoys me. Here you have this group that is putting a ton of effort into going through HOURS of footage on so many video cameras, stationary cameras, digital recorders, looking into the history, etc... Not to mention piecing all of this together to make an enjoyable show. Of course, some parts are slow at times. You can't expect to have evidence every minute. But the evidence they do manage to catch is awesome! If they didn't have eerie background music playing it would feel like the show is dragging along. The only negative I have to say is that they have to come up with better questions to ask & have to present themselves to the "spirits" as more friendly. Accusing them right away of making guests feel "creeped out" & saying "you won't scare me off these stairs" doesn't help get evidence... It sounds very defensive.  The best evidence in this one was the chandlier swaying, the ghost hand that looked like it was trying to sneak it's hand around the doorway to turn on a light switch without being caught, the bookcase moving forward, & the computers/machines turning on by themselves.  Overall, great show for a good scare & learn about one of the historic cities in Michigan. Before this show I had no idea about these places in my own state.

text: I love film noir and it's offshoots, and I really like Richard Carlson and Frank Lovejoy as actors, so I had high hopes for this film. The story was, in a way, the dark side of "The Best Years of Our Lives." Frank Lovejoy struggles to find work after WW2 and eventually meets a con-man and petty thief (Lloyd Bridges) who introduces him to a world of stick-ups, blackmail and eventually murder. Lovejoy is an everyman with a young son and wife who, not knowing he's become a criminal, thinks he's working the night shift at a local factory. Richard Carlson is the crusading newspaper reporter who sensationalizes the story of the murder and stirs up a tidal wave of emotion which crashes on an entire town when Carlson and Lovejoy are eventually captured and jailed. The descent into the black hole of crime is played out well and gives proof to the into on the old Philip Marlowe radio shows ... "Crime is a sucker's road, and those who follow it end up in the gutter, the prison or the grave. There's no other end." The ending of "Try and Get Me" is one that left me feeling deflated. But that's the point. I enjoyed this little gem .... Thank You Amazon for making available for Prime streaming.

title_x: Very well-made and acted, won't soon forget it
text:
***MILD SPOILER ABOUT THE NATURE OF THE ENDING*** Ravens is a very well-made Swedish film about the struggle of one family to eke out a living on a farm (dairy and potatoes), with a focus on the father, Agne. It's quiet, episodic, slow-moving, and provides an intimate look at their daily life and work. The acting is extraordinary, especially by Reine Brynolfsson as Agne- his face, his eyes. The film premiered at the Toronto film festival in 2013 to rave reviews. In an interview first-time director Jens Assur, a former photo-journalist and noted photographer, said that he sought to "challenge the audience when it comes to visual style, pace and content. And my vision is to make films that take the audience on a journey — intellectual, emotional, but also to another world, another life. The world in “Ravens” is really exotic, a small farm. But at the same time, it’s something we all have a relationship to. The farm is always just around the corner, and in that world, Agne played by Reine, is struggling to justify his own life and his own choices- something we all can relate to."

In a 2017 review Stephen Saito observed: "In introducing the family, Assur brilliantly uses time rather than geography to express distance, giving each member the individual space to stake their claim to the world “Ravens” immerses one in at the tail-end of the 1970s when thousands of farms across Sweden were falling by the wayside." Indeed, the movie held my interest from beginning to end, though I hoped it would have a happier ending than clues provided throughout hinted it might (it didn't).

The characters are stoic, impassive, express few emotions (yet I was riveted); there is little dialogue, and a sense of foreboding permeates the film. The suspense mounts steadily, nearly imperceptibly. The landscape is stark, remote, achingly beautiful. Tender-hearted animal lovers, especially those who love cows, and birds (ravens and crows in particular, like me) may find some scenes disturbing. The film is matter-of-fact about sex- has three relatively brief sex scenes, each explicit in its own way and none gratuitous (one tender, one illicit, and one involving cattle breeding), and is not appropriate for children or teens, IMO. I noticed only one use of strong profanity. Note- English captions must be turned on manually.

Three more noteworthy things about the film are: 1) it's so realistic, engrossing, immersive I forgot I was watching a film; 2) attitudes and behaviors that span generations still resonate in the film's present, though they're barely alluded to; and 3) the ending affords a very clear perspective on the psychological impact the father's decisions and behavior has on his family, his son in particular (rarely shown so clearly, and yet it's subtle, visceral). He "comes of age" in a way most profound. I won't forget this film any time soon. With the caveats above, highly recommended.
description: ['Hard working farmer Agne struggles with the harsh reality of his daily life, hoping his teenage son Klas will take over the farm and continue his legacy. Klas however, dreams of a world far away from this rural existence. Sumptuously lensed, this powerful coming of age story, written and directed by Jens Assur, paints a tangled web of shame, guilt, madness and the dreams of youth.']

text:
I somehow missed this until now. I thought everything about this mini-series was exceptional. I watched it straight through. Not over the top- utterly natural, simple and relatively subtle, its gravitas just enough to make your hair stand on end and give you chills (me, anyway, and I'm not even a church-goer). The acting, pacing, writing and direction were superb. Narratively, the seamless interweaving of action with historical developments, parables and Jesus's teaching tales to punctuate events was masterful, edge-of-your-seat stuff. No small feat when you know what's coming.

Someone on IMDB said Robert Powell looked/behaved more like Jesus than Jesus himself (!), to give you an idea of the integrity of his performance- splendid. Olivia Hussey was perfect as Mary, too, ditto with Ann Bancroft as an effective and affecting Mary Magdalene (I was surprised after Jesus' appearance to her after his resurrection, that the disciples' disbelief of her testimony was shown, 40+ years ago- I thought that knowledge and controversy were more recent than that). Anyway, all the actors were great. I noticed only one gaffe: someone said to an associate walking away, "keep in touch!" I thought that sounded awfully modern, looked up its origin and it comes from military drills in the 18th century (some 17 centuries beyond Jesus' time), wherein soldiers track their position in formation by brushing or touching those next to them.

I didn't care for The Passion of the Christ or The Last Temptation of Christ- too grandiose for me. I watched Godspell for the first time too recently, didn't care much for that either; this I LOVED. I don't think one needs to be a Christian to appreciate this film. Respectful, reverential, inspiring- HIGHLY recommended.

title_x: Info GALORE on the Royal Family
text:
I found this a little bizarre, but fascinating and informative. All about the royal family, with it's lynch pin, the Queen Mother (formerly "Queen Elizabeth", namesake of the QE1, wife of King George the VI, or Bertie of [[ASIN:B004R36QUE The King's Speech]], and mother of the current Queen Elizabeth, namesake of the QE2). This is ostensibly a biography of the Queen Mother, but it also details the stories of everyone close to her, i.e., the Royal Family for the last century- their proclivities, triumphs, scandals, etc. What is evident about this documentary is that some of it must've been taken from a documentary on fashion and the Royal Family, because the jewels, gowns, and especially wedding dresses of nearly every royal wedding in the last 100 years are discussed. Much is made of how the fashions reflected the times (for example, how the Queen Mother's HATS have evolved over the decades). The photos and film clips are wonderful and I found the discussion lively and very interesting.

Wonderful archival footage and interviews with people in the know. A LOT is crammed into 100 minutes. Though this will particularly tickle women's fancies, I think men who appreciate history and the historical record of the Royal's Family's participation in global affairs over the last 100 years will enjoy it too. I watched this to find out how Queen Mary was related to the present Queen, and to the QE1, the Queen Mary, and the QE2, and I learned that and a WHOLE lot more. Delves into the Queen Mother's personality in considerable depth- easy to see why she was so revered in Britain (a strong person, and quite a character). ***SPOILERS FOLLOW*** For example, she persuaded her husband the King to visit America at the start of WWII- the first Royal visit EVER to America (by ANY monarch, and in this case, by those from the country from which America won its independence, incredible. The Roosevelts served them hot dogs (!) and they and the King and Queen became friends as well as allies. This documentary includes archival footage of the Queen Mother meeting everyone from Errol Flynn to the Beatles (lots of footage of Princess/Queen Elizabeth too, from infancy on). Considerable detail on Prince Charles, who was very close to his Grandmother- his chief confidante and a kindred spirit, e.g., their shared favorite pastime was fly fishing. The film also suggests involvement by his grandmother in his choice of Diana (Diana's grandmother was her long-time lady-in-waiting), and later in his affair with Camilla, too. SCADS of information about the Royal Family from about 1900 on, beginning at the end of Queen Victoria's reign. Highly recommended!

text:
Succeeds on so many levels and for so many reasons. Steven Soderbergh did a masterful job of taking a story that could have easily dissolved into gratuitous farce/exploitation and imbuing it with humanity and compassion, along with narrative punch. An acting tour de force by both Damon and Douglas, especially Douglas. Douglas has Liberace's mannerisms, walk, movements etc. down to a T, astonishing. Both actors play their roles with just the right amount of pathos and passion, flaws intact. A powerful depiction of one person (a narcissist, likely) using another for his own selfish purposes, leaving him with nothing. The supporting actors, e.g., Rob Lowe, Debbie Reynolds, Scott Bakula, Dan Akroyd, Bruce Ramsay (the jaded houseboy), all concerned, were superb.

Add to this glitz, glamor, Liberace's phenomenal playing, and his charismatic persona (especially in the final scene), and it is plain to see why Liberace was a superstar. I saw him perform in 1979 on the Queen Mary (I worked behind the scenes as a concierge and met him- an experience right up there with meeting John Carradine and Natalie Wood. Thorsen was likely there, but I don't remember). Liberace had his white baby grand piano lowered by crane onto the ship for use in his show (and possibly his Rolls Royce, though I may be imagining that). He wore the white ermine robe with the yards long train, and absolutely wowed the crowd, the consummate showman. A revealing and incisive look at a moment and place in time- if you like stories about Hollywood, celebrity, or gay culture in the drug-infused 70s and 80s, you may find this as provocative and fascinating as I did. I recommend it for the acting alone- phenomenal.

text:
To each his own- I read other reviews, ranging from "hilarious" to "mean-spirited". I haven't seen other of these blokes' offerings (except Coogan's hapless director in [[ASIN:B001O6W9QC Tropic Thunder]]) and don't know their routines but found it alternately clever, funny, touching and bittersweet. I found it absorbing from beginning to end, and thought the character development incisive, inspired. *** SPOILER ALERT*** My husband was a Yorkshireman and he and his good friend from the east end of London often bantered this way, including impressions (Michael Caine at the top of the list, marvelous). In The Trip Steve has seeming ego and intimacy problems, is less than comfortable with himself, and though he treats his friend Rob quite shabbily at times, the latter takes little offense, happy enough to play Rhoda to his mate's querulous Mary. Beneath the humor, the wonderful Yorkshire scenery and the changing restaurants and locales is an undercurrent of pathos, of existential angst. It reminded me very much of Christopher Guest's [[ASIN:B00FWPML0A Family Tree]] (though the latter's tongue in cheek, more a parody). Guest ([[ASIN:B002CMXAYW This Is Spinal Tap]], [[ASIN:B0058YKE36 A Mighty Wind]]) grew up in both England (he's an English lord) and the U.S. and has a canny eye/ear for British characterizations. Anyway there's not a lot of action in The Trip but there's loads of conversation, character development and charisma between the two leads. Loved it.

Update: I've since become a fan of Coogan's, after seeing the absurd [[ASIN:B00IOH83AK Alan Partridge]] and especially, [[ASIN:B00IGI3LMC Philomena]]. In reading about the true story behind Philomena, I learned that the reporter Coogan plays in the film, Martin Sixsmith, purportedly embellished the story and added unsavory, gratuitous elements in writing the book This, according to people interviewed by Sixsmith. Coogan optioned the book, co-wrote the screenplay and produced the film, and CLASS ACT that he is, did so with respect for everyone involved. He ignored the sensational, cheesy elements of the story and instead focused on the relationship between Sixsmith and Philomena (it was a photograph of the two together in the newspaper that instantly drew him in). I couldn't have been more impressed with the film's subtlety, pathos, and inherent compassion for human beings, flawed though they are. The Trip bears the same subtle Coogan nuances as Philomena- utterly natural in the way real relationships are, in the details, and simply wonderful. I've since watched The Trip several times and see more and appreciate it more with each viewing. Highest recommendation.

text:
The focus of the first two episodes of Ken Burns's acclaimed series is the friendship between these two great women, from youth to old age and death, punctuated by highlights and lowlights of the women's suffrage movement, which they founded. Fascinating, the women very different- tiny Stanton ultra-radical, militant, well-off, married, with children, a brilliant writer; towering Anthony single, thrifty, more pacific, pragmatic, a gifted speaker. The issues they championed are detailed too, e.g., how women's rights paralleled and yet diverged from abolition and civil rights. SUCH muddy waters, and as in the 1960s, involving strained relations between women and men within each movement. The issues involved are complex (likewise involving race relations within the women's movement), and Burns brilliantly, eloquently, GENTLY teases it all apart.

This is a quiet, thoughtful production, not exciting, but momentous, we mustn't forget what women like Stanton and Anthony did to help secure women the right to vote. "Women's history" ("herstory") is given short shrift, considered a specialty area of study in school and college, even today (imagine if the same were true of "Men's History", though perhaps that's a redundancy, since the word "history" stems from the Greek for wise man and story). Every school child knows what Abraham Lincoln and Martin Luther King accomplished, securing rights for some 5-15% of the population, why do they not know of Susan B. Anthony and Elizabeth Cady Stanton (and Sojourner Truth), who championed and secured many of the same rights for MORE THAN HALF of the populace? Perhaps a "Woman's Day", a holiday honoring the likes of Stanton & Anthony is in order.

Women have come a long way, but some contend that they've still a considerable ways to go- especially globally, in other countries, some of which are our allies and trading partners, in spite of the fact that women are kept as chattel and scarcely deemed human. Were MEN being held in such bondage and denied even the most basic of human rights presumably it would be a different story. On a more personal note, I live across the street from a park playground and at any time of the day can be heard kids of all ages jeering at each other, leveling the biggest insult possible, "You're just a GIRL," or "You _____ like a GIRL!" (insert any verb). Anthony and Stanton envisaged the vote as the first step in securing equality for women. There's a lot of work yet to do to eradicate misogyny and sexism in our world.

A point of interest: Sweden was the first country that extended voting to women (tradeswomen) in 1718, 200 years before the United States (though it was rescinded in 1771). Our founding fathers debated and rejected allowing them to vote. A little known "herstorical" fact is that women fought alongside men in the Revolutionary War, women accompanying the troops not only as soldiers but as cooks, laundresses, providers of sex, etc. and expected to be accorded equal rights as citizens of the brave new republic. No spoiler alert given because Burns's film focuses on Anthony and Stanton, the Civil War era and after. MUST viewing, in my opinion.

I'll say just one thing of the ***SPOILER*** variety: fascinating that the measure FINALLY granting women the vote came down ultimately to the vote of just ONE courageous man (a Republican), inspiring. Burns paints a very detailed, rich portrait of these two women and their cause, as different as night and day, each very special, brilliant in her own way. A revealing portrait of two extraordinary people, whose work improved the lives of all Americans. HIGHLY recommended.

Phenomenal acting by Denise Newman in the title role, playing a "coloured" (mixed race) mother in the slums of South Africa. She has an extraordinary, expressive face (the unflattering photo on the DVD's cover doesn't do her justice). All the acting is superb, the son's too. I thought I'd like this, read a critic's view saying it was never maudlin, that despite the harrowing subject matter it was optimistic, ultimately uplifting. Not for me.

I struggled with how many stars to give it- I could see how some would give it five, but ultimately, due to my emotional gut reaction and discomfiture I settled on four. I'm mindful of the fact that my ambivalence towards it doesn't mean it's not a great film, it may well be. It's undeniably powerful.

[SPOILER ALERT] Shirley cares for her son who's been paralyzed in a gang shooting. The film (jerkily shot, with odd, myopic camera angles) is unremitting in its gritty depiction of the details of their existence- the poverty, the endless effort, toil required to procure food and help and to care for the son's physical needs. It's slow-moving, tedious at times, yet always intense, uncomfortably so.

Shirley is indomitable, rises to meet every challenge, but it's an uphill battle all the way and arguably a thankless one. I never had the sense I was watching a film, it seemed so immediate and real. I actually tend to like sad films, this one was too much for me, very depressing. When it was over I just cried.

I read once that Margaret Mitchell said that [[ASIN:B002MSD0ZK Gone With the Wind]] was about one thing- survival; she sought to contrast those whom had what it takes to survive with those who didn't. Although Shirley has what it takes, the feeling I was left with was, why bother? Shirley's strength and courage in the face of nearly insurmountable odds did not inspire or buoy me, rather the reverse, but perhaps it will you. I doubt if I'll be forgetting it any time soon, though, and the film did provide much food for thought, so I guess ultimately it was worth seeing (for me, anyway).

title_x: MESMERIZING, but not everyone's cup of tea
text:
Depending on where you are on life's journey, and/or your deepest sensibilities, this film may be profoundly moving, even gut-wrenching, or NOT. **Spoilers Follow**

Themes that resonate for us tend to be far different when we're young than when we're older, for one thing (duh). When you have everything ahead of you, issues such as your ability to wield personal power, who am I, really, will I find someone to love and love me, what am I going to do with my life, etc. are of the utmost saliency, urgency. This movie has to do with the LOSS of things in life that lent it meaning, the water in which you've swum, as ubiquitous as the air you breathe, suddenly drained away. Shocking. What now? Whether you love it or not may depend not only on your age but what you have lost, or if loss looms on your horizon.

I found it PROFOUNDLY moving and meaningful, a testament to the fact that life is in our interpretation of it and that to which we choose to attach symbolic meaning. What is left when everything that seemed to give your life meaning is gone? Only you, and your ability to experience life as a living work of art of your own creation. The cremation scene was just one of many I found achingly poignant. Ticking down to life's conclusion, the protagonist could have just slunk off into old age, gone home and opened a can of beans and turned on the TV, no longer a participant but a spectator in life's pageantry.

Instead, he blossoms thru the alchemy of a friendship with a prescient young Butoh dancer, a performance artist (her performances on the toy phone are AMAZING)- and partly as a result of her generosity and courageous example comes to realize that he himself is on stage. He prepares the performance of a lifetime (literally). I get chills just thinking about it.

This film strikes chords that are simultaneously Japanese and reminiscent of Ingmar Bergman, I thought, no less profound. If you liked Bergman's [[ASIN:B002R2FQNA Wild Strawberries]] I think you'll like this. But instead of merely accepting the inevitable and going quietly into that good night, Rudi TRIUMPHS over life's vicissitudes, including that biggest one of them all- death. He crafts a swan song that is not only the culmination and celebration of a life well-lived, but a testament to love. The film is utterly original, bizarre, even shocking at times, and for me, GLORIOUS, absolutely mesmerizing, but it's definitely not for everybody.

title_x: Characters in the movie behave unrealistically
text:
I thought about why this movie (and last jedi and rise of skywalker) suck. The problem is the guy in charge, JJ Abrams. All of his movies are like this. Things do not make sense. For example, even right in the opening text, it says that the empire is desperately searching for Luke. Why? He is hiding on a remote island and hasn't done anything in years. It doesn't make any sense. Throughout this movie, and all of JJ's movies, people act in ways that don't make sense, and then the next five minutes of the movie I am thinking 'oh come on, that xxx wouldn't do that' or 'why'. A girl who has never swung a lightsaber before beats Kylo Ren in a lightsaber duel. And then the ground conveniently opens up right between them creating an uncrossable cavern with perfect timing. Its like a joke.

You see, in good movies, everything makes sense. In the first 6 star wars movies, I never once thought these things. Now, if you combine this with the fact that none of the characters are cool or likable (in contrast to the first six star wars movies, where they have the coolest bad guys ever and very likeable heroes also), AND then add on top of that the fact that the only 'story' was just bits and pieces of the original star wars copy and pasted into the movie randomly. There is almost nothing at all original in the movie. You see, good directors like Lucas don't just rehash the prior successful movies. They create new stories and characters. They have a creative brainstorming team. That is how Lucas came up with the idea of Darth Maul, a totally awesome bad guy. You don't see a 'death star' etc in the prequels. Its all new stuff. The only thing left, as with all of JJs movies, is modern effects. So if you can forget about ALL of the above mentioned things and try to focus only on the fact that there are awesome cool effects and just focus on the battles, and try to forget about the first six star wars movies and pretend that they aren't just copying and pasting things, then it is worth the watch just for the effects. Oh and you also have to try to ignore the 'women are great' stuff being thrust in your face and an oversaturation of women in lead roles.

You need other people in charge to have a good movie, thats the bottom line, no JJ and no Kennedy.

text: Like many other reviewers I have experience with a family members with dementia and also have suffered multiple mild traumatic brain injuries (mtbi) myself. Alice's early symptoms were shockingly similar to my acute recovery from mtbi's. One family member had early onset Alzheimer's  while the other has elderly related dementia. The early onset is much more shocking and seems to progress far more quickly. Julianne Moore did a tremendous job as an individual experiencing and trying to manage this devastating disease. I felt that her part had depth and realism as did the part of her younger daughter. But the movie opens with this close-knit family and I expected to see myriad ways that they all experienced during the illness and how that interplayed between them as family members. There was hardly any of that. After about the first half hour, the son and oldest daughter were almost non existent in the film. The movie doesn't give you any sense as to why they just drop out of the story. So the viewer is left wondering if it's related to coping with disease or to life's business, or what? So their characters are not fleshed out at all. Spoiler alert - Alice's Alzheimer's is familial and one of these two have the gene. But that is never mentioned again. The husband is slightly aloof but attentive and I got the sense that he and Alice were such a high-powered couple that you couldn't relate to her decline. The ending was extremely abrupt and left me feeling unsatisfied. Perhaps that was intentional, there is no happy ending. But Alice was still living at home with a daughter and care-giver and then the movie just ended. Glad I watched it, but I was expecting a more fleshed-out story.

text:
I think this is turning out to be one of my favorite movies. Spoiler Alerts Ahead:

Indeed it is a twist on the original Sleeping Beauty, but all stories have two sides to them. I found the back story on Maleficent in this movie very compelling as to why a woman would want to curse an innocent baby. The concept makes all the characters "realistic" with real motives instead of just relying on pure good and evil to carry the story. It's a story with three very serious morals in it, if you can find them. The costumes, settings, special effects and sound track are classical Disney. The sound track, cinematography, and costumes in particular are Oscar worthy. While I'm not normally a fan of Angelina Jolie, she is probably the only one who I could think of who could pull off a real life version of Maleficient so well. Elle Fanning and Sharlto Copley also give very commanding performances, but I would have liked to see a little more screen time and character development with both of them in this movie. The use of Diaval as a "conscience" is ingenious and fits into the story so well that it even elevates a lowly crow that is only a snitch in the original story to a character that greatly adds to context of the story. While many people will decry that's it is not the same story as the original, I really think it's far better, even if Maleficent doesn't turn into the dragon at the end...again all stories have two sides and it's just the story teller who gets to pick the way events really might have happened.

This story is certainly from Maleficent's point of view. While by the end of the movie, she is not "good" by any means, as she does some really horrible things to Aurora, the three pixies, the soldiers, King Stefan and ultimately breaks the heart of Aurora's mother the Queen, this side of the story makes her a very real and likable individual. It becomes very clear that it is far better keep her on your side because she is certainly capable of being very dangerous if she's not your friend..

Two thumbs up for this realistic twist on an old fairytale.

title_x: The US leads the way in creation of National Parks
text: Stunning photography and a very good perspective on the history of our National Parks. Depicts how and why the first park, Yellowstone, was dedicated. Shows the way this historic place would have been lost if it were not for the act of creating National Parks. There is actual footage and photos of the original tourists in the Yellowstone area and how it was being destroyed at that time. You would not believe what a difference it made to create a National Park. It was a difficult process because there were no laws and no ideas how to do it at that time. The military was involved in maintaining order there. Yellowstone still has the old buildings from the military post at the north gate. And good to know.... the creation of this first National Park was actually a world wide event. The first of its kind in the world. Also points out that the dedication of national lands as parks has given the public equal access to the most magnificent land in the world. That is an outstanding feature of our country. It states that other countries had special places but they belonged to the wealthy. Be warned.... after seeing this you will definitely want to go see Yellowstone if you have not been there yet. Put it on your Bucket List.

text: This film takes a dark-humored approach at portraying the events of Stalin's death. Although who can say whether or not it is an accurate depiction of the dialogue and events, this movie does fairly portray the fear and brutality of living under a totalitarian regime. I am not really sure why it's classified as a comedy, so if you are looking for a lot of laughs, I would not suggest this film. I also would NOT recommend this film be presented to children as there are some extremely violent scenes as well as multiple scenes that do not explicitly show, but allude to the act of rape. There are some over the top things that happen in the film, under the context of the time period, some of which are comical in the context of the scene. However, overall I view this film as a dark-humored political satire that rightly criticizes fascistic governments, like the former USSR. The ultimate message of the film is that power hungry individuals ultimately devour their own (and anyone that gets in their way of seizing power) and that centralized government ultimately leads to dictatorship. If you are interested in the history of the time period and setting, I would highly recommend the film.

As I began writing this review, I realized I didn't like the film as much as I thought I did.

It's an interesting premise, but all in all I don't buy into the mechanic of time travel being used as a plot-defining device. It is for this very reason that I hated the movie Interstellar. For the same reason The Star Trek universe was totally ruined for me when they introduced time travel (TOS movies, TNG series finale).

All in all, this film was entertaining right up to the point where you realize Louis is actually seeing the future and not the past. This was a weird and dumb twist which made the character you had been following for the last 60 minutes pointless and void of any unique definition.

The ending is laughable. You have to ask, if she knew her child was going to die of a rare incurable disease, and she knew Ian was not going to make a good husband, then why would she continue to follow down that path to a future of sadness and disappointment? The ending in itself debases the whole premise of time altering mechanics being used in the plot. If you could see the future, wouldn't you intentionally make different decisions to make your own life better?

text:
In Free Guy, the titular Guy (played by Ryan Reynolds) is an NPC (non-playable character) in a Grand Theft Auto-esque sandbox game where he and his kind don't realize they are video game characters and the players rule the land bringing constant destruction. Guy starts to change and goes outside his daily routine when he becomes infatuated with player Molotov Girl (Killing Eve's Jodie Comer).

The story to this turned out to be a lot better than the commercials would have you think. I'm not saying this is a perfect movie, but there's an unexpected depth to this supposedly light comedy, particularly in the third act. There is a surprising amount of character work and effort put into the human world side of things. The world building for the video game is pretty well thought out and inventive at times. The movie manages to pay homage to sandbox games while giving the story room to breathe. (Congratulations to director Shawn Levy (Night at the Museum/The Pink Panther remake/Real Steel) for making a comeback after not having directed a theatrical film since 2014).

The humor can be hit-and-miss. There are a few pretty funny moments, but this is one of those films that work more based on it's general good-nature feel than a lot of memorable moments. I think the movie does suffer from giving Guy and his best friend Buddy (Lil Rel Howery), especially Buddy, I mean like rapid fire. It can be a little exhausting at times. (Especially Buddy! He won't stop with the jokes!) Also, Guy's crush at the beginning may feels a little too stalkerish and slightly uncomfortable.

Reynolds and Howery are both funny guys, and Reynolds in particular sells his character, but they also lean too much into the joke overload rather than reigning it in.

Comer delivers a stronger performance than you'd guess from the trailers. The character has more going on than just being a love interest. Props should also be given to Taika Waititi as the villain, scummy, corporate bro Antoine. Again from the trailer, I feared he'd be a little one note, and yeah the character plays out kinda like you'd think, but Waititi brings an energy that makes the character work.

Recommended, despite my criticisms this is an overall enjoyable and rather original film.

title_x: Not perfect, but entertains, so basically kinda like the original
text:
In this sequel to 1996's Space Jam, which has developed a loyal fan base over the years, basketball player LeBron James is trapped in the WarnerMedia Serververse (home to all WB IP), by a vengeful computer program Al G. Rhythm (get it?!) (played by Don Cheadle). He's also kidnapped James' son (his movie son, not real son) (played by Cedric Joe) and won't let them leave unless LeBron beats Rhythm's team at basketball. The athlete ends up teaming up with the Looney Tunes in order to save the day.

First off, LeBron is not a great actor. Michael Jordan in the original wasn't a great one either, but he fared better than LeBron. 'Course, I think the first film knew how to play better to the lead's strengths. This film feels more story heavy and Lebron is required to do a lot more. The movie have him at times to be a hard father who wants different things than his son and having LeBron be a bit of a jerk, albeit unintended, and do more serious stuff isn't a thing he can pull off. That having been said, the guy is definitely game for everything and doing his best and doesn't seem disinterested or like he's coasting. LeBron does better with the non-exposition scenes when he gets to be happy or mad. The star/Toon dynamic is also different. Jordan was more the cool mentor type who was weirdly chill when he met Bugs, LeBron's more likely to be a part of the lunacy and is legitimately thrilled to meet the rabbit (voiced by Jeff Bergman).

Cheadle on the other hand, is given some very basic bad guy dialogue with his material, but he's doing his best with what he's got here.

SJaNL is a lot like the original in that it's not perfect, but there's a lot to like about it. There are several clever or funny moments throughout this. The movie doesn't take itself too seriously and you shouldn't either. I appreciate that New Legacy tackles the same basic story as Space Jam but manages to do it in a different enough way, switching from an alien threat to computer programs and giving more of a video game theme to how the basketball game is played. Plus, the stakes feel a little bigger here than in the original. The father/son gap is predictable but is handled pretty well, and the script does a good job of explaining why LeBron has this tough style of parenting at the beginning. You can't get behind him, but you understand where he's coming from.

I know a lot of people are complaining about how much WB product is jammed into this and that this feels like an advertisement for the company. Personally, I'm not hating it. I won't deny that except for Bugs, the plot and other properties don't give the Looney Tunes enough time to shine with such characters as the Tazmanian Devil (Fred Tatasciore), Elmer Fudd (Eric Bauza) and Lola Bunny (Zendaya) barely getting anything to do. But, the various worlds and characters in this movie add a bit of fun to the proceedings and it's fun to see LeBron and the Toons interact with it all. There are a surprising amount of references for just the adults and that'll be fun for older audiences. However, expect kids to ask questions about properties that they don't know about. There are a a few selections in this that one can argue don't fit in a kids' movie (like Game of Thrones and a background cameo of the Droogs from Clockwork Orange). Also, they really try to squeeze in EVERY property WB owns, resulting in references that your kids won't get, such as background appearances by the kid from The Bad Seed and Baby Jane.

I think I liked The Monstars, the rival team from the first Space Jam, a little more than this films' team The Goon Squad. (The Monstars had more of a traditional Looney Tunes look and feel to them). That having been said, I liked the new guys. It took me a moment to warm up The Goon Squad 'cause their design was a different style than the Toons, but at the end of the day, credit has to be given to giving each character a distinct look and powers.

I think I preferred the original's use of cel animation and greater shadow work, which resulted in a more theatrical feel. Still, the animators definitely did a lot of work here, resulting in a slick, shiny look. For the 2D animation, I mean. The ads have been stressing the Toons' new 3D designs, which also look good, but they don't appear immediately. And that's the neat thing about this movie: it's mix of styles and media. You'll see LeBron switch between cartoon and live-action based on what world he's in. (By the way, I particularly liked the design of his cartoon version.) There is one particular world featuring Lola that particularly feels visually unique and really well animated. Going back to what I was saying about liking what they do differently between movies, I liked what they did with the basketball court here. It feels very different from the traditional indoor court of the first film and has a grander scale when it comes to the audience.

I think I liked the first film better, because it was simpler in it's story and more emphasis was put on the Looney Tunes, but I did have fun with this. Imperfect, but the highs are definitely highs. You're children will probably love this.
