text:
This is a period piece about a Soviet spy set in 1985 and that must end prior to August 1991, since that's when the Soviet Union fell and since the Soviet Union still remains unfallen at the end of the movie, despite the fact that doing the math according to the timelines given in the film would seem indicate the movie ends in the spring of 1992. But that's not actually one of the anachronisms of which I speak.

Towards the very beginning of the movie, we see Anna in a squalid public housing apartment in Moscow that she shares with her boyfriend in 1987. The movie is very non-linear, jumping back and forth in time with flashbacks and flashforwards to a dizzying degree, probably to try and distract from its many plot holes, but these are also not the anachronisms of which I speak. In that 1987 scene, Anna hasn't yet been recruited by the KGB and is an unemployed junkie, just like her boyfriend. She's sitting at the dining room table on her boyfriend's slim laptop PC with a color monitor running Windows or some Windows-like operating system and is using wi-fi and a browser to wirelessly access the Soviet Union's Navy's website to complete an online application to join the Soviet Navy. So how do a pair of lowlife junkies have a laptop that's still 13 years away from being invented and have a wi-fi router that's at least 15 years away from being at all commonplace to access a website that never existed, not just because the USSR never made it but because the Web itself wouldn't become public until six years later in April 1993, two years after the Soviet Union ceased to exist? It's ridiculous.

That's just the start of the anachronisms of which I speak.

In 1990, she breaks into the security room of a Paris hotel which has all its surveillance monitors networked on an ethernet server that wouldn't come out until 2001 and steals a removable hard drive that wouldn't be invented for 20 more years.

In 1990, long before anyone was walking around with cell phones, back when cell phones were those enormous bricks, so obscenely expensive to use only the richest people had them, and had coverage so poor coverage was not existent most places and at best spotty in the biggest cities, but in Anna cell phones are so common in 1990 that she not only is able to pick pocket a cell phone from the first random person she passes back when cell phones didn't even fit in pockets, the one she pick pockets is a Nokia candy-bar cell phone that wouldn't be invented for another 10 years, which she then uses to call her handler, who answers using a Motorola flip phone that wouldn't come out until 1996.

It goes on and on. It's like the makers of the movie were people who had no contextual idea about what technology developed when and didn't bother to look it up and didn't even bother to check the year the vintage props they'd purchased were made to make sure they weren't made AFTER the time period of the movie. What's more, none of it was necessary, like they could've had her filling out the Navy application on paper, could've had her pull a video tape out of a VCR recording the security camera footage, and could've had her use a pay phone to call her handler who could've answered a landline at his desk instead of at a dinner table.

I could maybe suspend my disbelief of how she repeatedly killed dozens upon dozens of assassins that would appear out of nowhere and everywhere in absolutely unbelievable onslaughts that were like the movie Kill Bill had a baby with a first-person shooter video game. I could maybe overlook the cliche characters and cliche plot filled with plot holes because that's just the kind of action movie this is. I could maybe even get past the very cringey and painfully implausible ending where she meets up with her KGB handler and CIA handlers, both of whom she's suddenly portrayed as being deeply in love when we've seen no such emotional interchange between them to that point save for a couple of seemingly meaningless and gratuitous sex scenes, leading to maybe the most ridiculous stand-off I've ever seen in a movie. But what I could not get past, could never get past, is anachronism after anachronism after anachronism.

I myself would only give two stars, but since anyone born after 1985 would probably not notice the many, many, many, many anachronisms and since that's its target audience, I figure to them, it's a 3-star action flick, it's plot holes, bad writing, implausible action scenes, unfounded emotionality, cliche characters, and cringey ending being par for the course for such films-- average, so an average rating.

Hayden Christiansen as Anakin comes across as some spoiled, smart mouth East Coast private prep school-type pretending, badly, to be a disciple and student of the Jedi Order. He’s always complaining and feeling sorry for himself instead of devoting himself to his art…how exactly like spoiled punk kids today.

Samuel L. Jackson as Mace Windoo is another character who has to constantly reassert his authority with menacing looks and sharp tones. I thought he was a Grand Master of the Jedi Council. How did he achieve that honor without being able to command respect the way Peter Cushing’s Grand Moff Tarkin did? (Tarkin told Vader to release his force-chokehold on that general at the counsel meeting, and Vader complied immediately and without question). Perhaps Windoo’s position was awarded based on a judgment of something other than his mastery of the force and leadership qualities?

Let’s not even discuss that imbecilic cartoon Jar Jar Binks. The Star Wars franchise should be fined $500M for inflicting that nonsense on its fan base.

Ewan MacGregor and Ian McDiarmid pick-up some of the slack in these films as Obi-Wan and Senator Palpatine, and Natalie Portman did a pretty good job with her Princess/Senator role (mostly because she’s cute and sexy…not a great actress).

In fact, if one looks at these films objectively, the Jedi, collectively, come across as the epitome of weakness. Many are defeated (killed) and don’t even see it coming (yeah, they can see the Chosen One but nothing else). And when suffering losses, they give up…Yoda goes into exile (hides), Obi-Wan goes into exile (hides), later Luke goes into exile (hides) in a future movie after considering killing one of his students (and nephew)…all while the war still rages. Instead of using their powers to organize, train, and lead small bands of resistance fighters like Special Operations Forces would do, they give up and go off somewhere to meditate (or whatever). That’s stunningly selfish and shamefully weak.

You know who has the never-say-die attitude? The Empire stormtroopers. No matter how many losses they suffer, they keep coming. And they have the strength of will to do what needs to be done to win a life and death struggle - ruthlessly.

If you weren’t there in 1977 in the theater with your $1.25 popcorn (what is it today? $15?) then you never saw the real thing. The characters today just aren’t the same, and the Woke-infused Disney productions are the worst of the genre…approaching nauseating, really.

text:
Let me start out by prefacing this review with the fact that I usually LOVE Guillermo Del Toro's movies, and I mean much more than your average viewer. They are consistently some of the best in modern fantasy escapist cinema and he understands the use of color like very few filmmakers do. Another rarity he practices is the implementation of practical FX, makeup and prosthetics BEFORE he will go to using CG, something special.

But to me this movie was just too easy, it was very low hanging fruit to be used very obviously and fairly forcefully as a commentary on "Trump's America". The story is incredibly simplistic and predictable, the characters are all pretty one dimensional clichés, and Michael Shannon's character was a prototypical "evil authority figure". Thats not to mention that he was filled with lots of generic attributes and dialogue.

Aesthetically the movie is pleasing, as you would expect it to be in the hands of Del Toro. Guillermo has a penchant for romanticizing time periods and he created a pretty, yet at times sterile and bleak, analog world of early Cold War era America. The film has some other strange "oddities" to it, even more than to be expected from the filmmaker. Unfortunately it fails with it's heavy-handedness creating essentially a story all too similar to "Beauty and the Beast" with elements of "Creature from the Black Lagoon".

As many other reviewers on here, Jumanji was a staple in my childhood VHS collection. Robin Williams was pure magic for kids of the 90's, between Mrs. Doubtfire, Hook and Jumanji he made movies fun for us. Seeing this now as an adult it really is no less special, Williams was a magnificent talent who had a penchant for bringing joy to the lives of others.

I can honestly and unbiasedly say that family films are just not made like this anymore. Jumanji is an adventure movie with the right amount of comic relief for both kids and adults, practically non-stop action, and all wrapped around a genuine heart warming core story about the strength and bond of family and how in the end, there is nothing more important.

Aside from some convincing performances from Williams and Jonathan Hyde (the poacher) something else that made this movie stand out was the incredible and “John Williams-eque” score from James Horner (a legend in his own right). Movies like this were meant to be passed down from generation to generation as the message here is a timeless one.

title_x: A Little Too Tame, True Story or Not
text:
True stories can be many things, they can be exciting and adventurous or they can be cliche and boring. What we are all used to in 'mountain climbing movies' is excitement, adventure and generally edge of your seat thrills. Through the first entire HALF of the movie, it hardly delivers on any of these things.

As a movie goer, I'm much less interested in the dialogue and backstories of these characters, who are supposed to be based on real people, and much MORE interested in the 'thrill of the climb' so to speak. This is why usually when true stories are adapted for the screen they are usually dramatized in one way or another to keep the audience engaged. It wouldn't have hurt to build the tension better for that first hour to take us to what would eventually happen in the second half of the movie.

With all that said, by no means is this a bad movie, it just isn't quite as thrilling as I expected or wanted it to be. But if you like true stories and you like movies about mountain climbing it is definitely worth your time.

title_x: A Seemingly Underrated Bond Flick That New Gens May Not Understand
text:
I am shocked and appalled at the negative reaction to this movie. Let me preface this review by saying, if your style of action movie is something like "Furious 7" you may have no interest in Spectre.

Lets start from the beginning.

Just because you don't understand a movie, doesn't mean it's not good. There are many reasons you might not understand this movie, if you're not a real Bond fan and are just looking for a good popcorn flick, this may not be for you. It's not really a multitasking movie, if you weren't paying attention, or were anticipating being force-fed the plot that would explain as to why you were lost.

What makes a Bond movie? What are the factual elements that comprise a James Bond film?

1. The cars. Spectre uses the all new (and Bond modified) Aston Martin DB10 and it is an absolute monster. There are several adrenaline pumping chase scenes in the movie (another Bond staple) that should keep you entirely enthralled. If that isn't enough wait til the end.

2. Bond girls. Spectre features not 1, but 2 Bond girls (although one with significantly less screen time). First you have Italian born actress Monica Bellucci, and next (the real Bond girl) you have the gorgeous Parisian Léa Seydoux, who not only looks good but was great for that role.

3. The gadgets. A lot of older Bond fans (specifically Moore fans) may be salty about the fact that the Craig-Bond doesn't use a ton of silly gadgets in his movies. While Spectre continues that trend, it is also not completely devoid of any Bond gadgets.

4. The attire. Like Skyfall, the production and costume design for Spectre was mesmerizing. Specifically for James Bond, who was outfitted in every scene courtesy of Tom Ford. There was not one shot in the film that he wasn't dressed to impress (unless otherwise intended).

5. The Bond. This is one that can not be changed, if you don't already know by now Daniel Craig IS James Bond. Everybody has their favorites but he is who he is and that isn't going to change unless he does indeed decide that Spectre was his last entry (which I don't think he will).

So to recap, the movie literally hit on everything that a James Bond movie is (and has been for over 50 years) and should be.

text:
The Ninth Gate works as a part detective, part thriller with overtones of the occult. Johnny Depp, in a very interesting role, plays Dean Corso, who is essentially a book detective that freelances in appraising and finding rare works. A wealthy, high profile client asks Corso to travel to Europe in search of 2 extremely rare books of a 3 book set, one of which he already has. But what happens on his journey may not be worth the money after all.

Not since Rosemary's Baby has Polanski made a picture this eerie. Though not as committed, the film could have been aesthetically darker and more stylized from a visual standpoint. The movie also could have easily gone on without the addition of the mysterious 'Girl' character, who left questions and more to be interpreted by the audience.

Frank Langella was probably the single most important ingredient to the overall success in the macabre ambience of the film. The operatic score (which I thought was even a little under-utilized) also helped round out a demonic path for this movie. As a persuasive thriller about demonology expect to be intimidated.

title_x: great documentary, thought-provoking on gender & running
text: Good documentary of one woman's challenge on the Long Trail: trying to beat the men's record. Not a whole lot of scenery, it's more about her, which is fine because she's engaged in such an intense endeavor, and there is plenty of drama (emotional/exhaustion). The best part of this is her ultimate focus on the organization "Girls on the Run", and how much meaning it has for her. In the end (spoiler warning), it is ironic that her achievement of setting a new woman's record became anticlimactic, almost a let-down. This is food for thought as to whether, or how, female athletes should compete against men for records. The film suggests that in long-distance running, there is less legitimacy to treating men and women separately, since men's advantage diminishes to almost nothing (at least, this is what is claimed), yet we see a top female athlete fall apart psychologically trying to compete with the men's record, and end up disappointed, even though she had an amazing performance and set a new record, relative to other women. I suppose the lesson of the film is that, at least on the Long Trail, women are not on equal footing with men (we're talking top athletes here). However, I'm sure this woman would say that it was competing mentally with the men's record that helped her do as well as she did. Which raises the question - does it hurt or help female athletes to not directly compete with men's records in certain sports, like long distance running?

It's scary to realize that not that long ago gay people in the US had few rights and suffered a lot of harassment, and had to live amazingly closeted lives. This documentary brings it home clearly by telling a cohesive narrative while weaving in firsthand accounts of living people and teaching us about one night when everyone had had enough.

I wasn't alive then and you can bet the Stonewall wasn't mentioned in school. It should have been, as it is as important today as any civil rights event. Anyway, my point is that like me, you might not know a lot about that time period, and I was really glad to find this production that covered it in a very human way. Yes, it tells the Stonewall's story, but it excels at giving you the atmosphere of the times as well.

It's funny too, to watch it in the context of today. There's one man, a purported expert on homosexuality, who claims to have tried it and realized it was not for him, but who advocated for gay acceptance anyway. At one point he talks about having enough mainstream acceptance of gays to allow them to have real relationships and not be driven underground. He follows that up with a chuckle, saying something to the effect of "After all, it's not like they want to get married, or adopt children." What a time capsule! You begin to understand the circular logic of the times - how forcing relationships to occur "in the dark" brought about the very behavior that made outsiders despise many gay people, and how fear led to many misconceptions as well.

A terrific story very well told. I appreciated it enough that when my first disc broke while popping it out of the box that I got another one.
description: ['In 1969, homosexuality was illegal in almost every state. But that was about to change. On June 28, 1969, New York City police raided a Greenwich Village gay bar, the Stonewall Inn, setting off a three-day riot that launched the modern American gay rights movement.']

We all knew that Lake Silencio was not the end of the Doctor. How they got around it was satisfying but it left more questions to be answered. And the bad part? They reveal how he does not die in the last almost 10 seconds of the show. The rest? Not satisfying.

I waited in eager anticipation for this episode. It was very very unsatisfying. Like wanting a hamburger with fries and being given a rice cake. Thin. Tasteless. Leaves you still hungry and not satisfied. This is how I felt after this finale.

The ending is interesting and is, actually, the whole episode. The rest of it, including the acting just felt unsatisfying. More than 3/4 of the episode was gone before any real answer-related action started. And what was shown, was a back story with little explanation or connection, except showing the Blue Man again.

Since most of the episode shows Matt Smith acting alone or with minor characters, the flaws in his acting abilities show up horribly. He needs the others to play off. Here he seemed uncomfortable and unreal, but I guess . . . ooops spoiler . . . Perhaps that is understandable. But it was noticeable how poorly he acts. In my view, they all seemed to act really poorly. Further, what is UP with the awful Doctor's dirty clothing? They are just awful and you can almost tell they spent very little time or money on that costume for him. It was annoyingly distracting.

And the oldest question in the universe, which is revealed? That was a big freaking joke. It is impossible that THAT is the oldest question in the universe Bah!

Overall, disappointing and unsatisfying. Compared to how the season started, this was grossly unsatisfying. We are left with huge holes of logic and lots of questions.

Lots of questions remained unanswered and not even addressed from this season. The only questions answered are we learn who River is to the Doctor, but in my view that isn't even clear given everything else we are shown in the last 10 seconds. We also learn what the question is. We have no hints as to the answer.

I'm for not having all spoilers and all plot twists revealed, but this was just ridiculous. When the episode was over, I kept thinking, IS THAT ALL? An unsatisfying finale. It was more a filler episode than anything else.

I give it 3 stars for the visual effects in the 1st half and the ending. The rest was just really disappointing.

text:
Just watched the fifth (final) season of Orphan Black.

SPOILER ALERT
SPOILER ALERT
SPOILER ALERT

This review will contain spoilers.

What I liked: Tatiana Maslany's acting, in her various roles. She's delightful, funny and complex as ever. Unfortunately, this season gives her little to do emotionally that's new.

What I didn’t: lots of things, unfortunately.

1. The writing seemed tired and a little hackneyed. In the first season, it sparkled. In this one, not so much. Characters explained and re-explained their own actions and motives. There were few surprises, and those that did occur strained credibility.
2. Many of the actors also seemed tired. I can imagine that they were, after five years of portraying characters whose actions often made little sense, as the storyline shifted around in circles. In the first few seasons, for example, Sarah's mother, "S," is a shapeshifter; we have no idea whose side she's on. This made her interesting and used her skills well as an actor. Not so much, this season... she's more one-note.
3. The violence in this season, like that in Season 4, is relentless and disturbing… huge amounts of blood. Lots of knives. Blood spurting everywhere. Characters are stabbed, stabbed again, shot, sliced up, then miraculously heal. Then they die again, or almost do... surprise... they're still alive, and aren't even limping after a few quick resurrection scenes. They are resurrected so often that when more deaths occur, they don’t seem real; the audience has an expectation somewhere that the characters are probably not really dead. The healing technology that saves them seems to do little for other characters who need it.
4. The character playing “S”, Sarah’s adopted mom, seems particularly tired and unfocused, and was just hanging around, doing very little, until the last couple of episodes before her death. The tension between her and Sarah was gone. This left her little to do but stand around looking and talking tough, till near the conclusion.
5. Ferdinand kills MK after following Sarah to where MK is hiding. This makes the killing partly Sarah’s fault; MK, if anything, was a survivor. No one, including Sarah, ever brings this up.
6. Ferdinand’s death was hard to believe. He knew what “S” was like, and how resourceful she was; it’s unlikely that he would have given her a chance to pull out one of her many hidden guns and kill him.
7. The notion that the board of Neolution would or could have believed, without proof, that someone was a couple of hundred years old, just because he said so, also makes little sense. If they did believe what's-his-name, the old guy on the island, was the world's oldest living man, they'd have kidnapped him and brought him in to be studied -- maybe even dissected him to get the answers they were looking for. They're scientists on the leading edge of evolutionary research, yet they believe without evidence?
8. Characters who did not really matter to the story, like one of Felix’s one night stands, and his biological sister, return for no apparent reason and do little to move the stories along. Complex characters with mysterious motives are reduced to simple ones who have little going on. They spend most of their time just hanging out together looking worried, while "worried" music plays in the background.
9. On a personal level, I didn’t like Allison, OB’s resident soccer mom, getting a new look. Her look was part of what defined her. I also didn't like seeing Delphine, Cosima's on-again, off-again girlfriend, another shapeshifter with implied deep secrets and connections to Neolution, reduced to such a simplistic character.
10. The second episode has a line that sums up the problem with this season. Sarah is getting ready to run off with her daughter (again) from Rachel and Neolution (again). No clear reason is established for this, since Rachel has been acting pretty nice. Her daughter doesn't understand why they're running. Sarah explains to her daughter: “We run on principle. It’s all we’ve got left.” The truth seems to be that they run to introduce some suspense where there is none.
11. So…. Not so much. I liked OB seasons 1 and 2. There were good things about seasons 3 and 4 (though season 4 was already starting to sag.) I'm glad they wrapped up the story, but it's lucky for them that they did; I don't think many people would have come back for more seasons if they hadn't.

text:
First I should say that Crack in the World is a fun movie. It's fast paced, well written, tightly edited, and reasonably well acted. (Not a lot is required of the actors, but they play their parts well.)

Second, I should confess that I originally saw it when I was 12 or thereabouts, so my perceptions may be colored by that bit of personal history. It's a good, straightforward SF story, the sort often appreciated by boys of that age. I liked it then, and still like it now.

In some ways it surpasses what one would expect from its genre, particularly when you compare it to other minor-studio SF movies produced and filmed in the 1960s. It's effective as a science fiction disaster movie, and also works well as a relationship drama. I have to say I like the character of Maggie, with her unapologetic and unconcealed love of two different men.

One reviewer criticized the movie for suggesting that an explosive device fired down into the earth, hitting pockets of hydrogen, could set off a hydrogen-bomb reaction. This is a valid criticism, and a glaring weakness in the storyline. It could have been avoided by simply saying that the hydrogen ignited, as it is flammable and explosive.

The notion of scientists doing stupid (risky) experiments motivated by either ego or the profit motive is, unfortunately, also plausible. So some of the science in the movie is borderline believable.

Apart from that, the science in the movie is reasonably straightforward. But it does have one logic problem that's difficult to overlook. Before discussing it though, here's a SPOILER ALERT: the end of this review reveals the end of the movie. Read below the asterisks at your own risk.

***********************************

So here's the SPOILER, and the problem:

***********************************

Let's say an event took place on Earth that was catastrophic enough to rip a sizable chunk of the planet, hundreds of miles across and who knows how deep, free; hurtle it into space with the violence necessary to escape the earth's gravitational field; and create a new moon.

What effect would the event, and the loss of a massive chunk of the world, have on the rest of the Earth?

What effect would a second (burning) moon in the sky have on the atmosphere, and on the tides?

If a huge chunk of our planet were torn free, could life as we know it possibly continue? Wouldn't oceans and continents slam in, driven by the earth's rotation, to fill the part that had been torn free, and make the globe round again? Wouldn't the Earth gyrate on its axis, trying to find a new rotational equilibrium? Wouldn't cities and populations be buried, asphixiated and drowned in such a catastrophe?

How could anyone survive an event like that, either on the part of the Earth that remained intact, or the part torn free?

The movie makes it clear that the new "moon" is molten. No life there. And these questions are raised, briefly, but they're dispensed with when the movie ends. A huge chunk of the earth tears free, and is propelled into orbit. The problem is that life seems to go on as usual a few hundred feet from where the even occurred. This is hard to accept, even giving the screenwriter some dramatic license. If a massive chunk of our planet, hundreds of thousands of miles across, were ripped free, ignited, and went hurtling into the sky, at the very least it would create a scorched earth effect for a vast distance around. It's also questionable whether our atmosphere would remain intact and breathable after such an event, as appears to be the case at the end. (Though maybe after the credits rolled and the screen went black, the hero and heroine fell over dead... you never know!)

Still "Crack in the World" is fun. It's also a perfect period piece, a better-than-average SF movie of the 1960s. I'm giving it five stars mainly because it's a wild ride and a novel scenario. It's also a valid cautionary tale, in spite of the story's scientific flaws.

text:
I have mixed feelings about "Blood and Chrome."

Considered as a "thing in itself," and forgetting for a moment about its connections with Battlestar Galactica, I like and respect it. It has good effects, reasonably good actors, and is a tightly told story.

But in the context of the regular BG series, overall it seems a little shallow. It's essentially BG re-imagined for a young male adult audience (18-23 year olds) (playing up the military experience, young men proving themselves, a (very) little sex and a lot of explosions). The story isn't bad - it makes a nice prelude to BG in its way, and also references the spin-off series Caprica. The plot is pretty good but suffers a little from having been broken into bite-size chunks due to its being originally formatted as a web series.

Are these things bad? Not necessarily. The unusual pacing (due to the webisode story story structure) is a little jarring at first, but once you get into it it's fine. The producers know their audience, and tailored Blood and Chrome effectively to that demographic. Like the title implies, there's lots of fighting and testosterone. I would say if you're young, and a guy, and can relate to the "young man goes to war" fantasy elements, you'll probably enjoy it... what's not to like? If you're female, and/or older, you may find it less engaging, lacking in some of the more subtle and disturbing elements that made Battlestar Galactica such an effective commentary on the human condition, and so interesting to watch.

title_x: Not quite up to the 5 star standard but close!
text:
Probably the most critical thing I could say about this series is that it suffers from the same thing to which many films produced today fall prey. And that is a serious over burdening of just too much hindsight. It's easy to make characters seem all-knowing and visionary when the past has already happened and you write their parts with the knowledge of what is still to come.

The other serious falter with this series is a lack of professional editing. There are only two genuine reasons for editing a film. One is the obvious location change when the shooting must end and start again or at the wrap up of a days schedule. The other reason is for natural scene changes as in the advancement of chapter one to chapter two etc. But when an edit ocurrs over and over in the same scene for no apparent reason there are two possible explanations - neither of which are really considered very professional. One is that the producer and director are working with a smaller budget than is necessary and instead of running multiple cameras from different angles, they try to film one angle for the closeup shots of one actor then reset for the closeup shots of the other actor(s) and piece them together in the editing bay to appear as if it was all done at the same time. The reality is it could have been done on different days - sometimes weeks apart. In this film it becomes very obvious when the main couple is on the dance floor and the editing keeps going back and forth from her to him and back. Most of the time it works and appears seamless except when you pay atttention to the orchestra in the background and realize that sometimes there are holes in the music because of the edits. I was just about to compliment the actors and the director because the couple really could dance as could most of the other couples on the floor - something that is seriously lacking and overlooked in most films today. Even when people can dance, on film, it looks clumsy because of the edits. Normally the dancers may be dancing to silence and the music is dubbed in later which makes it appear as if they're constantly out of step or time with the band. In this case, with the orchestra present in many of the scenes, they probably were dancing to live music while the cameras rolled. But it's very difficult to get the orchestra to be in the exact right place when the edits occur - so again they usually dub in the score after the editing. Sometimes it works, this time is almost worked but for a few miss-cues.

I was also about to compliment the wardrobe and makeup director because it appears as if most of the ladies hairstyles were appropriate for the time and place but then I noticed that the same was not true for the men. Most men in 1930s Europe did not have Hair Stylist haircuts. Those that could afford a barber still didn't have their hair "Styled" and look like they stepped out of the "Salon" in 2013. Instead they had what today is known as the "Bowl Cut" which is close cropped on the sides and back with a bit of a mop on top. Today's movie people seem to think that there have only been two styles of men's haircuts over all of time and that is the "Beatle" cut and the "military" cut. But a quick Google review would prove them wrong and since it's a free service, I fail to see why most don't take advantage and give their movies more credibility.

As far as spy movies go, and especially spy movies dealing with WWII Nazis this seems a bit on the tame side when it comes to blood and death. Yes, it's here but it's not nearly as graphic or as prevalent as one would expect it to be by 21st century movie standards. Perhaps because the director was a female, the perspective was not what we have been accustomed to seeing.

The last critique I'd like to point out is the fact that all of the French, all of the Germans as well as the Polish and the Russians in this film all seemed to have perfectly very very stiff-upper-lip-British accents. Somehow I thought all those nationalities would have a different type of accent when speaking English. Oh silly me, what would make me think that? But it does make this film a bit harder to follow when you're not quite sure who's who and on which side of the board they're playing. It would have been so much easier to watch and follow if they had taken some language diction lessons. It's a little trick that many directors will use to aid in the viewer's comfort level being where it needs to be for most optimum viewing. This film failed and for that reason, just cannot score a 5 star rating.

On the more positive side, the story is fairly well developed and for the most part can hold your interest. There is enough of the espionage mixed with the love story to keep both in balance. The filming locations looked to be as authentic as they could be with most of the shooting actually being in Poland. So the scenery is pleasant to look at.

Whether this has any historical accuracy or not, I am not sure but that's not important here. What is important is that it tells a story of likely events for the time and it does that fairly well.

title_x: Make no mistake - THIS IS A 5-Star MOVIE!!!
text:
If you thought this was a movie about BUILDING the Rabbit-Proof Fence in Australia, think agiain. Better yet, go back and re-read the title of the movie. It does not say anything about BUILDING!

TO KILL A MOCKINGBIRD is not about hunting fowl. CATCHER IN THE RYE is not about playing baseball in a grain field and THE ART OF RACING IN THE RAIN doesn't mention Mario Andretti, Dale Earnhardt, Secretariat or Seabiscut. So get over it already! To give this movie a 1-star rating based upon your own misgivings is incredibly lame.

This is a movie about the fence and the role it played in the lives of these three young girls and their mother. It also played a role in their attempted re-capture and had significance for the government agency hunting them down. SO IT IS ABOUT THE FENCE.

But it's a lot more. It's about the injustices delt upon the native population by misguided white people on power trips. It's also a reflective mirror in a way. The Aussies were not the first to remove tribal youth from their parrents and send them off to boarding schools. The United States started the practice with Native American Children in 1860 and continued until 1978.

This film is educational in a huge way even if there are dramatizations that were not actual occurances.

It's a sad movie in many ways and a movie about human perserverance and triumph. It's about how looking back makes it much easier to tell right from wrong.

This is one of two movies I know of that dealt with the Australian government's policy of removing Aboriginal children from their homes. The other is called: "The Sapphires". It is a 2012 Australian film which is loosely based on a real-life 1960s girl group that toured Vietnam military bases in the 1960s and early 1970s. (It's available on Amazon Prime for a small rental fee). Both movies are quite good in their production quality and storytelling and well worth watching.

This is a great movie to watch, learn and reflect in a group setting. With children or adults here are some starter questions to get the conversation going. Then just let each person come to their own realization of what the movie meant to them. It's more important that they own whatever feelings they gain from it than it is to belittle their contributions to the discussion.
Question 1) How did this movie make you feel?
Question 2) How would you feel if you were these girls' mother? (for adults)
Question 3) How would you feel if you were one of these girls? (for children)
Question 4) Do you think the tracker (who was aborigine) didn't find the girls on purpose?
Question 5) How do you think Mr. Neville would have felt if his own children were taken from him?

If you have a group discussion. Each person will get a lot more out of the film and it's meaning. Good luck!
description: ['At a time when it was Australian government policy to train aboriginal children as domestic workers and integrate them into white society, three girls escape their internment camp and embark on a dangerous 1,500-mile adventure back home.']

title_x: Not one of the better submarine movies and disrespectful to the era of WWII
text: Overacting, cheezy effects and lack of understanding of the period combine for a less than entertaining movie.  Over-use of today's technical ability to create effects and lack of quality directing makes this a very "sub-standard" submarine movie.  The effects of the depth charges exploding outside the sub and the crew being battered about inside the sub goes on and on and on way too long in each situation.  The crew whisper to maintain stealth and even the captain and radio man whisper into the microphone - until the sub springs leeks from the explosions, then they yell like hell.....guess the enemy cannot hear them over the noise of the explosions.  The explosion effects are about 10 times more powerfull than anything available in WWII.  We're supposed to believe that just one single topedo can blow up a battleship from stem to stern with a fireball half the size of the atomic bomb and the ship will sink in less than 20 seconds.  The flashlights all give off a bright blue-white hue - just like today's LED bulbs.  Yet anyone who knows, knows that WWII flashlights were incandescent and gave off a very yellow colored light....LED lights just don't work in a WWII movie.  Also, even though Matthew McConaughe's hair was cut short, it was TODAY's military haircut, not the style of WWII.  Others, who did not have hair cut as short, still had hair styles not appropriate for the period.  Barbers of the day used to do a great business because civilian men would get a haircut every 10 days.  Military men got it cut once a week at a minimum.  Some of these actors hadn't seen the clippers in over 3 weeks.  Then too, where was the Vitalis and the Brylecreem.  Men of the 1940's liked that slicked back wet look, not the freshly washed and blow-dried look seen in this movie.  Lastly, the amount of insubordination from crew would never have even been thought of in WWII much less tollerated.  This is another example of today's actors, directors and script writers not doing their homework.  Even if they don't have first hand experience, there are still plenty of people alive who do and would be able to consult if approached.  The culture differences are just too great to ignore and hope for a believable picture.  I don't know how, in good conscience, the producers could dedicate this film to the men who served and so completely disrespect the attitudes and perspectives that created the will for them to do what was necessary.  All in all I found this movie to be much less than expected especially from such name acters as Matthew McConaughey

In this last installment, Lisbeth Salander (Noomi Rapace) lies in critical condition, a bullet wound to her head, in the intensive care unit of a Swedish city hospital. She's fighting for her life in more ways than one: if and when she recovers, she'll be taken back to Stockholm to stand trial for three murders. With the help of her friend, journalist Mikael Blomkvist (Michael Nyqvist), she will not only have to prove her innocence, but also identify and denounce those in authority who have allowed the vulnerable, like herself, to suffer abuse and violence. And, on her own, she will plot revenge - against the man who tried to kill her, and the corrupt government institutions that very nearly destroyed her life. THE GIRL WHO KICKED THE HORNET'S NEST brings back Noomi Rapace in the starring role of the pierced and tattooed genius computer hacker Lisbeth Salander, Michael Nyqvist as Mikael Blomkvist, the crusading journalist and publisher of the magazine Millennium, and Lena Endre (Erika Berger) the editor of the magazine and Blomkvist's occasional lover."]

All of the characters were such a hoot. The story itself was equally enjoyable and hilarious. Such a gorgeous land looked as if straight from a fairy tale to a boy who grew up in south Texas and Arizona. Sure I loved where I grew up. This land though was so green it almost made the eyes hurt. Wherever the eyes feel, there were things I'd never seen. Streams everywhere, old bridges, churches, stonework, straw thatched roofs, quaint homes and old buildings; it all infatuating to a desert rat like me. How could beauty, humor, and quirky characters fail to delight? And through it all ran this stunning redhead I loved so.
It was an absolute delight to watch it again. For a little while I forgot I was grown to 60 years of age. Just for a couple of hours, I was again a redheaded boy, not yet ten. 💖

text:
I knew nothing about this movie going in. I don't watch TV anymore, so I don't see trailers on a regular basis. Only if I go searching for them online. I'm not usually into movies like this...referring to the type of violence. I don't like boxing. I mean, I can watch movie fighting, I'm not that sensitive, it's just not what I prefer. So, you might be wondering why I even watched it in the first place. Well...I have to be honest. It was because of Tom Hardy. I just think he's an amazing actor. He's like Daniel Day-Lewis plus Robert DeNiro and maybe even a dash of Lawrence Olivier thrown in for good measure.

I watched Bronson a couple of years ago, and I thought if I can sit through that for Tom Hardy, surely I can watch this movie. If you haven't seen Bronson, you won't know what I'm referring to. Not that it was very much like this movie, just that the character he plays is violent and angry and well, kinda crazy..okay, well, a lot crazy.

The character he plays in this movie isn't exactly crazy, but he is angry. I don't want to give anything specific away about the movie, but I'll just say his character has issues.

Well, I'm glad I gave it a chance, because I ended up liking it a lot. Yes, there are fight scenes that made me not want to watch, but I didn't exactly sit here with my eyes covered. The fighting, I thought, was realistic, not over-done or gratuitous. I found myself wanting certain things to happen, or characters to say what I thought they should say, but it was okay that they didn't. It makes it more real when it's not all tied up with a neat little bow. And that's what makes great story-telling.

And it is the story here that hooks you. I didn't even think of not finishing it. The script was excellent, and the acting superb. Nick Nolte's character was painful to watch, but Nick's performance was wonderful. I realized after it was over that Tom Hardy's character didn't really have much dialogue, but you don't notice that as you're watching. Joel Edgarton was awesome, and I thought Jennifer Morrison (who currently plays Emma in the TV series Once Upon a Time) who plays his wife here, was perfectly cast. She was just right.

It's hard to find a movie that brings it all together so well and makes you feel like it was time well spent. I felt that this really was one of those movies. Just good entertainment.

Watch and enjoy!

title_x: How should we understand "All is Lost"?
text:
An engaging but intense allegory. Unfortunately, much of the symbolism would require another viewing. For example, there are several shots from under the life raft with the bottom of the life raft in a circle of light as a focal point and the dark blue of the ocean around that circle. The shots are progressive in that the first shot is a close up with tiny crustacions, then a farther removed shot, then a shot of a school of minnows, then a school of minnows pursued by larger fish, then larger fish pursued and captured by a larger fish, then a school of sharks. In the final scenes, the shot is of the life raft in a circle of fire with Redford falling into the depths. Just what had the director intended with these progressive shots? The wonderful problem solving of Redford on the yacht to each obstacle that arose was an encouragement for the viewer to anticipate a happy ending. Yet, with a great deal of skill, the director left our household wondering and arguing about whose hand it was that reached into the water: was it a man or was it God?
Perhaps, the title itself is a reference to Job on his dung heap surveying his ruin? Perhaps it is an allegory about human life and its ultimate point -- meaning what?

I am not getting how this movie got such a terrible low number of stars from reviewers. Were they looking for Shakespeare? It is clearly a light comedy, and on that level I thought it delivered in spades. I found myself laughing out loud several times. The chemistry between the actors added to the believability of the preposterous plot, a plot that Abbott and Costello or the three stooges would have found themselves comfortable in. The writers dodged cliches and stayed on the edge and I only caught the drift of the surprise twist about three quarters of the way through. I write and I know plot devices, there are only so many and the makers of "Horrible Bosses" managed to find a few new twists and keep the dialog fresh. That is if the viewer can dispense with a few levels of disbelief that anyone could be so moronic or deranged. In fact there are many people who are as moronic and deranged as the actors characters, so it wasn't that much of a stretch.
Jennifer Aniston in the sexiest role I have ever seen her in. Kevin Spacey shined as the machiavellian manipulator, as did Colin Ferrel, who takes a part way out of his usual range. the three principals were consistently funny, playing off each other like real friends would. title_x: A fascinating drama about the family secrets behind a megachurch dynasty
text: This is a family drama that opens with the return of an estranged daughter to a family that has built a dynasty from a megachurch that is under investigation and hiding an explosive family secret. Merle Dandridge plays the role of the daughter, and she is simply stunning as a point of view character who leads you through the cast of characters, who at first are a bit confusing, but quickly come into focus, like a novel that gets better as you read it. Oprah plays the role of an aunt who keeps encouraging her to speak truth to power. It's refreshing to watch a television show that examines contemporary issues that are playing out in real time, like the Black Lives Matter movement. Noah Kendall and Desiree Ross are just two bright lights in a very strong cast of actors. The existence of this program is a sign that we are truly in a golden age of television.

text:
Entertaining Western. Rated R for violence, cussing (some GDs and a couple of "F" bombs), three brief scenes of surgery, and a post-love, so to speak, scene without nudity.

I like Russell Crowe best as the good guy, heroic figure, like in "Gladiator" (2000), or "Cinderella Man" (2005). But here, he shows that he's quite an effective bad guy as the ornery villain Ben Wade. Before watching the movie, I was paging around a bit in the Book of Proverbs in the Bible, and what do you know, Wade mentions the same book early in the movie during a saloon scene:

"Proverbs 13:3 He that keepeth his mouth keepeth his life; He that opens his lips too wide brings on his own destruction."

A little later, Wade mentions the same Bible book again in speaking at table to Byron McElroy (Peter Fonda):

"Every way of man is right in his own eyes, Byron. The Lord ponders the heart. Proverbs 21."

But is Wade a villain with a soft spot for God's Word, or is he just quoting it to manipulate people. He later insults McElroy by accusing him of being a man of one book, the Bible:

Wade: "Byron's like a song with one note. You ever read another book in your life, Byron, sides' the Bible?"
Byron: "No need."

The good guy in "3:10" is Dan Evans (Christian Bale). Bale's Evans is a Civil War veteran with a gimpy foot from battle, who is struggling to provide for his wife Alice (Gretchen Mol), 14-year-old son William (Logan Lerman), and younger son Mark (Ben Petry), who has tuberculosis. As the movie begins, William has a barely suppressed, smoldering/simmering contempt for his father, who he subtly taunts as not doing good enough for his family. In an early scene, Dan tells Alice that he's tired of his family looking down upon him and God's seeming silence to his plight:

"Now I'm tired, Alice, I am tired of watching my boys go hungry. I'm tired of the way that they look at me. I'm tired of the way that you don't. I've been standing on one leg for three damn years, waiting for God to do me a favor. .. And He ain't listening."

By capturing and bringing to a train for transport to prison the outlaw Ben Wade, will Dan be able to earn sorely needed reward money for his family and raise himself in their eyes? That's the movie's plot.

Ben Foster as Ben Wade's chief sidekick, the brutal, cold, even psychopathic Charlie Pierece, is a scene-stealer.

Spoiler Alert**********************************************************************************************************************************************************

With Ben Wade in custody, and needing to get him on the 3:10 to Yuma by going through a seemingly impossible gauntlet of Wade's men and townsfolk who are promised a bounty if they will kill those trying to get Wade to the train, Evans receives a memorable monologue from Wade. Maybe sensing the type of words Dan spoke to his wife earlier, Wade gives the story of the beginning of his life and of how his mother and God let him down. Obviously tempting Dan to give up his mission in discouragement, Wade says:

"You ever read the Bible, Dan? I read it one time. I was eight-years-old. My daddy just got hisself killed over a shot of whiskey and my Mom said we're going back East to start over. So she gave me a Bible, sat me down in the train station, and told me to read it. She was goin' to get our tickets. But I did what she said. I read that Bible from cover to cover. Took me three days. .. She never came back."

As the movie moves towards its climax, you wonder who's going to give Wade's sidekick Charlie Pierce his comeuppance, who's going to kill him? Dan? His son William? Wade? Someone else?

Also, as the movie moves towards its peak, Ben Wade is thrown a gun. Looking at its handle, one sees welded to it a gold crucifix.

title_x: Excellent, based on a true story
text:
Excellent movie based on the true story of Walter Keane (Christopher Waltz) becoming a celebrity in the late 50s by taking credit for the "Big Eyes" Children artwork of his wife Margaret (Amy Adams), who won a Best Actress, Musical/Comedy Golden Globe for her performance.

Margaret's conscience is bothered by the fraud and though she's a "Methodist", she talks to a Catholic priest in a confessional in San Francisco saying she is most bothered about lying to her daughter. In an extras interview on the disc, the real life Margaret Keane, still alive, says, "If they're (people are) doing something wrong, admit it, turn around and start over and do the right thing."

In addition to effectively portraying Margaret Keene's inner emotions, Amy Adams is given some memorable dialogue to deliver, including the following about her "Big Eyes" Children artwork early in the movie to her husband-to-be, Walter:

"I believe that you can see things in the eyes. The eyes are the window to the soul. ... The eyes are how I express my emotions."

I've read that more than 90% of communication is non-verbal. The late Catholic psychiatrist Conrad Baars (1919-1981) wrote: "[P]eople are very little aware of the way in which their eyes mirror their inner feelings. ... for the will can mask or control the expression of the eyes only very slightly ... tender love leaves its unmistakeable mark in the expression of the eyes. The tender gaze is characterized by repose and tranquility in the delight of contemplating the good. It reflects ... the joy of love."

In a brief role as a New York Times art critic, John Canady (Terence Stamp), says "Art should elevate". Indeed it should, but too much modern art drags down by denigration and even blasphemy. Do some artists try to cover up a lack of artistic talent by creating controversy? In the movie, not wanting his (mostly Margaret's) artwork to be hung by the bathrooms of a nightclub, Walter Keane says, "When people see art they shouldn't think of s**t."

But too often, they do. I think of the infamous "Piss Christ".

St. Thomas Aquinas defined beauty as "that which being perceived, pleases." And, "the nearer they (all things) are to God, the more beautiful they are."

Artists and those interested in art will probably particularly enjoy "Big Eyes".

title_x: Procative, Painful, and Very Difficult to Watch
text:
Directed by Swedish-Danish couple Frida and Lasse Barkfors, PERVERT PARK (2014) profiles several child molesters who have been arrested and convicted of sex crimes. They are now on parole and living in a Florida trailer park, which functions as a sort of half-way house as they struggle to return to society. The subjects speak frankly about the crimes that brought them into the legal system. One man raped a five year old girl. Another man, a homosexual who was trying to pass as straight, molested two boys. Two men, one young and one in late middle age, were arrested in an internet sting, after conversations with people who turned out to be police officers in disguise. But the emphasis is on two people, William Fuery and Tracy Hutchinson.

Fuery is a man in late middle age who works for the trailer park, half security guard, half maintenance office. He describes an extremely abusive childhood, a devastating family tragedy, and years of ‘acting out’ behavior that ultimately led to two charges of sexual battery against two girls. His account of his life and his crimes are detailed but very matter-of-fact, and his tone is one of exhaustion. Hutchinson is a woman in early middle age who describes childhood molestation by her father. Even as an adult she was unable to completely break from him, and she ultimately acted out the same behavior with her son, who in turn molested a child younger than himself. Her telling of the story is deeply, painfully emotional.

Fuery and Hutchinson believe their criminal behavior is rooted in the molestation and abuse they themselves experienced in childhood and was furthered by substance abuse. At the same time, they do not excuse themselves on that basis. Fuery in particularly is very plain: I was the adult, he says. Explanation is possible; understanding what brought them to that point is essential; but there is no possible excuse, and although some of the subjects seem to conceal certain depths, none of them try to shift blame away from themselves.

Some years ago I had a discussion with a psychiatrist who specializes in issues pertaining to children. He said, in his opinion, there were two types of molesters. The first was usually a middle-aged man who underwent a personal crisis of some sort—a divorce, a death, a job loss—and who began to molest a child as a means of demonstrating personal control. My friend felt that such people, who were often shocked by their own behavior, responded well to treatment. The second was a person for whom molestation was ingrained. “The only sure way to control them,” my friend said, “is to put a sword over their head. You have to make them know that if they do it again, they’re going to be so deep under the jail they’ll never see sunlight again.”

It is difficult to know to which category the subjects of PERVERT PARK belong. Some have been victims of childhood molestation—but to what extent does that imply “ingrained” behavior? Some seem to have been involved in isolated events that may have been prompted by loss of personal control—but to what extent can we truly believe what they say? I think the film is an important one, because it reminds us that child molesters are in fact human beings. When you consider the overall scope of the lives and behavior of these particular people, it becomes difficult to define them as “monsters.” (When asked if she has met any ‘monsters’ in the park, Hutchinson says “Only me.”) But there are a couple of things we have to note about this documentary.

There is no “fact check.” We must take the subjects entirely at their word, and while they certainly seem honest and sincere, it is difficult to have a valid opinion of their behavior, or of appropriate treatment or punishment, without a firm knowledge of the background facts. Similarly, and excepting Hutchinson, we really do not know anything about the victims or the impact the crimes had on them, which also prevents us from forming a clear opinion re the appropriateness of their sentencing. We also have to remember these particular people are actually the ones deemed unlikely to re-offend—but there are others who remain incarcerated because they are deemed too dangerous for release.

PERVERT PARK left me with a deep sense of pity for its subjects, particularly for Tracy Hutchinson, who bares her emotions so painfully. It also forced me to reconsider some of my thoughts on how child molesters should be treated by the justice system and by society in general, and I left the film with the belief that each offender must be dealt with on a truly case-by-case basis. Even so, my pity and my new assesment did not translate into sympathy. As Fuery said, they were the adults, and we expect adults to protect and defend children, not damage them or prey upon them. When all is said and done, they are responsible for their own actions.

The other half-hour is the worst episode of Ghost Adventures ever. 20 minutes is random tours with random people and the actual "investigation" is Zak's overnight, which was over 8 hours, but yielded 10 minutes of footage. True Facts: I don't believe in ghosts, but I love this "Paranormal Investigators" junk, much in the same way i love Sci-Fi and Fantasy, but suspension of disbelief will not be enough to make Demon House what you want it to be. text:
When this movie was first released in theatres, my husband and I saw it about four or five times. We even bought a copy of the poster to display in our home.

We liked it that well.

However, my current husband (yes, a different one) had never seen the film.

I wasn't sure if it (the film, not the marriage) would hold up well if we watched it so many years after its release.

Nervously, I set it up with our large-screen projector, to see it large on our home theatre screen.

And then...

It was even better than I'd remembered. The scenery, the music, and the styling of it were all breathtaking. The dry humor adds to it, and Sean Connery actually plays the role convincingly.

It's like being immersed in a magnificent setting, in a cultural context from a century ago, but where everything seems seamlessly odd and logical at the same time.

If you've seen this before, it's worth revisiting. And it's best on the largest TV or screen you have. The scenery is still astonishing and grand.

title_x: Guardians of the Galaxy Vol.2-In My Own Words
text:
I vividly remember seeing Guardians of the Galaxy in a packed theater back in 2014. I wasn't sure what to expect, but I ended up leaving the theater thoroughly satisfied.

Much of James Gunn's ambition carries over into Guardians of the Galaxy Vol.2, and it ends up being a relatively bigger sequel than I'd originally thought it would be.

Chris Pratt is as humorous as he was in the 2014 film, but the movie harbours more serious moments for his character; which in turn benefit Vol. 2. Zoe Saldana and Karen Gillan both return as Gamora and Nebula respectively. What I liked more with these two characters is that James Gunn chose to make Nebula more inclusive to the film; and her scenes alongside Gamora adds to the depth the movie has.

As expected, both Rocket Raccoon (voiced by Bradley Cooper) and Baby Groot (voiced by Vin Diesel) bring their usual comedic antics to Vol. 2, but even Dave Bautista's character Drax adds to the humor. One of the biggest surprises of the movie ends up being Michael Rooker's character Yondu.

The movie is very well designed, perhaps even moreso than the previous film. It is certainly larger in scale and the character design is nicely done. It is one reason why Kurt Russell's character Ego and Pom Klementieff's character Mantis fit right into Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2. Elizabeth Debicki's Ayesha is another well designed character.

Though it is much larger in scale, Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2 doesn't shy away from what made the first film a success. James Gunn's sequel packs more humor and a lot more unexpected emotion.

And while viewing the film, Gunn's ambition is very evident. Its unfortunate that the sequel has jokes that don't always land, and the movie doesn't always progress as smoothly as the original did.

Those criticisms aside, Guardians of the Galaxy Vol.2 still manages to be a mostly successful sequel.

Coming in at 2 hours and 16 minutes long (not including the 5 post-credits scenes), Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2 is an entertaining and emotional sequel that further expands the Guardians of the Galaxy series. There are a ton of easter eggs and other characters that appear; and I have no doubt Guardians of the galaxy Vol. 3 will continue to expand both the Guardians of the Galaxy and the Marvel Cinematic Universe.

title_x: Kong Skull Island-In My Own Words
text:
Kong: Skull Island succeeds where a lot of films of this genre don't always-and that benefits the movie in a lot of ways.

This star-studded film stars Tom Hiddleston (James) Brie Larson (Mason) and Samuel L. Jackson(Preston) to name a few of the many big names in the movie; though it's well worth noting the supporting characters leave a highly impressive mark on the movie. Shea Whigham's character Earl being one example of this, as is John C. Reilly's character Hank Marlow. The
additions of both Toby Kebell(Jack) and Jason Mitchell(Glenn) add to Kong: Skull Island's humor.

Not to take away from the monster himself either, Kong Skull Island's main success comes from how effective the movie is at bringing the iconic ape to life on the big screen. The movie's best moments are whenever Kong is going at it with one of his opponents; even better the movie gives Kong a considerably enormous size that makes the ape a sight in itself to behold. Finally, the movie does a better job of ensuring that Kong gets enough screentime-and isn't overshadowed by his human co-stars. As a fan of monster films, I very much enjoyed this.

The scenery and camera angles combined with Kong Skull Island's CGI go on to further benefit the movie.

What disappointed me with Kong Skull Island is certain of the character arcs become thinly developed as opposed to some of their other respective co-stars.

And despite this shortcoming-that does not hold the movie down. Where Kong: Skull Island falters in characterization occasionally, it still impressively delivers sheer entertainment and knows well what it wants to be as a movie.

title_x: Despite some slick action sequences and a nice outing by Rupert Friend, Hitman Agent 47 is only just average
text:
As the summer draws to a close, Fox ends its summer run at the movies with the movie: Hitman Agent 47.

What works surprisingly well for Hitman Agent 47 as a movie is that Rupert Friend's portrayal of the popular assassin is spot on in more ways than none. While Timothy Olyphant's 47 was bald in the 2007 film much like the video game character, Rupert Friend is able to convey 47's mannerisms and style in a more believable manner. Hannah Ware's character Katia makes for a solid, though not entirely satisfying supporting character. And as a movie, Hitman Agent 47 delivers some timely action scenes. I also like how "Diane" (a nod to Diana from the games) is utilized in this movie as opposed to the 2007 movie.

Unfortunately, not all of Hitman Agent 47 is good. Aside from an uneven story, Hitman Agent 47 lacks an interesting supporting cast. Despite being mostly indestructible, Zachary Quinto's character John Smith never really feels as imposing or threatening as the antagonist. The story never feels as exciting as it tries to be, and it does lacks certain qualities of the games. Though it doesn't always entertain, Hitman Agent 47 ends up being only just average despite a good performance by Rupert Friend and some nice action scenes.

While Fox has ended its summer run at the movies on a particularly disappointing note(this and Fantastic Four), I do think their upcoming movies like The Martian and Joy will entertain audiences better than Fantastic Four and Agent 47 have. We have yet to have a thoroughly good video game adaptation, and as a fan of both Michael Fassbender and the Assassin's Creed games I hope Fox does justice to that particular series with the 2016 movie adaptation. Hitman Agent 47 gets

2.5 Stars

title_x: Though It may not be perfect, San Andreas is an thrill-a-minute movie that is one of the better disaster movies to date
text:
The last disaster movie I saw in recent memory was the 2009 movie 2012. Frankly, I think at that time I was more scared of the events in the movie itself as opposed to the supposed "Mayan Prophecy". I like disaster films that cause you to think as a viewer and allow your mind to ponder about all the possibilities if such a disaster could occur. And with no further adieu, here is my review on the movie San Andreas.

After rescuing a girl from almost falling from her car to her death, Ray later calls his daughter to talk about their trip to San Francisco. Ray soon arrives at his soon to be ex-wife Emma's new home belonging to her new boyfriend Daniel. Over at the Hoover Dam, Dr.Park and Dr.Hayes are both currently investigating a possible earthquake, when suddenly a fault ruptures starting an earthquake. Upon further realization, Dr.Hayes realizes that the San Andreas fault is shifting; thereby on the verge of causing a massive earthquake.

Over the past couple of years, Dwayne Johnson has made quite the name for himself. And he does a really good job as the helicopter rescue pilot Ray. Also starring in the movie is actor Paul Giamatti as Dr. Hayes and I definitely enjoyed his performance; due to how well his character is able to explain the cause that ultimately lead to the disastrous effects. Alexandra Daddario plays Ray's daughter Blake alongside actress Carla Gugino who portrays her mom Emma. I enjoyed Alexandra's performance, though there were times I felt that Carla Gugino could have done a bit more in certain scenes. Overall though, I was satisfied in terms of acting.

In terms of story, there is not necessarily a major plot line to follow, but then again this IS a disaster movie. In that, you get these enormous earthquakes that cause massive destruction that ultimately ends up being really marvelous to look at; thanks to the impressive visual effects. Visually, San Andreas can do no wrong and is a gorgeous watch.
And believe me when I say, once San Andreas DOES take off, there is no slowing it down. Even better, I found the third act of the movie to be executed exceptionally well; because of the still growing suspense, and due to a few touching moments between the main characters. And just so you know, San Andreas is a movie I encourage you to GO SEE because of the acting(just remember Carla Gugino does only just enough), the visual bravado, the pacing of the movie, the timely manner in which the story is executed, and the the exceptional payoff of the third act. It may not be a perfect disaster film or even the best disaster film, but it is one of the better disaster films in recent memory and that is why San Andreas is

A GOOD Experience

text:
This 2008 offering, based on a book by Phillipa Gregory, depicts the lesser-known aspects of the tragic saga of King Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn, played here respectively by a relatively staid Eric Bana and a sparkly, and appropriately vivacious Natalie Portman.
The film, directed by Justin Chaddock, is, as many have noted, rafe with inaccuracies. But it begins with a view of the early lives of the three surviving (two died in childhood) Boleyn children, Anne, George, and Mary(Daisy Doidge-Hill,Finton Reilly, and Kizzy Fassett), romping in a field. Anne, the most agressive of the trio, comes out on top in the game they were playing, winning the praise of their father, Sir Thomas Boleyn(Mark Rylance), and episode that precludes the main events of the childrens' lives in certain ways.
Several years later, we see the now-grown children on Mary's wedding day to William Carey(Benedict Cumberbatch).
In viewing this film, as well as another period piece featuring Scarlett Johansson--"Girl With a Pearl Earring", I've often felt that another blonde actress--namely Kate Hudson, with her squarer jawline, bore a stronger resemblance to both Mary Boleyn and Vermeer's muse( and Hudson had been slated to play at least one of them).But in view of the speculativeness and/or inaccuracies of either film, Johansson aptly acquitts herself.
In actuality, the Boleyn sisters' dubious careers as royal courteseans began during their father's years in France--at least Mary's, during her time of service in the court of Queen Claude. Mary's first conquest was the French King Francois, but she had been sent home because of the Queen's resentment of the situation.
Here, the Boleyns encounter Henry when he is injured during a hunting accident on their estate, which Anne unintentionally caused.Henry desires a liason with the married noblewoman, Mary as she nurses him.They both become ladies-in-waiting to Queen Catherine(Ana Torrent).
Elizabeth Howard ( played by Kristin Scott-Thomas with the reputedly blonde good looks of the Howard family), expresses her disapproval as the sexual and political intrigues involving her children begin, and then escalate, but is sadly ignored.Under the scheming machinations of her Uncle, the Duke of Norfolk(David Morrissey), Mary becomes King Henry's mistress, and bears him a son.
We deal with the inaccuaracy of Anne marrying her sweetheart Henry Percy(OliverColeman), when, in fact, she was only betrothed to him.Confiding the news of her marriage to her brother, George(Jim Sturgess), George tells Mary, who reports this to her father and uncle due to fear that Anne's marrying a prominent nobleman without the King's permission will compromise the family.Anne has her marriage annuled and is exiled to France.
Mary's pregnancy by the King leads to the increased wealth of her family at the King's pleasure.We observe the ritual of her confinement when the pregnancy becomes a high risk one.
Norfok has his other niece returned home to help keep the King's attention from wandering to other mistresses, but ultimately this backfires, and as Mary gives birth to her son, Henry, the King's attention turns to Anne, and they two begin to plot to dislodge Queen Katherine, who can no longer give the King a son.
Mary, who is widowed by this point is sent to the country to live with her child. Eventually, she will marry the kindly William Stafford(Eddie Redmayne), who offers her security and a peaceful life away from court intrigues.
Amid the annoying array of inaccuacies is the scene of The King raping Anne after he has broken with Rome, declared himself the Head of the Church of England, and exiled Catherine after she still refuses to consumate their relationship.
Anne and Henry marry, and Anne is coronated, and the latter gives birth to a daughter, Elizabeth, much to Henry's dismay.A second child -- a boy--- is stillborn--leading the desperate queen to consider incest with George(which history relates was a fabrication) in the hope of the pretense of maintaining the pregancy, and hiding the miscarriage from the King for fear of being burned.
But George's long neglected wife, Jane(Juno Temple), reports her suspicions, setting the events leading to the downfall of both George and Anne.
As Mary's marriage to William Stafford earned her the ire of her family, as she did it with out permission, it is unlikely that she was present during her sister's miscarriage, or during Anne's final moments, or that she had any hand in rearing her niece, Elizabeth. But the emphasis is on the fact that ultimately, the lesser-acknowledged Boleyn sister led the happiest and most stress-free life of any of the Boleyn siblings, outliving all members of her immediate family.
What this tale lacks in accuracy, it makes up for in being a cautionary tale about the tragically high price of glory.

title_x: Addiction to This Stylish Series?...Must Be Catchin'!
text:
This stylish series about those working for the now-defunct airline for which an uncle of mine once worked, and on which I myself flew a few times in childhood(my sisters and I were given pins with the Pan Am logo and wings at the end of one such flight) successfully holds a viewer's interest.
It follows the adventures of flight crew members, including pilots Dean Lowrey and Ted Vanderway(Mike Vogel and Michael Mosely), and focuses mainly on their female flight attendants, including the head flight attendant, Maggie Ryan ( a mouthy Christina Ricci), sisters Kate and Laura Cameron (Kelli Garner and Margot Robbie), one of whom is a CIA agent, and the other of whom is a runaway bride, who finally took a stand against their domineering mother(Kate Jennings Grant), and jilted her fiance at the altar on her wedding day, the mysterious Bridget Pierce (Annabelle Wallis,who shows the acting ability of her late uncle Richard Harris has not been lost on her), and finally, the strong, intelligent, romantic French war orphan, Colette Valois( Quebequoise actress, Karine Vanasse), as they literally jet set around the globe in 1963, when Pan Am was at the height of its glamour and prestiege.
It could easily be dismissed at the "'Mad Men' of the Airways", but its plots are intriguing, as are many of Kate's adventures as a CIA agent, the relationship between the two pilots, one a son of priviledge, and the other, a farm boy, the women having to deal with weight and girdle checks by their boss, Miss Havermeyer(Veanne Cox), the Bohemian Maggie's street smart attitude which gets her into trouble,and the kind Laura's(who makes the cover of "Life" Magazine when they do an article about the airline) final confrontation with her fiance, as well as dealing with an incident of racism at the height of the Civil Rights era.A budding romance between two of the crew members may have whetted the interests of many as well.
We see episodes of both heroism and tragedy, as well as the witnessing of history, although some have complained about inaccuracies,such as the idea of passengers having to throw luggage off the plane to reduce the weight, which was apparently stolen from "The High and the Mighty". title_x: An Excellent Golden Oldie about Teen Angst
text:
The 1980s were a sort of Golden Age much like the 1950s. Indeed, in some ways, the styles were alike-especially with the flat-top haircut. This movie is an excellent teenage coming of age film about the social interactions in an upper class/middle class high school. The story itself is somewhat predictable. Boy (Keith-played by Eric Stoltz) has a crush on Girl (Amanda-played by Lea Thompson)-a classy but less wealthy in-crowd chick. Keith's best friend is a tom-boy (Watts-played by Mary Stuart Masterson) who is blossoming into becoming a woman with the needs of women.

The movie's plot thus orbits around a highly anticipated date between Keith and Amanda with Watts volunteering as chauffeur. Meanwhile, the stuck up rich kid (Hardy-played by Craig Sheffer) and rival to Keith has invited Keith to a party where Hardy plans to beat up and socially humiliate Keith.

Keith must face his rival, win the girl-or perhaps win the right girl and make the right choices as to what he plans to do following high school. Unlike so much of Hollywood's cultural poison which glorifies self-destruction and family breakup, this movie gets the family to be civil to each other even with disagreements. Keith's connection to the "bad boys" in detention is also well done and reminded me-and of course many others-of their own high schools. Indeed the "bad kids" normally are the ones that make the most loyal of friendships. It's the leather jacket wearing skinhead with the heart of gold trope that seems to accurately reflect the real world.

I really enjoyed this movie and the styles and technology contemporaneous to the time of the movie (1987) filled me with an enjoyable nostalgia. Don't see this as a silly teen movie. The characters grow in this film and the audience-especially the young get a pretty solid message from the film.

It's also nice to look back at the 1980s-when peace and prosperity was the norm.
description: ['A young tomboy’s feelings for her best friend are complicated when he lands a date with the most popular girl in school.']
