title_x: Very Moving...and Excellent Portrayal of the Importance of Sadness
text:
I went to see Inside Out mainly because the kid wanted to see that film instead of any other movie and I didn't want to argue. I was pleasantly surprised by how good the film is.

The movie personifies the mental and emotional make up of Riley, a tween girl who is uprooted with her parents from Minnesota to San Francisco. Her emotions are thus Fear, Anger, Joy, Sadness, and Disgust. The five emotions control Riley's state and manage her memories. They also manage her important core memories that have a decisive influence on her personality. As the seriousness of the move starts to wear on Riley, the emotions, normally steered by Joy, start to interact in a different way. Importantly, Sadness gets in the way. This leads to the accidental loss of the core memories into the long term storage of Riley's mind. The movie does a decent job of explaining how the external things impact the internal emotions. This sets the stage for a surreal adventure.

Having grown up in a family that moved around a great deal I found the climactic scene where Sadness takes over and saves the day pretty moving. This is a great film, excellent acting and very interesting.

title_x: Completely Un-expected, Completely Frightening, and Totally Entertaining
text:
Imagine you are the subject of a criminal investigation and target of wrath for a furious, judgmental Crime TV spokesbimbo and you have Gone Girl. This movie is quite possibly the most intense, mind bending, thriller I've seen on screen in a very long time.

The movie tells the story about Nate Dunne (Ben Affleck) and his wife Amy (Rosamund Pike). Amy is the daughter of a pair of authors who used her as the inspiration for a famous children's book series called the Amazing Amy. Due to the 2008 recession, Amy and Nate lose their jobs. Nate's mother gets cancer and so the Dunnes relocate to Nate's hometown of North Carthage, Missouri (actually Cape Girardeau). The marriage wears thin. Amy has a detailed diary of the marriage-from its happy honeymoon to its cooling.

We learn from a barside conversation between Nate and his sister Margo Dunne (Carrie Coon) that Amy is a kill-joy wife. Nate can do nothing right, and he feels dread upon returning home due to the fear of what argument his wife wishes to start. Home for Nate is not a peaceful sanctuary, but a burdensome place of strife. When Nate returns home he discovers his wife missing. The crime scene appears to be a fake kidnapping and the police instantly suspect Nate. The case becomes a media sensation and the story brings in two excellent characters, Ellen Abbott (Missi Pyle) and Tanner Bolt (Tyler Bolt). Both play their roles excellently. Abbott is a vicious TV personality on the model of Nancy Grace and she moves against Nate with furious purpose. Tanner Bolt is a lawyer, a high rolling lawyer who specializes in celebrity cases. His character is the best in the movie, he is funny, intelligent, entertaining, competent, and all around wonderful.

Eventually Nate gets the idea that he is being framed by his wife. She has staged everything. Indeed we learn this is true as the movie cuts into her life. In most cases, when the antagonist gets shown and reveals the evil plan, the show falls into cliché as the good guy triumphs against the bad. In this case, Amy has everything worked out, but at (presumably) her hideaway around the Lake of the Ozarks, she has a run in with some opportunistic criminals who thwart her plan. She devises a new one, one that turns out to be even better than before. The ending of the film is completely un-expected, completely frightening, and totally entertaining.

We Were Soldiers is an enjoyable Mel Gibson movie which is based on the book We Were Soldiers Once...And Young. It could be beyond enjoyable-a transcendent study of war-but the movie deviates from the book in several significant ways. As a result it is more of a pre-Iraq Attack propaganda flick.

Mel Gibson stars as LTC Hal Moore the commander of a squadron of the 7th Cavalry who first battles the North Vietnamese Army using the US Army's Airmobile Tactics as well as heavy fire support in the Battle of the Ia Drang Valley.

The film is a bowdlerized version of The Nam, ignoring the important realities of the war as well as the critical study of the political limitations at the start of escalation that so warped the American effort. The book is far more frank of this reality.

The film also pays surprising homage to contemporary America's civil religion of "diversity." Of course, racial tension nearly crippled the US Army in Vietnam and may have contributed to the ultimate defeat of American objectives therein. This un-necessary but included inversion of reality seems to stem from the current of deliberate denial of diversity's problems that was a major part of the Bush Administration's actions following 9-11.

The film also ignores the remainder of the Battle at Ia Drang-in particular the devastating ambush at LZ Albany.

Of course, it is only a movie and there are great parts to it. It does highlight the valor of the Americans in Vietnam, it shows the home front, and the necessary building of trust necessary for successful operations. Superb acting, casting, wardrobe and set.

text:
A good adaption with such originality but the reason I gave this one 4 stars and not 5 is because for me, it didn't entirely live up to the praise and recognition it got from other reviewers.

***Spoiler Alert***

I watched this at the Cinema a while back and I was truly annoyed when people left their seats midway of the movie because the scenes and the creature "grossed" them out. Why did they not feel the same way about Beauty & the Beast? Was it because the Beast became a human or because there were some adult scenes (Reptilian on Human) in this one?

Nevertheless, this movie was slightly on the stranger side. I had mixed feelings at first (when Elisa got her pleasure on in the bathtub every morning) and having boiled eggs for breakfast & lunch every single day. This was very odd behaviour. There was just something about Elisa that I didn't quite get.

We then meet Elisa's neighbour, Giles who is a struggling artist. He tells Elisa that she is the only one who cares for him. Kinda sad in a way but the two get along exceptionally well. I think Giles is more like family to Elisa than just a neighbour or friend.

Elisa works as a cleaner in some Government sort of underground Laboratory and we then meet her friend / co-worker Zelda. This is when we realise that Elisa is a mute because Zelda serves as her interpreter. While cleaning one of the bathrooms, Colonel Strickland enters and says a few words to Elisa and Zelda. Later on, the sirens go off and the two see Strickland walking towards them and his two fingers have been ripped off. The two are asked to clean a secret Lab (where Strickland was attacked) and Elisa comes face to face with the male Reptilian. Elisa is not afraid of it. She leaves the Reptilian one of her boiled eggs and we see him grab it and return to the water.

And so the friendship between Elisa and the Reptilian begins. She secretly sneaks into the Lab and teaches the Reptilian sign language, she gives him boiled eggs everyday and even though the friendship is turning weirder and weirder, there was an absolute sweet feeling about it. Elisa proved that you should love someone / something for who they are and not what they look like!

Then Strickland is instructed to continue experimenting on the Reptilian for the betterment of America. He has already used shock therapy and the worst sort of abuse on the Reptilian. Elisa sees this and she is livid. She asks Giles to help her free the Reptilian and Giles mocks her. But Elisa says that the Reptilian is just like her and he can hear but is mute. She says she feels something when she is around him and he is the only one who understands her. Giles disagrees but eventually helps Elisa and a reluctant Zelda take the Reptilian to Elisa's apartment. They cannot take him to the river just yet because the water is low. They will have to wait until the rains flood the river.

And so the magic begins. Elisa slowly but surely falls in love with the Reptilian. They share a magical moment in the shower. I remember LMAO when Zelda asked Elisa about the Reptilian and if he has a PP. This was weird but at the same time, freakin' funny!

I am not going to tell you any more. You have to watch this yourself to feel the magic, live the fairy-tale and most of all, it's a sorta movie that you just have to scratch off from your bucket list.

Happy viewing!

text:
I loved Stranger Things and Arrival and the producers have not disappointed me in this one.

It was a brilliant performance by ALL characters and various plot twists that I didn't anticipate would happen!

***Spoiler Alert***

What if someone told you that there was a virus (IAAN) which could give children super powers and make them superior to adults? Many children couldn't adapt to the virus and died but the remaining survivors were feared by adults and therefore sent to various secluded camps to be controlled and rehabilitated. The children would only be allowed to return to their homes once they were ultimately cured.

10 year old Ruby Daly loves her parents. But the night of her birthday, she is given her favourite toy keychain but Ruby notices the despair in her parent's eyes and just to comfort them, she erases their memories of her. We are not told this until later on in the movie. But this is the main reason why she chooses not to touch other people. She is afraid of her powers. The only times she would touch people is when she would manipulate them into doing something good for her. Each child with an ability is categorized by colour. The Blues, Greens and Golds are fairly harmless but the Orange and Red must be terminated immediately as they pose as a danger. Ruby is an Orange but she is a different kind of Orange who has the ability to manipulate situations - she made the doctor change her colour from Orange to Green so she would not be terminated.

6 years later, Ruby is found out to be an Orange as she is the only one who is affected by the frequency. She then meets Dr. Kate Bigby who leaves a small note inside Ruby's chart stating that she must meet her tonight so they can escape the camp. We then see Kate drive Ruby to the front gate of the camp and Ruby uses her powers to manipulate the Captain into letting them leave. I thought this was brilliant.

We are then introduced to Zoo (a Gold with electrical powers), Liam (a Blue with telekinetic powers) and Chubbs (a Green who is a smart ass) after Ruby runs away from Kate and her partner after Ruby touches his hand and sees him capture a girl. Before this, Ruby was given a chain with a tracking device from Kate. Kate told her that if she is ever lost, she should press on the pendant and Kate will find her. But after the encounter with Kate's partner, Ruby runs away and meets Zoo and she allows Ruby to enter their van. Unsuspecting Liam and Chubbs don't know Ruby is in the van until they meet up with Lady Jane who is a tracker. Trackers are like bounty hunters employed by the government to bring in children to the camps. I liked the part where Ruby manipulated Lady Jane - that was brilliant.

Okay, I am not going to spoil anything else for you. What I didn't like and my reason for giving it four stars was that we never heard Liam's story. Ruby did not want to touch him just in case she erased his memories. I wanted to know more about Liam. He played a major role in the movie and I felt slightly robbed about not knowing about him.

This was an original Sci-Fi Thriller with tons of unexpected twists and if you are a fan of the genre then I highly recommend you watch this.

Enjoy!

text:
Star Wars rebels has done something that the Clone Wars couldn't do. It brought me back into Star Wars. The somewhat tepid Star Wars universe that has existed since Revenge of the Sith has eroded my enthusiasm and the increasingly labyrenthine comic and literary universe has left me feeling less enthused. I couldn't even get my kids interested in watching the films or Clone Wars, so I was out in the cold.

One day the trailers for Rebels began appearing on the Disney Channel, and my kids were interested. They were talking about it, and I had no idea what they were talking about. Until I happened to catch one of the promos and ask them. They were excited and wanted to watch. After we watched the first episode, they waned more. They wanted toys and books, they wanted to watch the movies with me. It was just like 1980 all over again when i stood in line to watch Empire Strikes Back.

But that's enough of my nostalgia. The episodes are fun. Sure they have their problems, but honestly, what in Star Wars doesn't? Watching the characters come together has been fun and interesting. Seeing all of the nods to Ralph McQuarrie's original vision of Star Wars, and the Kenner toys, and even the original Star Tours attraction at Disneyland are fun. The action is spot on for grabbing the attention of younger kids, it's well conceived and animated. The character models pull in elements of Disney Characters that the kids know as well as Star Wars characters that the parents know.

At its heart, it is exactly what it should be to carry on the tradition of the original Star Wars. Fans believe that they are so much more sophisticated and need more "adult" entertainment from the show, but that's not what they are nostalgic for. I cannot wait to see more, and I hope that it ties in with the upcoming Sequel trilogy. This show has restored me to the world of Star Wars, and I look forward to going on this journey with my kids.

title_x: Horror Masterwork, Boris Karloff in an Iconic Role
text: This is an inarguable horror classic, one that takes inspirations from other Universal monster tales, but crafts a vision that is unique and would inspire countless other movies in its own right. The narrative is effective, but the atmosphere is what drives The Mummy, a slow burn, but intense and gradual eerieness, all while Boris Karloff turns in one of his best performances. The opening sequence is iconic, with Karloff in the wrappings and the famous “He…he went for a little walk!” line that will echo through all of horror as long as the genre exists. The deliberate pace is never a concern in the least, thanks to the tense mood and at only 73 minutes, there’s no filler or downtime whatsoever. Even in a slow burn approach, The Mummy is efficient and makes every scene count. Of course, this would launch numerous sequels and remakes, but the original remains my personal favorite, thanks in large part to Karloff, the visuals, and the overall atmosphere. The Mummy is a classic for a reason and without question, is a cornerstone of the genre. Visit my site for a full review!

text: The genesis of one of horror’s most enduring franchises and one of the genre’s most iconic characters, Hellraiser is a horror classic that hasn’t lost even a little of its impact in the decades since it was released. Although Pinhead would be the front man for the entire series, this first installment uses both Pinhead and his fellow cenobites in measured doses. This ensures their presence always commands attention, but it is also because the main narrative is quite strong, so the movie doesn’t suffer when the cenobites aren’t around. I love how unique Hellraiser looks and feels, as it is so far removed from the usual slash & stalk elements of its 80s horror peers, it is such a welcome change of pace. The cenobites are beyond bad ass and creepy, much more intense and otherworldly than a masked maniac, again helping the movie stand out and burn some images into the viewers’ brains. The atmosphere is tense and unsettling, leaning on tension and mood to drive the horror elements, rather than cheap jump scares. The cast is also terrific, with Doug Bradley shining as Pinhead, while Ashley Laurence is fantastic and conveys fear so well. But man, Andrew Robinson steals the show at times and is simply masterful in the wild finale, with one of the movie’s most memorable moments. Hellraiser has endured as a horror classic for a reason, it is a must see even for the most casual of genre fans. Visit my site for a full review!

title_x: Pre-Code Sizzler with a Great Barbara Stanwyck Performance
text: If you’re curious about pre-code Hollywood, Baby Face is an ideal place to start and to me, is one of the best examples of what pre-code cinema is about and has to offer. The narrative is likely to divide audiences even decades later, as Lily is driven by selfish reasons and leaves a lot of wreckage behind her, but to me, she is more than justified in what she does. She endured the abuse of men, including her own father since she was a young girl, so to see her take back her power is liberating and the men she uses are all to willing to be used. This movie is about Lily’s use of sex and allure to get what she wants, but the men line up to tear down their marriages, businesses, and personal lives, so they’re not sympathetic characters, at least to me. The story is always interesting and the pace is brisk, so even if you’re not usually into older movies, this one will hold your interest. Barbara Stanwyck is fantastic in the lead and just goes for broke in the role, embracing the character and making the most of the material. She truly shines here and commands the screen, this is the kind of screen presence you rarely find, truly remarkable work. The rest of the cast is fine as well, but Stanwyck owns this one and outshines even the best of her costars. Baby Face is a bold, dynamic movie that lets Stanwyck showcase her talents and tells a memorable narrative, all with no punches pulled. Visit my site for a full review!

title_x: Started Out Good, Rapidly Descended into Cliches
text:
It was a glamorous job to be a stewardess with the most exclusive airline in the world during the 1960's. The trademark blue skirt and a big smile could take you to the skies, a means of seeing the world and being paid for it. But life wasn't all fun and games for the women who weighed in each morning and came home exhausted on weekends.

Dreams have become reality for Dean (Mike Vogal) on his first assignment after his promotion: piloting the Majestic on its inaugural New York to London flight. The world certainly looks different from inside a cockpit, and the mood of the flight crew is a positive one... even though not everything goes as planned. The woman he loves and hopes to marry, Bridget (Annabelle Wallis), is a no-show, leaving the formerly grounded Maggie (Christina Ricci) to fill in for her. Little does Dean know there's more to the beautiful blonde than he first surmised; she is an intelligence officer working undercover whose assignment has become too hot to handle. Her replacement is Kate (Kellie Garner), who is distressed to discover that her beautiful younger sister, Laura (Margot Robbie), is working the same flight. Known best as the face of Pam Am on a magazine cover, Laura is escaping demons of her own having literally run out on an engagement and left her controlling mother behind.

Meanwhile, Collette (Karine Vanasse) finds matters complicated when she discovers the man she has been dating is on board with his wife and child. In the weeks to come, we grow to know each character more intimately and appreciate their different backgrounds and personalities. The cast is lovely and while at times the series is melodramatic, there is no mistaking the charm of the setting. Let's face it, the 1960's were glamorous and Pan Am isn't afraid to remind us of this, whether panning a crowd or lingering on a bubbling glass of champagne in first class. Pencil skirts and bright smiles play out against dangerous operations for the government, while delving into the politics of the age... JFK running for president, the height of the Cold War, it's all here and then some.

Unfortunately, it didn't take this series long to descend into immorality and political correctness, ranging from the lax morals of everyone involved to a sanitized look at some of the serious events of the era. What struck me as I waded through the thirteen episodes was how far off the mark it got. I could not root for any of the guys to win the women they professed to love, because none of them would be faithful. The costumes are cute and it has a nostalgic air to it, but this is one flight you may want to delay indefinitely.

text:
Getting ready to watch the remake of "Poltergeist", I wanted to revisit the original films again. The first "Poltergeist" was, and is, a fun and fantastically scary film. The second film tries to rehash what we loved about the first film and fails, but it still had some nice moments. The third film simply misses the mark completely.

I guess the Freelings had enough of their ghost-attracting daughter and ship her off to some relatives living in a high rise in Chicago. It's not long before the ghost are back, and Kane from the second film makes some appearances as he's leading his followers to haunt Carol Anne for vague reasons. This time they get to live in the mirror lined hallways of the skyscraper instead of the closets of a single family home. Before you can say "....hey I know that woman from Robocop"...Carol Anne and her cousin are pulled into the mirror world with the ghosts.

This movie actually has a decent cast, and the premise isn't bad at all, but the execution is just awful. The one thing I liked about the previous two films, and actually a keystone of their plots, was that the Freelings felt like a real family, and the previous two entries was all about how their love for each other protected them from the harmful spirits, and right off the bat we are supposed to believe that Diane and Steven wanted to rid themselves of their youngest daughter? Beyond that, nothing really works in this film. No scares, Kane get rehashed, but it's a stand in, and what made Kane work in the second film was Julian Beck's charisma and presence, something you don't get here.

title_x: "It's Just Like a Bad Horror Movie.....Isn't It?"
text:
There are some really great ideas in "Hellworld", easily the most imaginative "Hellraiser" sequel since "Bloodline". With Lance Henriksen thrown into the mix, and an early performance by "Man of Steel" star Henry Cavill, this is one of the better "Hellraiser" sequels.

As the movie opens we see a young man digging a grave, and then killing himself. We flash to his funeral where several of his friends blame themselves for not stopping the boy from taking his own life. It seems that Adam was obsessed with an online computer game called "Hellworld", a game that allows players to wander through Hell's labyrinth searching for the LaMerchand puzzle box and avoiding the cenobites. All of the friends have been playing the game as well, but Adam's obsession pushed him over the edge. Flash ahead two years and while most of Adam's friends have continued playing "Hellworld", Adam's former girlfriend, Chelsea is still struggling with the guilt of not helping stop Adam's suicide. When three of Adam's other friends find and unlock the puzzle box online, they receive invitations to a secret "Hellworld" party, and Chelsea decides to attend as well. Once there, they meet the mysterious Host who is steeped in Hellraiser lure, and seemingly decorated an entire mansion to reflect the "Hellworld" game. Once inside though, the friends begin to wonder if there if "Hellworld" is more than simply a game.

I really liked the idea of updating the series, and taking it out of the "Hellraiser" world. In this movie, "Hellraiser", "Pinhead", "Cenobites" and "Engineers" are simply characters out of the movies and game. It was a fun way to bring the story into current times. With that said, I think the film tries to be more clever than it's script, and while the idea is fantastic, the execution is poor. There are brief glimpses of some pretty effective ideas, but more often than not, they are buried under too much extraneous scenes or dialogue. The ideas here are fun, the movie is just good enough that you wish there were more talented people behind the camera to make it better.

With that said, I like the direction this film takes, and it's always fun to watch Lance Henriksen chew up some scenery.

The world's favorite angler is at it again. Tracking down rumors of a "monster" that has been attacking swimmers in the northern part of the United States. This is Jeremy Wade at his best.

Many people want to be Jeremy Wade. He lives a life of adventure, tracking down and fishing for some of the world's most elusive, most dangerous, and most challenging river monsters. Jeremy is down to earth. You won't see this guy driving around in a Range Rover, wearing a Rolex Submariner, and being followed by serving men and women. No, Jeremy doesn't try to pass himself off as some wealthy, gentleman adventurer with nothing better to do. In his interviews, he candidly tells his fans that he made a great deal of personal and financial sacrifices to get to this point. He is knowledgeable and one of the world's top ranked anglers.

In this episode, swimmers have complained of getting bit by an unknown creature while swimming on the lake surface. Jeremy's investigation takes him to a river where people actually trap and collect the creature. And some consider the creature a delicacy. I do not want to spoil the episode for you, since part of the fun is guessing what Jeremy will pull up on his hook. Suffice it to say, this is one of the better episodes of the season.

Highly recommended.

I love the show. It is very educational. The format is basically a real-life case study of people who have become infected. The outcomes are usually good. The culprit is discovered, the victim is cured, and so on. However, there are some cases that end sadly. The victim did not make it. And that adds drama, and brings on some needed harsh reality, to the serious topic of the show. If "Game of Thrones" shy away from "comfort fiction", then this show certainly is a departure from the normal reality TV shows out there.

This is a show that should be made available to health educators out there. Perhaps even to high school science classes. Dan Riskin presents his commentaries in a very informative manner. There's a lot to be learned from these episodes. What you can't see, can hurt you.

However, the negative side to it is that the show can make you paranoid. So, it is not for everybody. If you have someone in your family who is already paranoid and scared of life in general, then this should not be recommended to that person.

I have a dog. I also have numerous fish tanks. Watching the beautiful, young Hanale Cox contract an infection from her fish tank did make me paranoid. After a while, that paranoia turned into caution. Ever since, I take great care when cleaning my tanks. I always apply a bandage to broken skin, and I make sure that I do not have any uncovered cuts before sticking my hands inside the fish tank. Being a horseman, I also got overly worried when mucking out the manure. All kinds of thoughts were going through my head, imagining the potentially infective larva, eggs, and cysts contained in one shovel of the nasty stuff. But common sense prevailed with some rational thinking. People have been keeping horses for thousands of years. And with that husbandry, people have been cleaning out stalls for the same amount of time. And while we will never know how many people throughout the millenia have contracted diseases from horse manure, common sense tells us that it must be comparatively low.

So, watch the show. Learn from each episode. But please, do not kick your dog out of the house. Just make sure that you take care of the dog carefully and be consistent with his/her de-worming schedule. Talk to your vet. Keep your dog on a broad-spectrum de-wormer. There's no reason to get rid of your fish tanks. Just be careful when doing maintenance. Think carefully before you jump into the local pond, or lake. Stay healthy and keep your immune system in shape. And eating raw crayfish is never a good idea. Arm yourself with knowledge. Exercise caution. But please do not let the knowledge make you paranoid. Caution, yes. That is good. But not fear.

text:
Silent Hill is a movie inspired by the video game of the same name. The game came out on the original Sony Playstation console. It was one of the first of the so-called "survival-horror" genre of games, which included Resident Evil and Parasite Eve. The genres popularity, as well as the dominance of the Sony Playstation console, ensured that the movie already had a large fan base even before it opened.

Chris and Rose DaSilva are concerned with their adopted daughter's sleepwalking habits. During these episodes, Sharon keeps referring to "Slient Hill", a town in nearby West Virginia. Rose then takes it upon herself to drive to Silent Hill, with Sharon in tow. Miles outside of Silent Hill, she stops at a gas station. While there, the attendant warns her not to proceed to the town. Evidently, the town was evacuated many years before. This is coal mine country. Fire got started in the coal mines, deep beneath the town. The fires continue to burn to this day, making Silent Hill a danger zone.

Rose drives through the barricades and proceeds to the ghost town. Meanwhile, a mysterious motorcycle police officer is in pursuit. Rose swerves to avoid hitting a child, and runs off the road. When she wakes up, Sharon is missing. Rose starts to walk down the empty streets. She meets up Dahlia, who informs her that she believe Sharon is actually Alessa. With fog blanketing the town and ashes falling from the sky, Rose runs back to the car. There, she meets up with Officer Cybil Bennett. Together, they continue the search for Sharon.

They learned that the town is not empty. Silent Hill is populated by the members of a cult. As darkness descends, they follow the members to the safety of a church. While there, they are captured by the cult, led by the insane Christabella. Slowly, the story of Silent Hill and Alessa begin to unfold. Dahlia had a daughter out of wedlock. Condemned by the town as an abomination, Alessa grew up without friends. Other children tormented her, while the adults did not do anything to stop the bullying. Christabella convinces Dahlia that the cult can help. She proposes a ritual that would "cleanse" Alessa. Dahlia agrees. The cult takes Alessa into their church and straps her to an iron wheel. Dahlia realizes too late that the cult intends to burn Alessa to death. The cult proceeds with the ritual and sets Alessa aflame. During the ritual, an explosion rocks the town. The fire gets out of control. Dahlia and the police arrive to stop the ritual. Alessa, horribly burned but still alive, is taken to the hospital by Officer Gucci. Alessa's anger and rage pulls the entire town into an alternate reality, created by her mind. Her powers, fueled by anger and hate traps the town and the cult members into her dreamworld, filled with horrors. Meanwhile, Alessa takes that part of her soul which is still good and manifests it into another child, Sharon. Sharon is the "good" half of Alessa.

Meanwhile, Chris arrives at the outskirts of town to look for his wife and daughter. Stopped by the same Officer Gucci, Chris learns the tragic story of the town. Unable to proceed into town, he then returns home.

This is a very good horror movie. Sean Bean, Radha Mitchell, Laurie Holden, Alice Kriege, Kim Coates, and Deborah Kara Unger make up the all-star cast. Laurie Holden probably gave the best performance out of the group, playing the role of a dedicated police officer. She plays the tough but very beautiful policewoman, Cybil Bennett. Laurie Holden, with her short blonde hair and slender figure, looked sexy in her motorcycle policewoman's outfit. Kim Coates was also very good as the compassionate Officer Gucci.

text:
I'm sure everybody starts off their review this way, but there's no crying in baseball! Well, it's a shame I broke that rule several times while I watched this movie. It's just really good at being inspiring and tugging at the heart strings at the same time.

In World War II, when a majority of the athletes joined the service and went off to war, the baseball associations brought in women to fill their positions. And at first everyone was skeptical, games weren't selling well and it looked as if the whole notion would be dead on its feet. But then people started paying attention to just how good these girl's were. And history changed. This movie spends time on two sisters who join the league and their ups and downs with the game and each other.

Characters:
Tom Hanks: Jimmy Dugan
Geena Davis: Dottie Hinson
Lori Petty: Kit Keller
Anne Ramsey: Helen Haley
Megan Cavanagh: Marla Hooch
Rosie O'Donnell: Doris Murphy
Tracy Reiner: Betty Horn
Madonna: Mae Mordabito
Bitty Schram: Evelyn Gardner

The cast in this movie is fabulous. All of them play their parts so well and you can believe all of them truly love baseball (and if they didn't before the movie they probably do now). They had a lot of fun out there. Hanks was a convincing alcoholic used to be pro ballplayer turned coach. He has a lot of funny lines, although I'm not sure I enjoyed watching him pee for five minutes. Davis as Dottie was perfect. She had attitude and wasn't actually perfect. She fought with her sister but still loved her, it was very much a real looking sibling relationship. The same with Kit, she was the spoiled little sister who never quite feels good enough when compared to her older sibling. Since that's a feeling a lot of younger siblings have it was very believable. The only characters I couldn't quite get on board with were Rosie O'Donnels and Madonna's. They did an ok job. But I feel like they were there because they were famous and not because they were the best choices for the movie.

Normally I'm not big into movies on sports. Unless they're inspiring and about the underdog. Which considering the time period and who was actually playing ball in this movie, they were the underdogs. And I liked that they told some personal stories with the movie too, the sisters and the women with their husbands off at war. It was very emotional and you may tear up several times during the movie. There actually wasn't a ton about the sport itself, it was more about the people who played it. But that just means it would be good for a wider audience.

The sets on this film were very authentic. Down to the cars and the clothes they fit into the movie just like you were transported back to the World War II era. Even the music fit the period. I'm glad they took the time to focus on the details and made sure that the movie was just right.

A wonderful movie about a group of athletes that you don't think about too much. But just like they won a spot in the Baseball Hall of Fame, this movie should also win a spot on your to-watch list.

Review by M. Reynard 2013

text:
My nearly-two year old loves the Thomas episodes. We watch them independently on PBS, but also stream them via Netflix and Amazon Instant. This is a great collection of newer episodes, and introduces two new characters (Stafford and Winston).

This collection includes:
Gordon Runs Dry - Diesel and Gordon avoid a serious accident, but Gordon is struck by some slate that flies out of the car Diesel is pulling behind him. Gordon thinks he's invincible, and ignores the fact that his boiler keeps running dry. He learns that big, strong engines can need help.

Kevin's Cranky Friend - Cranky is having an unusually busy day at the docks, and Sir Topham Hatt sends an enthusiastic Kevin to the docks to help. Cranky is rude, condescending and downright hateful to Kevin when all Kevin does is try to help. Cranky later relents, but never actually apologizes for his behavior. I think that's a huge misstep by the writers of this episode, so I'm docking a star for that. Bad behavior, especially unwarranted bad behavior, should never be condoned, not when the audience is primarily impressionable, young children who idolize these characters. It is a great teaching point for parents to point out that Cranky doesn't apologize, and walk their children through what he should have said to Kevin.

Scruff's Makeover - Scruff is rusting so Sir Topham Hatt orders him repainted. Scruff is, at first, reluctant to be cleaned and repainted but when the other engines compliment him, he decides he can't work at the waste dump with Whiff anymore because he doesn't want to get dirty again. He spends the remainder of the episode trying to find where he fits in on the island. A good lesson to kids about how "the clothes don't make the man" or "it's what's inside that really matters."

Wayward Winston - Sir Topham Hatt and his new car, Winston, are having trouble working together to drive smoothly along the tracks. Winston gets teased by the other engines for his bumpy driving, and Winston decides he wants to see what it's like to be without a driver. When Sir Topham Hatt gets out and forget to put on the brake, Winston takes off on his own around the island. After nearly causing a couple of serious accidents, he realizes the drivers and cars/engines need each other.

Steamie Stafford - Stafford notices the children seem to enjoy the puffs, chugs, whistles and wheeshes the engines make all over the island. He decides he wants to be like the other engines, and he has them teach him their signature sounds. Later, he is sent on a special to Farmer McColl's, making quite a racket along the way. When he frightens the sheep, he learns that he is valuable and appreciated just the way he is.

Mr. Perkins' Clips- In the scenes with Mr. Perkins in the Engine Driver's Common Room, Mr. Perkins is preparing to stand in for Mr. Arkwright as referee for the annual Engine Driver's soccer match. He spends the time between episodes gathering his gear and searching for a whistle, finally asking Thomas if he'll use his train whistle because Mr. Perkins can't find a traditional referee whistle.

text:
Last year, when the second Hobbit came to theaters, I couldn't wait to see it. We saw it right after Christmas when our Dad came to see us, and ate at Olive Garden afterward. It was worth it. The second Hobbit is the best movie of 2013 (maybe one of the best of all time), with the exception of a possible tie with Thor 2: The Dark World.
I've never been a huge Lord of the Rings fan (although I do enjoy them a little), but I really like how the Hobbit movies have a tie in with the Lord of the Rings films, and The Hobbit films have become my favorite series of all time. The actors that Peter Jackson casted really make even the smallest characters seem important (except for Bifur), and it even included new characters, not in the book, and still helped move the story along with them too.
Gandalf's story may not have been so in depth in the book, but in the appendixes of the third Lord of the Rings book, it does mention that Gandalf fought at Dol Guldur. I may have had an idea of how it was going to end before it came out, because I estimated how many chapters in the book each movie would cover, but that didn't make it any less awesome.
The only thing in it that could have been better would be if they had included the theme music from the first film in it, but the rest of the music is great, and I can still hope it'll be in the third.
Overall, it is five stars, and I hope that the third will be the same.

text:
I first saw the preview for The Hobbit when I saw Journey 2 in theaters, and I didn't know what to think. I had seen Lord of the Rings, but I didn't find them that exciting, because they had too much war, and not enough peril. I loved the 2003 Hobbit video game, and that was my vision of the Hobbit.
My sisters saw the preview for the Hobbit when they went to see Brave, and they had a totally different reaction. They knew right away that they had to see it.
So, on New Years Eve, my sisters saw the Hobbit in theaters, and they loved it. My younger sister instantly decided it was her favorite movie, and highly encouraged the rest of the family to see it.
Well, we did see it on Valentines Day two and a half months later, and it was not what I had expected at all. Like I said earlier The Hobbit video game was my The Hobbit. Furthermore, it hardly could even be compared to Lord of the Rings. It caught me completely off guard.
But after the movie, I knew something else. The next time I watched it, I was prepared, and it was decided. It was probably my favorite movie of all time.
First of all, Martin Freeman did a perfect job for Bilbo, and Gollum was absolutely hilarious. When reading the book, you hardly know of any of the dwarves, but in the movie, each actor puts so much into their character, that I memorized all of the Dwarfs names.
But best of all, the movie was awesome; My favorite part was the escape from the goblin mine.
The movie was emotional, and exciting, and I give it five stars. A lot of fans wonder why Peter Jackson had to make one book into three movies, but you cannot capture the depth that is captured here in anything less.

Man, I was super excited for this when it was first announced. I love slashers, I love Christmas, and I love Christmas slashers. Blumhouse did so well with 'Halloween' I could only imagine how epic Black Christmas would've been. Boy, did they mess this up! I heard it was going to be bad, because it was slapped with a PG13 rating and I knew it had a feminist agenda, but this movie was stereotypically feminist to the point where they are practically shoving it down your throat. They took away Billy, the original killer and replaced him with a cult of college boys who are misogynistic and under a spell due to some black sludge coming out of a statue of the founder of their college. I'm dead serious!

Our hero is Riley, a sorority woman who was sexually attacked by the AKO fraternity president Brian Huntley. She and her sorority sisters enter a singing contest that mocks the fraternity. Soon after, they all start getting harassed and threatening texts. Some of the girls start to go missing, and that's when the cult of he-man woman haters start attacking. It's up to Riley and her gang of strong independent women to fight back. This movie was not made with a good story or to be scary, it's just made to appease the Feminazi's, and that's just sad. I'm sure I'll watch this again someday, but just do yourself a favor and watch the original classic instead. This re-remake makes the 2006 version look like 'The Godfather Part II' I would not recommend BLACK CHRISTMAS!!!
